lessons.summary: Generics are easy to write and hard to write well. The difference is inference: a good generic signature lets callers write plain values and get precise types back, while a bad one forces explicit type arguments or, worse, quietly hands back whatever the caller asked for. This sector is about designing the good kind.

# V3·TB1 — Generic APIs that stay inferable

You already know how to write `function first<T>(items: T[]): T`. That was the
mechanics. This sector is about the design question that comes next, and it is
the one that separates a library people enjoy from a library people fight:
**where does each type parameter come from, and does the caller have to say it
out loud?**

An API is *inferable* when the caller writes ordinary values and TypeScript
works out every type parameter on its own, precisely. It is not inferable when
callers end up writing `getThing<User>(...)` at every call site, or — the worse
failure — when they do not have to write anything because the type parameter is
never checked against reality at all.

```ts
// Inferable. The caller writes values; T and K fall out.
const names = pluck(users, "name");      // string[]

// Not inferable, and unsound. T is whatever you claim it is.
const user = parseJson<User>(text);      // a cast wearing a costume
```

Both compile. Only one of them is doing work.

## Concept — inference sites, and the golden rule

TypeScript infers a type parameter by matching the *arguments* you passed
against the *parameter types* that mention it. Each place a type parameter
appears in the parameter list is an **inference site**. Return types are not
inference sites — nothing flows backwards from the return position into `T`,
except in the narrow case of contextual typing from an assignment target.

That gives you the single most useful rule in generic design, sometimes called
the golden rule of generics:

> A type parameter that appears in only one place is doing nothing useful. A
> type parameter that appears only in the return position is an `any` in
> disguise.

Check the rule against real signatures:

```ts
declare function firstOr<T>(items: readonly T[], fallback: T): T;   // 2 sites, related
declare function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(xs: readonly T[], k: K): T[K][];
declare function parseJson<T>(text: string): T;                     // 0 sites - a lie
declare function log<T>(value: T): void;                            // 1 site - just use unknown
```

`firstOr` earns its `T`: the parameter and the fallback are *tied together*, so
`firstOr(users, null)` is a compile error rather than a surprise at runtime.
`pluck` earns both: `K extends keyof T` is a relationship, so the key is
checked and the element type follows from it. `parseJson<T>` has no site at
all — the caller's claim is accepted whole, which is exactly `as T` with extra
syntax. `log<T>` has one site and no relationship; `log(value: unknown)` says
the same thing more honestly and produces better error messages.

## Concept — inference through callbacks

The most valuable inference in day-to-day TypeScript flows through function
arguments. When you write

```ts
const byRole = groupBy(users, (user) => user.role);
```

TypeScript infers `T` from `users` first, then uses that `T` to **contextually
type** the parameter of the arrow function, so `user` needs no annotation, and
finally infers `K` from what the arrow returns. Argument order matters here:
inference proceeds left to right in passes, so the array must come before the
callback for the callback's parameter to be typed for free. Flip the arguments
and `user` becomes an implicit `any` — the same function, a worse API.

## Concept — the three modifiers that fix the awkward cases

Ordinary inference has three well-known failure modes, and modern TypeScript
has a tool for each.

**Widening.** `defineRoutes(["/health", "/users"])` infers `string[]`, and the
literal information you cared about is gone. `const` type parameters
(TypeScript 5.0) fix this at the declaration site rather than making every
caller write `as const`:

```ts
declare function defineRoutes<const T extends readonly string[]>(paths: T): T;
defineRoutes(["/health", "/users"]);   // readonly ["/health", "/users"]
```

**Poisoning.** When a type parameter has several inference sites, every one of
them votes, and a sloppy argument can widen the result:

```ts
declare function chooser<T>(options: readonly T[], fallback: T): T;
chooser(["red", "green"], "purple");   // T = "red" | "green" | "purple". No error.
```

`NoInfer<T>` (TypeScript 5.4) removes a site from the vote while still
checking it: mark `fallback` as `NoInfer<T>` and the call above becomes the
error it always should have been.

**Loss of shape.** `Parameters<F>` and `ReturnType<F>` look like the way to
write a wrapper, and they flatten generics and overloads on the way through.
Capturing the argument list as its own type parameter — `<A extends readonly
unknown[], R>(fn: (...args: A) => R)` — preserves parameter *names* and arity
in tooltips, which is what people actually notice.

## The trap

The trap in this sector is that unsound generics are invisible. Nothing goes
red. `parseJson<Config>(raw)` type-checks perfectly and then your program reads
`config.port.toFixed(2)` on a string that came out of a YAML file. Every
generic you write is a promise about where the type came from; if the answer is
"the caller told me", you have written a cast and given it a nicer name.

There is a second, quieter version of the same trap. `function log<T>(value:
T)` is not unsound, but it is pointless: with one occurrence, `T` behaves
exactly like `unknown` while producing worse error messages and a worse
tooltip. When someone on your team adds a type parameter "so it works with
anything", that is usually what has happened. The cure is a question, not a
rule: *what relationship does this parameter express?* If you can finish the
sentence — the fallback matches the elements, the key exists on the row, the
decoder produces the result — keep it. If you cannot, the signature is asking
the caller to supply information the function will never check, and every
call site inherits the risk.

The eight exercises walk from the two-site generic that ties arguments
together, through keyof relationships and callback inference, into `const` and
`NoInfer`, and finish with an overloaded `pipe` — the classic proof that
sometimes a stack of overloads is the only way to thread types through a
variadic API.

# Reading - typescript/v3tb01_inferable_generics

Notes on how inference actually runs, why the golden rule holds, and the
places where the compiler will not help you.

## Notes

**Inference is a matching problem, run in passes.** TypeScript pairs each
argument's type with the corresponding parameter's declared type and collects
*candidates* for every type parameter it meets. Then it picks a winner: the
common supertype of the candidates if one exists, otherwise the union. Two
details matter in practice. First, candidates from different arguments are
pooled, which is why `chooser(["red"], "purple")` widens instead of failing —
`"purple"` is a legitimate candidate. Second, arguments that are function
expressions are processed in a later pass, so their parameters can be
contextually typed by what earlier arguments already fixed. That ordering is
why `(items, callback)` works and `(callback, items)` does not.

**Return positions do not infer.** There is exactly one route by which
information flows from the outside in: contextual typing from an assignment
target or from an enclosing call. `const xs: string[] = empty()` can fix a type
parameter of `empty`. That is a fragile channel — it disappears the moment the
call is passed to something else — so no serious API should depend on it.

**Constraints are not inference sites; they are filters.** `T extends
{ id: string }` narrows what a candidate is *allowed* to be and gives you
`.id` inside the body. It does not create a candidate. A signature whose only
mention of `T` is in `extends` clauses infers nothing.

**Defaults are the quiet killer.** `function make<T = string>(): T` never
fails, never infers, and silently produces `string` when the caller forgets.
Type parameter defaults are for *type-level* APIs — a generic interface with a
sensible common instantiation — and rarely belong on a function.

**`const` type parameters are not `as const`.** The modifier asks inference to
prefer the literal, immutable interpretation of the argument. It only affects
inference at that site; the caller can still pass a widened variable, and
nothing is frozen at runtime. It also has no effect on a parameter whose
declared type already forces widening, which is the usual reason it "doesn't
work": `<const T extends string[]>` (mutable array) undoes half of it. Write
`readonly` in the constraint.

**`NoInfer<T>` is a filter, not a cast.** It is implemented as an intrinsic in
`lib.es5.d.ts` since 5.4; before that, people faked it with
`T & {}` or with a two-parameter trick. It removes the annotated position from
the candidate pool while still requiring assignability, so you get "Argument of
type '"purple"' is not assignable to parameter of type '"red" | "green"'" —
the error a reviewer would have written by hand.

**Variance annotations are for speed and clarity, not correctness.** `interface
Box<out T>` documents that `Box<Cat>` is assignable to `Box<Animal>` and lets
the checker skip structural work. Getting one wrong is a compile error, so they
are safe to add; adding them to types that do not need them is noise.

**Overloads beat conditional return types for readability.** A conditional
return type is more precise and much worse in a tooltip: the caller sees the
unevaluated conditional. Overloads show a concrete signature per case, which is
why the standard library, `pipe` implementations and `document.createElement`
are all written that way. The cost is that the implementation signature is
unchecked against the overloads beyond crude compatibility, so the body needs
care.

## ex1 — two sites, one relationship

`firstOr(items, fallback)` is the smallest interesting generic: two inference
sites for one `T`. The point is not the implementation, it is that
`firstOr(users, null)` now fails. Notice the deliberate absence of `??` in the
reference answer. `items[0] ?? fallback` is shorter and wrong for
`firstOr([0, 1], 99)` and `firstOr([null], "x")`, because `??` asks about the
value and you meant to ask about the length.

## ex2 — keyof as a relationship

`K extends keyof T` is the pattern that makes property access safe without
casts. Two things are worth noticing. The return type `T[K][]` is an *indexed
access*, so `pluck(users, "name")` really is `string[]` and not
`(string | number)[]`. And `K` is inferred as a literal, not widened to
`keyof T`, because a string literal argument in a position constrained by
`keyof T` keeps its literal type — the constraint acts as a hint that literal
inference is wanted.

## ex3 — inference flowing into a callback

Two type parameters, inferred in different passes. `T` comes from the array;
`K` comes from what your callback returns. Constraining `K extends
PropertyKey` (that is, `string | number | symbol`) is what allows
`Record<K, T[]>` in the return type. The implementation detail worth arguing
about is the one cast: you build a `Partial<Record<K, T[]>>` because that is
the truth while the object is half-built, and you assert the full `Record` on
the way out. One narrow, deliberate cast at a boundary you control is fine; a
cast at every read is not.

## ex4 — `const` type parameters

Without the modifier, the array argument widens and the whole exercise
collapses to `string[]`. With it, `T` is `readonly ["/health", "/users"]`, and
`T[number]` gives you the union of routes for free — which is what makes
`Record<T[number], number>` and the `path is T[number]` predicate meaningful.
This is the mechanism behind route tables, permission lists and design-token
maps in real codebases.

## ex5 — `NoInfer`, and why the error is the deliverable

The runtime behaviour of `chooser` is three lines. The exercise is the
signature. Mark `fallback` as `NoInfer<T>` and a typo in a fallback becomes a
compile error at the call site instead of a value that silently joins the
union. Say that in an interview and you have said something most candidates
cannot.

## ex6 — the return-position lie

`parseJson<T>(text): T` is the most common unsound generic in the ecosystem,
and it is worth being able to explain why in one sentence: **the caller supplies
the type and nothing supplies the evidence.** The fix is to add an inference
site that carries proof — a decoder function `(value: unknown) => T`. Now `T`
is inferred *from the decoder*, the decoder is the thing that has to be right,
and the call site loses its type argument entirely. That is the shape the next
sector builds on.

## ex7 — preserving a signature through a wrapper

`<A extends readonly unknown[], R>` captures the whole parameter list as a
tuple, so `withRetry(fetchUser)` returns something that still takes
`(id: string)` and still says `id` in the tooltip. Compare with `(fn: (...args:
any[]) => any)`, which type-checks any call at all, and with
`Parameters<F>`/`ReturnType<F>`, which work but resolve overloads to the last
signature and drop generics. Also worth knowing: `A extends readonly unknown[]`
rather than `any[]` keeps the wrapper honest under `strict`.

## ex8 — why `pipe` needs overloads

You cannot express "each function's input is the previous function's output"
with a single variadic signature; there is no way to thread a type through a
tuple of unknown length without recursive conditional types that degrade
tooltips and hit the recursion limit. So every real `pipe` — RxJS, fp-ts,
Effect, lodash/fp — is a stack of hand-written overloads, usually up to nine or
ten arguments, with a loosely typed implementation signature underneath. Having
written one, you know why every library has that odd wall of nearly identical
declarations.

## challenge and review1

The challenge stacks three mechanisms in one small API: `Row` inferred once
from the data, a `const` type parameter so `select(["id", "name"])` yields
`Pick<Row, "id" | "name">` rather than `Pick<Row, keyof Row>`, and a `V`
threaded from a projection into a comparator. The review comes at the same
ideas from the literal-preservation side: a registry built from a `const`
array, with a derived order map and a sort that only accepts names in the
registry.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Generics](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/generics.html) — the mechanics, including constraints and defaults.
- [TypeScript 5.0 release notes: `const` type parameters](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-5-0.html#const-type-parameters) — the motivation and the `readonly` caveat.
- [TypeScript 5.4 release notes: `NoInfer`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-5-4.html#the-noinfer-utility-type) — with the colour-picker example this sector borrows.
- [TypeScript wiki: FAQ on type inference](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/FAQ) — the pooled-candidate rule stated by the people who wrote it.
- [Effective TypeScript, Item 33: avoid unnecessary type parameters](https://effectivetypescript.com/) — the golden rule, argued at length.

# V3·TB1 — Generic APIs that stay inferable (archive)

The deep version of this sector: the model of inference, worked examples of
every failure mode, the interview answers, and a self-test bank.

## 1. The model

Think of a call as a small constraint-solving problem. TypeScript walks the
argument list, pairs each argument type with the declared parameter type, and
whenever it meets a naked type parameter it records a **candidate**. When the
walk is over it picks a result per type parameter: if one candidate is a
supertype of all the others it wins, otherwise the candidates are unioned, and
if there were no candidates at all the parameter falls back to its default, its
constraint, or `unknown`.

Three refinements make the model useful:

1. **Priority.** Not all candidates are equal. Candidates inferred from a
   return type of a contextually typed callback have lower priority than
   candidates from ordinary arguments, which is why the array wins over the
   callback in `groupBy`.
2. **Passes.** Function-expression arguments are inferred in a second pass, so
   they can be contextually typed by results from the first. This is the entire
   reason "data first, callback second" is the convention.
3. **Literal freshness.** A string literal argument keeps its literal type when
   the parameter position wants a literal (a constrained type parameter, a
   `const` type parameter, a literal-typed parameter) and widens otherwise.

## 2. The golden rule, with counterexamples

> If a type parameter appears in only one place in a signature, question it. If
> it appears only in the return type, it is unsound.

```ts
// Bad: one site, no relationship. `unknown` says the same thing.
function logIt<T>(value: T): void { console.log(value); }

// Bad: zero sites. The caller invents the type.
function fetchAs<T>(url: string): Promise<T> { /* ... */ }

// Good: two sites, tied together.
function firstOr<T>(items: readonly T[], fallback: T): T { /* ... */ }

// Good: a relationship between two parameters.
function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(xs: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][] { /* ... */ }

// Good: T inferred from evidence, not from a claim.
function fetchAs<T>(url: string, decode: (v: unknown) => T): Promise<T> { /* ... */ }
```

The `fetchAs` pair is the one to memorise. Both signatures are used constantly
in real code; only the second one can fail when the server changes.

## 3. Failure mode: widening

```ts
declare function defineRoutes<T extends readonly string[]>(paths: T): T;
const r1 = defineRoutes(["/a", "/b"]);           // string[]  - information lost
const r2 = defineRoutes(["/a", "/b"] as const);  // readonly ["/a", "/b"] - caller did work

declare function defineRoutes2<const T extends readonly string[]>(paths: T): T;
const r3 = defineRoutes2(["/a", "/b"]);          // readonly ["/a", "/b"] - free
```

The caveat people trip on: `<const T extends string[]>` — a *mutable* array
constraint — forces the result back to a mutable array type, which cannot be a
readonly tuple, and you get much of the widening back. Always write `readonly`
in the constraint of a `const` type parameter.

## 4. Failure mode: poisoned inference

```ts
declare function chooser<T>(options: readonly T[], fallback: T): T;
chooser(["red", "green"], "purple");    // T = "red" | "green" | "purple" - compiles

declare function chooser2<T>(options: readonly T[], fallback: NoInfer<T>): T;
chooser2(["red", "green"], "purple");   // error: "purple" is not "red" | "green"
```

The same mechanism explains a class of confusing errors in React and in state
libraries: an initial value widens a state type, and every later assignment is
allowed. `NoInfer` is the scalpel.

## 5. Failure mode: lost signatures

```ts
// Loses everything.
function wrapAny(fn: (...args: any[]) => any) { /* ... */ }

// Works, but flattens overloads and drops generics.
function wrapUtil<F extends (...args: any[]) => any>(fn: F):
  (...args: Parameters<F>) => ReturnType<F> { /* ... */ }

// Preserves arity, names and the return type.
function wrap<A extends readonly unknown[], R>(fn: (...args: A) => R):
  (...args: A) => R { /* ... */ }
```

None of the three can preserve a *generic* function through the wrapper —
`wrap(identity)` gives you a concrete instantiation, not a generic. Higher-rank
polymorphism is the long-standing missing feature here; the practical workaround
is to wrap at the call site or to hand-write an overload.

## 6. Failure mode: the escaping generic

```ts
declare function withResource<T>(open: () => T, use: (r: T) => void): void;
withResource(() => openFile(), (file) => file.read());   // fine

const use = (file: unknown) => {};       // once it escapes into a variable,
withResource(() => openFile(), use);     // T is pinned by the wrong site
```

Contextual typing only reaches into function *expressions* written at the call
site. Extract the callback into a `const` and the free typing disappears. This
is the most common reason people say "inference broke when I refactored".

## 7. Overloads versus conditional return types

```ts
// Conditional: precise, unreadable in a tooltip.
declare function parse<T extends "json" | "text">(
  body: string, as: T
): T extends "json" ? unknown : string;

// Overloads: one concrete signature per case.
declare function parse2(body: string, as: "json"): unknown;
declare function parse2(body: string, as: "text"): string;
```

Rule of thumb: overloads when the cases are few and named; a conditional type
when the cases are generated by the input (mapped keys, tuple lengths) or when
the function is itself generic in a way overloads cannot spell.

## 8. Interview answers

**"When would you not use a generic?"** When the type parameter has one
occurrence. A single-site `T` is `unknown` with worse error messages; a
return-only `T` is `any` with better manners.

**"How does TypeScript infer type arguments?"** It collects candidates by
matching arguments against parameter positions, in priority order and in
passes, then picks the best common supertype or the union. Return types are not
inference sites; contextual typing from the assignment target is the only
backwards channel.

**"What does `const` on a type parameter do?"** It asks inference at that site
to prefer the literal, `readonly` interpretation of the argument — the effect of
the caller writing `as const`, moved into the declaration. It changes inference
only; nothing is frozen at runtime.

**"What problem does `NoInfer` solve?"** It excludes a parameter position from
the candidate pool while still checking assignability, so a secondary argument
can be validated against a type fixed by a primary argument instead of widening
it.

**"Why is `pipe` written as ten overloads?"** Because threading a type through a
variadic argument list requires the output of argument *n* to be the input of
argument *n+1*, which a single signature cannot express without recursive
conditional types that produce unreadable errors and hit recursion limits.

## 9. Common mistakes

- Adding `<T>` to a function that never relates `T` to anything.
- Writing `as const` at every call site instead of `const T` once.
- Putting the callback first, then annotating its parameter by hand forever.
- `Parameters<typeof fn>` on an overloaded function and wondering why only one
  signature survives.
- Reaching for a type argument (`f<Foo>(x)`) as a *fix* when the real problem is
  that the signature has no site to infer from.
- Type parameter defaults on functions, which convert an inference failure into
  a silent wrong answer.
- Constraining with `any[]` where `readonly unknown[]` would do, then losing
  every `strict` guarantee inside the body.

## 10. Check yourself

1. Name the inference sites in `function zip<A, B>(as: readonly A[], bs: readonly B[]): [A, B][]`.
2. Why does `logIt<T>(value: T): void` not deserve its type parameter?
3. What does TypeScript infer for `T` in `chooser(["a", "b"], 42)` and why is that not an error?
4. Rewrite `fetchAs<T>(url: string): Promise<T>` so that `T` is inferred from evidence.
5. Why must a `const` type parameter's constraint use `readonly`?
6. Give a call where contextual typing of a callback parameter is lost, and say why.
7. What is the difference between a constraint and an inference site?
8. When does a return-position type parameter get fixed by the assignment target?
9. Why does `<A extends readonly unknown[], R>` beat `Parameters`/`ReturnType` for a wrapper?
10. What do variance annotations `in`/`out` buy you, and what do they not?
11. Why can no wrapper preserve the genericity of the function it wraps?
12. Give one case where overloads are clearly better than a conditional return type, and one where the reverse holds.

# The long read: how inference actually runs, and what it costs

TypeScript's type argument inference is one of the oldest parts of the compiler
and one of the least documented. It has no formal specification any more — the
old spec document was retired in 2016 — so the working model most engineers
carry is folklore assembled from release notes, issue threads and the reactions
of the compiler itself. This essay tries to make that model explicit, because
almost every "why is my type `unknown` here" question is answered by it.

## The algorithm, roughly

When you call a generic function, the checker performs the following, in order.

First it establishes the **context**: if the call sits in a position with an
expected type (the right-hand side of an annotated `const`, an argument to
another call, a `return` in a function with a declared return type), that
expected type is matched against the declared return type, and any type
parameters that show up are given low-priority candidates. This is the only
backwards flow in the system, and its low priority means an ordinary argument
will always beat it.

Then it walks the arguments. For each argument it runs *inference from the
argument's type to the parameter's declared type*, structurally: `T[]` against
`User[]` produces the candidate `User` for `T`; `(a: T) => K` against a supplied
arrow produces a candidate for `K` from the arrow's return type. Function
expressions whose parameters lack annotations are skipped in this first pass —
their types are not known yet — and revisited afterwards, once the parameters
they depend on have been fixed. That second pass is where contextual typing
happens: the arrow's parameter is *given* the type the signature says it should
have, rather than inferred from nothing and defaulted to `any`.

Finally it resolves each type parameter from its candidate set. If some
candidate is a supertype of all of them, that one wins; otherwise, in the
common inference position, the candidates are unioned. Literal candidates are
widened to their base primitive type unless the position asks for literals.
Any parameter left with no candidates falls back to its default, then to its
constraint under some circumstances, and finally to `unknown`.

You can see every piece of this in the compiler's error messages if you read
them literally. "Argument of type 'X' is not assignable to parameter of type
'T'" means inference already fixed `T` from an earlier argument and is now
*checking* this one. "Type 'unknown' is not assignable" usually means a type
parameter had no candidates at all.

## Why the ordering convention exists

Every functional utility library in JavaScript settled on the same argument
order — data first, function second — for `map`, `filter`, `groupBy`,
`sortBy`. Lodash's `_.map(collection, iteratee)` is not merely a stylistic
choice inherited from Underscore; in TypeScript it is load-bearing. Put the
callback first and its parameter cannot be contextually typed, because the
collection's element type has not been inferred yet. The `lodash/fp` variant,
which reverses the order to enable currying, pays for it with far heavier type
definitions and worse inference — a real, measurable tradeoff that shows up as
slower editors on large codebases.

The same principle is why `useReducer(reducer, initialState)` types poorly
compared to a config object, and why builder APIs (the next-but-three sector)
have to think hard about which method fixes which parameter.

## The history of the two modifiers

For most of TypeScript's life the only way to keep literal types was `as
const`, added in 3.4. It works, but it is a *caller* obligation: an API author
who wanted literal keys had to document "remember to write `as const`", and
half of all users forgot. `const` type parameters, shipped in 5.0, move that
obligation to the declaration, which is where it belongs. The implementation is
narrow on purpose: it changes the inference *priority* at that site toward the
literal, readonly interpretation, and it explicitly does nothing at runtime and
nothing to the mutability of the value.

`NoInfer` has an even more interesting history. The technique circulated for
years as a userland trick — `type NoInfer<T> = [T][T extends any ? 0 : never]`
and several variants — that abused the fact that inference does not descend
into certain conditional and indexed positions. Those tricks worked but broke
error messages, and every one of them had a case where it also blocked
*checking*. In 5.4 the team made it an intrinsic, so the compiler now knows
what you mean, and errors point at the argument instead of at a mangled
conditional type.

## Performance

Generic-heavy APIs are the main reason a TypeScript project's editor becomes
slow, and inference is where the time goes. A few concrete effects, in rough
order of how often they bite:

- **Deep conditional and recursive types.** Each instantiation is memoised, but
  a recursive type over a long tuple instantiates once per element, and the
  50-deep recursion limit exists because the alternative is a hang. A `pipe`
  written with recursive conditional types can cost tens of milliseconds *per
  call site*; the overload wall costs almost nothing.
- **Large unions crossed with mapped types.** `Record<T[number], X>` where
  `T[number]` is a 200-member union of literals produces a 200-property type at
  every use.
- **Inference into large object literals.** Every property is a matching
  problem; a config object with 300 keys and a `const` type parameter is a
  measurable pause.
- **Variance.** Without `in`/`out` annotations, assignability between two
  instantiations of a large generic interface is checked structurally, member
  by member. Annotating turns that into a single variance check. This is why
  the compiler's own source gained variance annotations in 4.7.

`tsc --generateTrace` and the `--diagnostics` flag will tell you which of these
is happening in your project rather than making you guess. The usual finding is
one file, one type, one call site.

## When not to be generic

There is a bias in the community toward maximum precision, and it is worth
resisting. Some rules that hold up:

**Do not make a function generic to avoid writing `unknown`.** If the body
does not use `T`, and no other parameter relates to `T`, the generic only
weakens error messages.

**Do not make internal helpers generic.** A function with one call site should
take the concrete type. Generality is a cost paid by every reader.

**Do not encode business rules in types when a runtime check will do.** A type
that proves "the discount is between 0 and 1" is possible, expensive to write,
and impossible for the next person to modify. A branded type produced by a
validator gets you most of the benefit for a tenth of the complexity.

**Do not use a generic where a union is clearer.** `function area(shape:
Circle | Square)` beats `function area<S extends Shape>(shape: S)` unless the
return type genuinely depends on `S`.

**Do prefer an options object once you have four parameters**, even though it
inferences slightly less well, because the readability at the call site is
worth more than the last increment of precision.

The through-line is that a type parameter is a *promise about a relationship*.
If you can state the relationship in a sentence — "the fallback has the same
type as the elements", "the key must exist on the row", "the decoder produces
the result" — the generic is earning its place. If you cannot, delete it and
watch how little you lose.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## ex1 — two inference sites, one relationship

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Write two functions whose type parameter is inferred
from the *values*, never from a type argument:

- `firstOr<T>(items: readonly T[], fallback: T): T`
- `atOr<T>(items: readonly T[], index: number, fallback: T): T` — negative
  indices count from the end, like `Array.prototype.at`

Behaviour:

- `firstOr(["a", "b"], "none")` → `"a"`
- `firstOr([], "none")` → `"none"`
- `firstOr([0, 1], 99)` → `0` — not `99`
- `firstOr([undefined, 1], 7)` → `undefined` — not `7`
- `atOr([10, 20, 30], -1, 0)` → `30`
- `atOr([10, 20, 30], 5, 0)` → `0`
- `atOr([10, 20, 30], -9, 0)` → `0`

The type gate also checks that `firstOr(["a"], 3)` is a **compile error**. That
is the whole point of tying `fallback` to `T`: a mismatched fallback should
fail at the call site, not become `string | number`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb01_inferable_generics ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two of the gate cases exist to break the obvious one-liner. `items[0] ??
fallback` answers "is the value nullish", and you were asked "is the array
empty". `firstOr([0, 1], 99)` and `firstOr([undefined, 1], 7)` are the two
values where those questions disagree.

## Hint 2

Length first, value second:

```ts
function headOr(xs: readonly string[], fallback: string): string {
  if (xs.length === 0) return fallback;
  return xs[0];
}
```

Make it generic and the fallback follows the element type automatically.

## Hint 3

`atOr` needs one normalisation step and one range check. Resolve a negative
index to `items.length + index`, then reject anything outside
`0 .. items.length - 1` before indexing.

Left to you: whether `firstOr` uses a `length` check or a `for...of` that
returns on the first iteration. The second is shorter and behaves correctly
even under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, which is worth knowing about before the
last sector of this volume.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read the signature as a contract before you write a line of code:
`(readonly T[], T) => T` says *the fallback is one of these things*. Every
behaviour in the prompt follows from taking that sentence literally.

## Hint 2

Ask what `T` is inferred as in each call. In `firstOr(["a"], 3)` the array
offers the candidate `string` and the fallback offers `number`; with both in
the pool, TypeScript would happily union them. The gate expects an error, so
your job is to make sure both arguments really do mention the same `T` — no
`fallback: unknown`, no second type parameter.

## Hint 3

Write `atOr` first and define `firstOr` in terms of it if you like — `atOr`
covers index `0` already. Watch the boundary: `-items.length` is the first
element and `-items.length - 1` is out of range, which is exactly the
`atOr([10, 20, 30], -9, 0)` case.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## ex2 — a relationship between two parameters

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement the `keyof` pair:

- `pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][]`
- `pluckUnique<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][]` —
  same, but each distinct value appears once, in first-seen order

With `const users = [{ id: 1, name: "ada" }, { id: 2, name: "grace" }, { id: 3, name: "ada" }]`:

- `pluck(users, "name")` → `["ada", "grace", "ada"]`, typed `string[]`
- `pluck(users, "id")` → `[1, 2, 3]`, typed `number[]`
- `pluckUnique(users, "name")` → `["ada", "grace"]`
- `pluckUnique([], "name")` → `[]`

The type gate checks three things: `pluck(users, "email")` is an error, the
result of `pluck(users, "id")` is `number[]` and not `(string | number)[]`, and
neither call needs an explicit type argument.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb01_inferable_generics ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`K extends keyof T` does two jobs at once. It rejects keys that do not exist,
and it keeps `K` as the *literal* key you passed rather than widening it to
`keyof T` — which is what lets the return type be precise.

## Hint 2

The return type is an indexed access:

```ts
type Name = { id: number; name: string }["name"];   // string
```

`T[K][]` reads as "an array of whatever lives at key `K` on `T`". That is why
`pluck(users, "id")` is `number[]` and not the union of every property type.

## Hint 3

`pluck` is one `map`. For `pluckUnique`, a `Set<T[K]>` remembers what you have
emitted and an array preserves order.

Left to you: whether `pluckUnique` builds the `Set` up front or as it goes.
Building it up front and then filtering loses first-seen order unless you are
careful — try it and see which version survives the duplicate `"ada"`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the failing case rather than the working one. What would go wrong
if the signature were `pluck<T>(items: readonly T[], key: string): unknown[]`?
Everything still compiles at the call site, `"email"` is accepted, and every
caller has to cast the result. Each part of the real signature exists to remove
one of those problems.

## Hint 2

Try writing the return type as `Array<T[keyof T]>` and look at what
`pluck(users, "id")` becomes. You get `(string | number)[]`, because
`keyof T` is the union of all keys and the indexed access distributes over it.
Precision comes from carrying the *specific* key in its own type parameter.

## Hint 3

Both functions are three lines or fewer. The interesting part is that
`item[key]` inside the body type-checks without a cast: the constraint proved
the key exists, so the compiler already knows the result is `T[K]`.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## ex3 — inference that flows into a callback

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export function groupBy<T, K extends PropertyKey>(
  items: readonly T[],
  keyOf: (item: T, index: number) => K,
): Record<K, T[]>
```

With `const files = [{ name: "a.ts", size: 10 }, { name: "b.md", size: 3 }, { name: "c.ts", size: 7 }]`:

- `groupBy(files, (file) => file.name.split(".").pop() ?? "")` →
  `{ ts: [a.ts, c.ts], md: [b.md] }`
- `groupBy([1, 2, 3, 4], (n) => (n % 2 === 0 ? "even" : "odd"))` →
  `{ odd: [1, 3], even: [2, 4] }`
- `groupBy([], () => "x")` → `{}`
- The second callback parameter is the index: `groupBy(["a", "b", "c"], (_, i) => i % 2)`
  → `{ 0: ["a", "c"], 1: ["b"] }`

Two type requirements the gate checks. The callback's `item` parameter must
need **no annotation** at the call site — that is contextual typing doing its
job — and the returned object must be keyed by the literal union the callback
produces, so `result.even` is `number[]` and `result.nope` is an error.

Order within each group is input order.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb01_inferable_generics ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two type parameters inferred from two different arguments. `T` comes from the
array in the first inference pass; `K` comes from the callback's *return* type
in the second pass, which is also when the callback's parameter gets its type
for free.

## Hint 2

`PropertyKey` is the built-in `string | number | symbol`. It is the right
constraint for `K` because `Record<K, T[]>` needs a key type an object can
actually have:

```ts
declare function tally<K extends PropertyKey>(keys: readonly K[]): Record<K, number>;
```

## Hint 3

Build into a `Partial<Record<K, T[]>>` while the object is incomplete, then
assert the full `Record<K, T[]>` on the way out. That one assertion is honest —
the object is complete by the time you return it — and it is the only place a
cast belongs.

Left to you: `{}` or `Object.create(null)` as the starting value. The second
avoids a group called `"constructor"` colliding with a prototype property. Try
`groupBy(["x"], () => "constructor")` against both.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Swap the parameters in your head: `groupBy(keyOf, items)`. Write that version
and the callback parameter becomes an implicit `any`, because nothing has told
the compiler what an item is yet. That thought experiment is the reason every
collection library in JavaScript takes the data first.

## Hint 2

The runtime part is a single pass with a lookup-or-create step:

```ts
const bucket = groups[key];
if (bucket) bucket.push(item);
else groups[key] = [item];
```

Everything else in this exercise is the signature.

## Hint 3

If the compiler complains that `groups[key]` might be `undefined`, that is
correct and it is why the working type is `Partial<Record<K, T[]>>` rather than
`Record<K, T[]>`. Fighting that error with `!` works and teaches you nothing;
letting the type be honest and asserting once at the boundary is the pattern
you will reuse in the parsing sector.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## ex4 — `const` type parameters keep the literals

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Finish the route table:

```ts
export interface RouteTable<T extends readonly string[]> {
  readonly paths: T;
  readonly index: Readonly<Record<T[number], number>>;
  includes(path: string): path is T[number];
}

export function defineRoutes<const T extends readonly string[]>(paths: T): RouteTable<T>
```

With `const routes = defineRoutes(["/health", "/users", "/orders"])`:

- `routes.paths` is typed `readonly ["/health", "/users", "/orders"]` — no
  `as const` at the call site
- `routes.index` → `{ "/health": 0, "/users": 1, "/orders": 2 }`, and
  `routes.index["/nope"]` is a compile error
- `routes.includes("/users")` → `true`; `routes.includes("/nope")` → `false`
- After `if (routes.includes(input))`, `input` is narrowed to
  `"/health" | "/users" | "/orders"`

Duplicated paths keep the **first** position: `defineRoutes(["/a", "/b", "/a"]).index["/a"]`
→ `0`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb01_inferable_generics ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Delete the `const` modifier from the type parameter and look at what happens to
`routes.paths`. It becomes `string[]`, `T[number]` becomes `string`, and the
index map and the predicate stop saying anything. The whole exercise hangs on
one keyword.

## Hint 2

`T[number]` on a readonly tuple is the union of its elements:

```ts
type Paths = readonly ["/a", "/b"];
type Path = Paths[number];    // "/a" | "/b"
```

That union is what makes `Record<T[number], number>` a three-key object type
rather than a string index signature.

## Hint 3

Inside the body, `paths.forEach((path) => ...)` gives you `path: string`, not
`T[number]`, because the body only knows the *constraint*. One assertion when
you write the key is the accepted cost; keep it to that single line.

Left to you: how to make duplicates keep the first position. A membership check
before assigning is one way; iterating in reverse is another, and it is wrong —
work out why before you use it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The predicate is the part that pays off. `includes(path: string): path is
T[number]` is a user-defined type guard whose *result type is derived from the
type parameter*, so a table of three routes narrows to those three strings and
a table of thirty narrows to those thirty. Nothing is hard-coded.

## Hint 2

Two independent things need to hold at runtime: `includes` must be a real
membership test (a `Set` built once beats `paths.includes` inside a loop), and
`index` must be a plain object so property access works. Build both in the
factory and close over them.

## Hint 3

Remember the constraint caveat: `<const T extends string[]>` — mutable — would
undo half the work, because a mutable array type cannot be a readonly tuple.
The `readonly` in the constraint is not decoration.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## ex5 — `NoInfer`, or how to stop one argument widening another

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface Chooser<T> {
  readonly options: readonly T[];
  readonly fallback: T;
  choose(value: unknown): T;
}

export function chooser<T>(options: readonly T[], fallback: NoInfer<T>): Chooser<T>
```

`choose` returns `value` when it is one of `options`, and `fallback` otherwise.

- `const theme = chooser(["light", "dark"], "light")` — `T` is `"light" | "dark"`
- `theme.choose("dark")` → `"dark"`
- `theme.choose("solarized")` → `"light"`
- `theme.choose(null)` → `"light"`
- `chooser([1, 2, 3], 1).choose(3)` → `3`

The gate's real assertion is a *negative* one: `chooser(["light", "dark"],
"purple")` must be a **compile error** saying `"purple"` is not assignable to
`"light" | "dark"`. Remove the `NoInfer` and that call compiles, with `T`
quietly becoming a three-member union — run the experiment before you move on.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb01_inferable_generics ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every position that mentions a type parameter casts a vote for what it should
be. Two voters here — the options array and the fallback — and the loser of a
disagreement is not an error, it is a union. `NoInfer<T>` withdraws a voter
while keeping its ballot subject to inspection.

## Hint 2

`NoInfer` is an intrinsic in the standard library since TypeScript 5.4; you do
not define it. Its shape in a signature:

```ts
declare function seed<T>(values: readonly T[], initial: NoInfer<T>): T;
seed(["a", "b"], "c");   // error - "c" is not "a" | "b"
```

## Hint 3

At runtime `choose` is a membership test plus a fallback. A `Set<unknown>`
built from `options` in the factory gives you an O(1) test and accepts an
`unknown` argument without a cast on the way in — the cast belongs on the way
out, once membership has proved what the value is.

Left to you: whether `choose` should take `unknown` or `T | null | undefined`.
The prompt says `unknown` because the values arrive from outside the program;
narrowing that decision is the whole subject of the next sector.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about where this bug shows up in real code. A state hook with an initial
value, a config helper with a default, a select component with a placeholder —
all of them have one argument that should *define* the type and another that
should merely *conform* to it. Naming those two roles is the design skill here.

## Hint 2

`choose` receives `unknown`, so nothing can be done with the value until
membership is established. Once `allowed.has(value)` is true you know the value
came from `options`, so `value as T` is justified by a runtime check rather
than by hope. Write the comment explaining that, because a reviewer will ask.

## Hint 3

If you want to see the mechanism rather than take it on faith, hover the
result of `chooser(["light", "dark"], "purple")` with `NoInfer` removed. `T` is
`"light" | "dark" | "purple"`, `theme.choose("purple")` returns `"purple"`, and
nothing in the program ever notices the typo. That is the failure the modifier
exists to prevent.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## ex6 — replacing a return-position type parameter with evidence

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. The file starts with the most common unsound generic in
the ecosystem:

```ts
export function parseJson<T>(text: string): T {
  return JSON.parse(text) as T;      // the caller's claim, unchecked
}
```

Replace it with a version that infers `T` from something real, and add the two
pieces of evidence it needs:

- `isRecord(value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown>` — true for plain
  objects, false for `null`, arrays and primitives
- `decodeUser(value: unknown): User` where `User` is `{ id: number; name: string }`
  — throws a `TypeError` with a useful message when the value is not a user
- `parseJson<T>(text: string, decode: (value: unknown) => T): T`

Behaviour:

- `parseJson('{"id":1,"name":"ada"}', decodeUser)` → `{ id: 1, name: "ada" }`,
  typed `User` with no type argument at the call site
- `parseJson('{"id":"1","name":"ada"}', decodeUser)` throws
  `TypeError: id must be an integer`
- `parseJson('{"id":1}', decodeUser)` throws
  `TypeError: name must be a non-empty string`
- `parseJson('null', decodeUser)` throws `TypeError: expected an object`
- `isRecord([])` → `false`, `isRecord(null)` → `false`, `isRecord({})` → `true`

`decodeUser` must return a **fresh** object containing only `id` and `name`, so
extra keys in the JSON do not travel onward.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb01_inferable_generics ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Count the inference sites in the original signature. There are none: `T`
appears only in the return type, so nothing about the argument can contradict
the caller. `parseJson<Config>(raw)` and `JSON.parse(raw) as Config` are the
same statement with different punctuation.

## Hint 2

Adding a decoder parameter creates the missing site:

```ts
declare function decode<T>(input: unknown, decoder: (v: unknown) => T): T;
decode(payload, decodeUser);   // T = User, inferred, not claimed
```

Now the thing that has to be correct is `decodeUser`, which is code you can
test.

## Hint 3

`isRecord` needs three checks, and the order matters because
`typeof null === "object"` is a JavaScript wart. Arrays are objects too, so
exclude them explicitly with `Array.isArray`.

Left to you: whether `decodeUser` throws or returns a `Result`. This exercise
says throw, because the message text is asserted; the next sector argues the
other side at length.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A useful way to audit any generic: cover the return type with your hand and ask
whether the remaining signature still determines every type parameter. If it
does not, the parameter is an instruction from the caller rather than a
conclusion from the code.

## Hint 2

Write `decodeUser` before you touch `parseJson`. Destructure after the
`isRecord` guard — `const { id, name } = value` gives you two `unknown`s, and
each check that follows narrows exactly one of them. The final `return { id,
name }` then type-checks with no cast at all, which is the signal that you did
the narrowing properly.

## Hint 3

The "fresh object" requirement is not busywork. Returning `value as User` after
checking two fields would pass every runtime assertion in the gate while
smuggling every other key in the payload into your domain model — including,
in a real system, the ones an attacker chose. Constructing the result is what
makes the decoder a boundary.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## ex7 — preserving a whole signature through a wrapper

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Implement a retry decorator that does not damage the
function it wraps:

```ts
export function withRetry<A extends readonly unknown[], R>(
  fn: (...args: A) => Promise<R>,
  attempts: number,
  onRetry?: (error: unknown, attempt: number) => void,
): (...args: A) => Promise<R>
```

Behaviour:

- Calls `fn(...args)`; on a rejection, calls `onRetry(error, attempt)` and
  tries again, up to `attempts` total calls
- Resolves with the first successful result
- After the last failure, rejects with the **last** error thrown
- `attempts` less than 1, or not an integer, throws a `RangeError` immediately
  when `withRetry` is called — not when the wrapped function is called

Given `const flaky = async (id: string) => { ... }` that fails twice then
succeeds:

- `withRetry(flaky, 3)("u1")` resolves; `onRetry` was called with attempts `1`
  and `2`
- `withRetry(flaky, 2)("u1")` rejects with the second error
- `withRetry(flaky, 3)()` is a **compile error** — the wrapper still requires
  the `id` argument

The type gate hovers the wrapped function and checks the parameter is still
named `id` and typed `string`, and that the return type is `Promise<User>` and
not `Promise<unknown>`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb01_inferable_generics ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`A extends readonly unknown[]` captures the entire parameter list as a tuple
type, including names and optionality. That is why the wrapper's tooltip still
says `(id: string)` instead of `(...args: any[])`.

## Hint 2

Spreading a generic tuple into the call is legal and needs no cast:

```ts
function twice<A extends readonly unknown[], R>(fn: (...args: A) => R) {
  return (...args: A): [R, R] => [fn(...args), fn(...args)];
}
```

## Hint 3

The loop keeps a `let lastError: unknown` outside it, calls `await fn(...args)`
inside a `try`, and returns on success. After the loop, `throw lastError`.
Validate `attempts` before returning the wrapper so the `RangeError` fires at
decoration time.

Left to you: whether `onRetry` fires after the final failure too. The prompt
says attempts `1` and `2` for three tries, so it fires only when another try
follows — a small decision that changes every log line in production.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Compare three candidate signatures before you pick one:
`(fn: (...args: any[]) => any)` accepts anything and checks nothing;
`<F extends (...args: any[]) => Promise<unknown>>(fn: F) => (...args:
Parameters<F>) => ReturnType<F>` works but flattens overloads and drops
generics; the tuple form in the prompt keeps arity, names and the resolved
type. Being able to say why the middle one is second best is an interview
answer.

## Hint 2

`lastError` is `unknown` because that is what `catch` gives you under
`useUnknownInCatchVariables`, which `strict` turns on. Do not narrow it, do not
wrap it — rethrowing an unknown preserves whatever the caller's own handler
expects to receive.

## Hint 3

Think about the failure ordering. If `attempts` is 2 and both calls fail, the
gate expects the *second* error, not the first, and not an aggregate. Assign
into `lastError` on every catch and the ordering takes care of itself.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## ex8 — the overload wall: `pipe` and `flow`

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Implement left-to-right composition twice, once over a
value and once over a function:

```ts
export function pipe<A, B>(value: A, ab: (a: A) => B): B;
// ... up to five stages
export function flow<A extends readonly unknown[], B>(ab: (...args: A) => B): (...args: A) => B;
// ... up to four stages
```

Behaviour:

- `pipe(" 42 ", (s) => s.trim(), (s) => Number(s), (n) => n * 2)` → `84`,
  typed `number`, with **no annotations** on any of the arrows
- `pipe([1, 2, 3], (xs) => xs.filter((x) => x > 1), (xs) => xs.length)` → `2`
- `pipe(1, (n) => n.toFixed(1))` → `"1.0"`, typed `string`
- `const parseAge = flow((raw: string) => raw.trim(), Number, Math.round)`;
  `parseAge(" 41.6 ")` → `42`, and `parseAge` is typed `(raw: string) => number`
- `pipe(1, (s: string) => s)` is a **compile error** — stage inputs must match
  the previous stage's output

Write the overload declarations by hand for 2, 3, 4 and 5 arguments to `pipe`
and 1, 2, 3 and 4 to `flow`, then one implementation signature underneath each.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb01_inferable_generics ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Try to write `pipe` with a single variadic signature first, and notice what you
cannot say: there is no way to express "argument *n*'s input is argument
*n−1*'s output" over a tuple of unknown length without recursive conditional
types. That failure is why every real library ships a wall of overloads.

## Hint 2

The pattern for each overload is mechanical — a fresh type parameter per stage,
each function taking the previous one and returning the next:

```ts
export function pipe<A, B, C>(value: A, ab: (a: A) => B, bc: (b: B) => C): C;
```

Write them in increasing arity. TypeScript picks the first overload that
matches, so ordering shortest-first is the convention.

## Hint 3

The implementation signature sits under the declarations, is not visible to
callers, and is allowed to be loose: `(value: unknown, ...fns:
ReadonlyArray<(input: unknown) => unknown>): unknown` plus a `reduce`. For
`flow`, take the first function separately so you can spread the caller's
arguments into it and then thread single values through the rest.

Left to you: how many stages to support. Real libraries stop somewhere between
nine and twenty; the interesting question is what the error message looks like
when a caller goes one past your last overload.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`flow` is the harder of the two and the reason is worth naming: its *first*
function may take several arguments, and every later one takes exactly one.
That asymmetry is why the first type parameter is a tuple (`A extends readonly
unknown[]`) and the rest are plain types.

## Hint 2

Watch what inference does with a bare `Number` or `Math.round` passed as a
stage. They are ordinary functions with declared types, so nothing has to be
inferred for them — but `Number` accepts `any`, which means a wrong stage
before it will not be caught. Test the chain with a stage you wrote yourself if
you want the error.

## Hint 3

Overload resolution stops at the first match, so a call with three arguments
never reaches the four-argument declaration. If a correct call is rejected, the
usual cause is an overload listed out of order or a missing one at that arity —
read the error's "Overload 2 of 4" prefix, it tells you which one it tried.

## Challenge — a tiny table API where nothing needs a type argument (hard)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Build a query-shaped wrapper over an array in
which every type parameter is inferred from a value:

```ts
export interface Table<Row> {
  readonly rows: readonly Row[];
  where(predicate: (row: Row, index: number) => boolean): Table<Row>;
  select<const K extends readonly (keyof Row)[]>(keys: K): Array<Pick<Row, K[number]>>;
  sortBy<V>(project: (row: Row) => V, compare: (a: V, b: V) => number): Table<Row>;
  indexBy<K extends PropertyKey>(keyOf: (row: Row) => K): Map<K, Row>;
}

export function table<Row>(rows: readonly Row[]): Table<Row>
```

With

```ts
const people = table([
  { id: 3, name: "ada", team: "core" },
  { id: 1, name: "grace", team: "core" },
  { id: 2, name: "alan", team: "ops" },
]);
```

- `people.where((p) => p.team === "core").select(["name"])` →
  `[{ name: "ada" }, { name: "grace" }]`, typed `Array<{ name: string }>`
- `people.select(["id", "name"])[0].team` is a **compile error** — `select`
  returns `Pick<Row, "id" | "name">`, not `Row`
- `people.sortBy((p) => p.id, (a, b) => a - b).rows.map((p) => p.name)` →
  `["grace", "alan", "ada"]`
- `people.indexBy((p) => p.team).get("core")?.name` → `"ada"` — first row wins
- `people.select(["nope"])` is a compile error
- Every call above works with no explicit type argument and no annotated
  callback parameters

`where` and `sortBy` return a new `Table` and never mutate `rows`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb01_inferable_generics challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three mechanisms from this sector, one API. `Row` is inferred once, from the
array. `select` needs a `const` type parameter, or `["id", "name"]` widens to
`string[]` and `K[number]` collapses to `keyof Row`. `sortBy` threads `V` from
the projection into the comparator, which is why the comparator's parameters
need no annotation.

## Hint 2

`Pick<Row, K[number]>` is the return element type, and it is worth checking
what each piece contributes:

```ts
type Row = { id: number; name: string; team: string };
type K = readonly ["id", "name"];
type Out = Pick<Row, K[number]>;   // { id: number; name: string }
```

Take the `const` off `K` and `Out` becomes `Pick<Row, keyof Row>` — the whole
row, which is the bug the gate checks for.

## Hint 3

Implement `table` as a factory returning an object literal, with `where` and
`sortBy` calling `table(...)` again on a copy. `select` builds a plain object
per row and asserts the picked type once, on the way out; there is no way to
write that loop without one assertion, and one is the right number.

Left to you: whether `indexBy` keeps the first or the last row for a duplicate
key. The prompt says first — implement it with a `has` check rather than
reversing the input, because reversing also changes nothing else you can see.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build it in the order the types depend on each other: `rows` and `where` first
(no new type parameters), then `indexBy` (one, from a callback), then `sortBy`
(one, threaded between two arguments), then `select` (a `const` tuple crossed
with `keyof`). Each step is a mechanism you already used in an earlier
exercise.

## Hint 2

If `select` returns `Pick<Row, keyof Row>` in your editor's tooltip, do not go
looking for a bug in `Pick`. The tuple widened. Confirm it by hovering the
argument itself: `string[]` means the `const` modifier is missing or the
constraint forgot `readonly`.

## Hint 3

Inside `select`, the natural loop assigns into an object whose key type is
generic, and TypeScript will not check that assignment for you. Accumulate into
a `Record<PropertyKey, unknown>` and convert once at the end, rather than
sprinkling assertions through the loop — the goal is that a reader can see
every unchecked step in a single glance.

## Review — a registry that remembers its own literals

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Same ideas, approached from the literal-preservation
side:

```ts
export interface Registry<N extends readonly string[]> {
  readonly names: N;
  readonly order: Readonly<Record<N[number], number>>;
  isKnown(value: string): value is N[number];
  sort<T>(items: readonly T[], keyOf: (item: T) => N[number]): T[];
}

export function createRegistry<const N extends readonly string[]>(names: N): Registry<N>
```

With `const stages = createRegistry(["queued", "running", "done"])`:

- `stages.names` is `readonly ["queued", "running", "done"]`
- `stages.order.running` → `1`; `stages.order.failed` is a compile error
- `stages.isKnown("done")` → `true`, and inside the `if` the argument is
  narrowed to the three stage names
- `stages.sort([{ s: "done" }, { s: "queued" }], (j) => j.s)` →
  `[{ s: "queued" }, { s: "done" }]`
- `stages.sort(jobs, (j) => j.title)` is a compile error when `title` is a
  plain `string` — the callback must produce a registered name
- The sort is **stable**: equal stages keep their input order
- `createRegistry(["a", "b", "a"])` throws a `RangeError` naming the duplicate

Nothing above requires an explicit type argument.

```

```

## Hint 1

Everything here hangs off one union: `N[number]`. It is the key type of
`order`, the narrowed type of `isKnown`, and the return type the `keyOf`
callback must produce. Get `N` inferred as a readonly tuple and the other four
requirements are consequences.

## Hint 2

`Array.prototype.sort` has been required to be stable since ES2019, so you do
not need to decorate with indices — but you do need to copy first, because
`sort` mutates and `items` is `readonly`.

```ts
const sorted = [...items].sort((a, b) => rank(a) - rank(b));
```

## Hint 3

Build the order map in one pass and detect duplicates in the same pass: if the
name is already a key, throw. Throwing at construction time is deliberate — a
registry with a duplicate has an ambiguous order, and there is no sensible
answer to give later.

Left to you: whether `isKnown` consults the `order` object or a separate `Set`.
Both work; one of them behaves oddly for the name `"toString"`. Try it.

## Hint 1

Read the `sort` signature closely: `keyOf: (item: T) => N[number]` constrains

If `order` refuses an assignment inside the loop, remember what the body knows:

lessons.title: V3·TB2 — Parse, don't validate: schemas and unknown boundaries
lessons.summary: Every type in your program is a claim about data you did not create. At the edges — HTTP bodies, JSON files, localStorage, message queues — the only honest type is unknown, and the only honest way out of it is a function that inspects the value and returns a narrower one. This sector builds that function from scratch.

# V3·TB2 — Parse, don't validate: schemas and unknown boundaries

The previous sector ended on a signature that looked harmless and was not:

```ts
function parseJson<T>(text: string): T { return JSON.parse(text) as T; }
```

The problem was that `T` had no inference site — nothing checked the claim.
This sector is about what to put there instead, and it turns out the answer is
a whole design discipline with a name: **parse, don't validate**.

The phrase comes from Alexis King's 2019 essay about Haskell, and it survives
the trip to TypeScript intact. The distinction is between two shapes of
function:

```ts
function validateUser(value: unknown): boolean;   // returns a fact you must remember
function parseUser(value: unknown): User;         // returns a value you can use
```

A validator answers a question and throws the answer away. The caller still
holds an `unknown`, and if they want to use it they must cast — which means
the check and the cast can drift apart, and nothing will tell you. A parser
returns *evidence in the type system*: after `const user = parseUser(body)`,
there is no path where `user` is not a `User`, because the only way to get one
is through the function that checks.

## Concept — `unknown` is the boundary type

`JSON.parse` returns `any`, and `any` is the type that turns the checker off.
Rule one at any boundary is to demote it immediately:

```ts
const raw: unknown = JSON.parse(text);
```

`unknown` is the top type with the safety on: everything is assignable *to* it,
nothing is assignable *from* it, and you cannot read a property, call it or
index it until you have narrowed it. That refusal is the feature. `any` says
"stop checking"; `unknown` says "prove it first".

Narrowing `unknown` uses the tools from the unions sector, with two traps
specific to this territory:

```ts
typeof value === "object"            // true for null - the famous wart
Array.isArray(value)                 // the only reliable array check
"id" in value                        // needs value narrowed to object first
Object.hasOwn(value, "id")           // ES2022; ignores the prototype chain
```

Prototype-chain checks matter here more than anywhere else, because JSON
payloads come from outside. A body containing `{"__proto__": {...}}` is a real
attack, and `key in object` will happily report `true` for `"toString"` on
every object you have ever seen.

## Concept — a decoder is just a function

You do not need a library to have a schema. A decoder is:

```ts
type Decoder<T> = (value: unknown, path: string) => T;
```

It takes an `unknown` and either returns a `T` or throws with a path saying
*where* the data was wrong. Everything else in this sector is composition:

```ts
const decodeUser = object({ id: integer, name: string, tags: array(string) });
type User = Infer<typeof decodeUser>;   // { id: number; name: string; tags: string[] }
```

The second line is the part that makes this pay for itself. The static type is
**derived from** the runtime check, so they cannot disagree. Write the type by
hand alongside a separate validator and you have two sources of truth that will
diverge on a Tuesday. This is exactly what `z.infer<typeof schema>` does in
zod, `v.InferOutput` in valibot, and `t.TypeOf` in io-ts — you are about to
build the mechanism they wrap.

## Concept — what the parser returns is not what it received

A parser is a *transformation*, and that has three consequences worth stating
before you write one.

**It constructs a new value.** Returning `value as User` after checking two
fields lets every other key in the payload travel into your domain — including
keys an attacker chose. Building `{ id, name }` strips them. That is the "strip
unknown keys" policy zod applies by default, and the alternatives (`passthrough`
and `strict`) are real design choices, not defaults to accept blindly.

**It can produce a richer type than the wire format.** A date arrives as a
string and leaves as a `Date`. An enum arrives as a string and leaves as a
literal union. A user id arrives as a string and leaves as a *branded* `UserId`
which cannot be swapped with an `OrderId`, even though both are strings at
runtime.

**It should report every problem, not the first.** A form with four bad fields
should not take four round trips. Accumulating issues with paths — `$.items[2].email`
— is the difference between a schema you can put behind an API and one you can
only use in a script.

## The trap

The trap is the cast that looks like a check:

```ts
if (typeof body === "object" && body !== null && "id" in body) {
  const user = body as User;      // "I checked it"
}
```

You checked that `id` exists. You did not check that it is a number, that
`name` exists, or that `tags` is an array of strings, and nothing in the
program will ever check again. Six months later somebody adds a field to
`User` and this line silently starts lying. The parser you are about to write
cannot drift like that, because the type is generated from the check.

There is a milder version of the same failure, and it is more common: two
sources of truth. Someone writes `interface User { ... }` by hand, someone else
writes a validator, and for a while they agree. Then a field becomes optional
in one place and not the other, and the compiler — which can only see the
interface — reports nothing at all. Deriving the type from the schema removes
the possibility rather than the symptom, which is the difference between a
convention and a mechanism.

The eight exercises build the library in order: errors with paths, safe
navigation of `unknown`, predicates versus assertion functions, the object
combinator with `Infer`, arrays and unions, issue accumulation, branded types,
and finally the mapped type that makes optional fields genuinely optional.
