# Reading - typescript/v3tb02_parse_dont_validate

Notes on the mechanism, the type-level machinery, and the places where
hand-rolled schemas go wrong.

## Notes

**`unknown` versus `any`, precisely.** Both accept every value. The difference
is what you may do next: `any` is assignable *to* everything and permits every
operation, while `unknown` is assignable only to `unknown` (and `any`) and
permits none. `unknown` also behaves better in unions — `unknown | string` is
`unknown`, whereas `any | string` is `any`, which is how one `any` in a large
codebase erodes everything it touches. The practical rule: `any` at a boundary
is a hole; `unknown` at a boundary is a door with a lock.

**Type predicates are unchecked promises.** `function isUser(v: unknown): v is
User` compiles even if the body is `return true`. TypeScript verifies that
`User` is related to `unknown` and stops there. That is why a predicate should
be small enough to read in one glance, and why generating the predicate and the
type from one schema is strictly better than writing both.

**Assertion functions have a declaration quirk.** `function assertUser(v:
unknown): asserts v is User` narrows the argument for the rest of the block,
but only when the compiler can see the declaration statically. Assign one to a
`const` without an explicit type annotation and you get *"Assertions require
every name in the call target to be declared with an explicit type
annotation"* — a real error people hit weekly. Function declarations and
explicitly annotated consts work; inferred consts, methods reached through
optional chaining, and imported-then-reassigned functions do not.

**The `Infer` type is one conditional type.** `type Infer<D> = D extends
Decoder<infer T> ? T : never` reads the return type out of the function type.
It composes because the object combinator's return type is written as a mapped
type over the shape — `{ [K in keyof S]: Infer<S[K]> }` — so nesting decoders
nests the inferred types automatically, to whatever depth you build.

**Optional properties are not the same as `| undefined`.** A decoder that
returns `T | undefined` produces `{ name: string | undefined }`, which requires
callers to *write* `name: undefined` explicitly. Making the key genuinely
optional needs key remapping: partition the shape's keys by whether `undefined`
extends the inferred type, then intersect a required mapped type with an
optional one. That is ex8, and it is the single piece of type-level machinery
in this sector that is worth memorising.

**Unknown-key policy is a security decision.** Three options, all defensible.
*Strip* (build a fresh object with only known keys) is the right default: extra
fields cannot reach your database, your logs or your JSON responses. *Strict*
(throw on unknown keys) catches client bugs and typos and is excellent in
internal APIs, and terrible on a public one, where adding a field becomes a
breaking change for nobody's benefit. *Passthrough* keeps everything and should
be reserved for proxies that genuinely need to forward data they do not
understand.

**Branding is how parsed data stays distinguishable.** `type Email = string &
{ readonly __brand: "Email" }` is not a runtime wrapper; it is a type that only
your parser can produce, because nothing else will satisfy the intersection
without a cast. It costs nothing at runtime and turns `sendTo(user.name)` into
a compile error. The cost is that branded values need unwrapping at the edges,
and that a cast still defeats it — branding is a guard rail, not a wall.

## ex1 — errors that say where

Decoders that throw `"invalid"` are useless in production; decoders that throw
`"$.items[2].email: expected a string, got number"` are a support ticket
answered before it is filed. Carrying the path as a parameter rather than
reconstructing it from a stack is what makes composition cheap. Note the
`Number.isFinite` check: `typeof NaN === "number"` is true, and `NaN` in a
price field is a genuine production incident.

## ex2 — walking `unknown` safely

`getPath` is the function everybody writes badly once. The lessons are that
each step must re-establish "this is an object" before indexing, that
`Object.hasOwn` is the check you want rather than `in`, and that a path
segment named `__proto__` must not be followed. The bug class here is not
theoretical: prototype pollution through JSON merge helpers has produced
critical advisories in several popular packages.

## ex3 — predicate, assertion, parser

Three shapes for one job, with three different call-site ergonomics. A
predicate composes with `filter` and `if`. An assertion reads well at the top
of a function and narrows for the whole body. A parser is the only one of the
three that can *change* the value, which is why it is the one this sector
builds on. Being able to say which you would choose and why is a good interview
answer; noting that all three are only as good as their bodies is a better one.

## ex4 — the object combinator

Two mechanisms meet here. At runtime you iterate the shape's keys and call each
decoder on the corresponding property, collecting into a fresh object. At the
type level, the return type is a mapped type over the shape. The single
assertion at the end is unavoidable and correct: the object is complete
precisely when you return it.

## ex5 — arrays, unions, and where the path goes

`array(inner)` decodes each element with a path of `${path}[${index}]`.
`union(...)` is the interesting one, because on failure you have several
errors and no single reason. Reporting "no variant matched" plus the collected
messages is more useful than reporting the last failure, which is what naive
implementations do.

## ex6 — collect, do not stop

Short-circuiting is right for a single scalar and wrong for a form. The switch
is small — accumulate issues into an array instead of throwing — and the
resulting API is a discriminated union with `ok` and `issues`. That shape is
the subject of the next sector; here it exists only so the parser can report
everything at once.

## ex7 — brands

The exercise's sting is that `asEmail("nope")` must fail while
`"nope" as Email` still compiles. Types are erased; a brand raises the cost of
being careless, it does not eliminate it. Its real value is in a large codebase
where three different `string` ids flow through the same functions.

## ex8 — optional keys, properly

The mapped-type partition is fiddly and worth doing once by hand, because every
schema library contains a version of it, and because the failure mode when you
get it wrong — every field becoming optional, or none — is instructive about
how `undefined extends T` behaves for `unknown` and for `any`.

## Further reading

- [Alexis King, "Parse, don't validate"](https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/) — the original argument, in Haskell, and still the clearest statement of it.
- [Handbook: `unknown`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#unknown) — including why it beats `any` at boundaries.
- [Handbook: assertion functions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-7.html#assertion-functions) — with the explicit-annotation requirement spelled out.
- [zod documentation: `strict`, `strip`, `passthrough`](https://zod.dev/) — the three unknown-key policies as a real library exposes them.
- [OWASP: prototype pollution](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Prototype_Pollution) — why `__proto__` deserves a special case in `getPath`.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·TB2 — Parse, don't validate (archive)

The deep version: the argument, the full combinator set, the type-level
machinery, the security angle, and a self-test bank.

## 1. The argument in one page

Consider two functions with identical runtime behaviour:

```ts
function isConfig(value: unknown): boolean { /* checks */ }
function parseConfig(value: unknown): Config { /* same checks, builds a Config */ }
```

With the first, a caller writes:

```ts
if (!isConfig(raw)) throw new Error("bad config");
const config = raw as Config;          // the cast is unavoidable
```

The cast is the problem. It is a separate statement from the check, it does not
know what the check tested, and it will keep compiling when the check stops
matching `Config`. With the second:

```ts
const config = parseConfig(raw);       // no cast anywhere in the program
```

There is no way to obtain a `Config` except by going through the code that
verifies one. That is what "parse, don't validate" means: **make the check the
only constructor**.

The same idea has other names. In domain-driven design it is a value object
with a private constructor and a `create` method. In Rust it is
`TryFrom`. In TypeScript it is a decoder plus, when you want the property to
survive assignment, a brand.

## 2. The combinator set

A usable hand-rolled schema needs about a dozen pieces:

```ts
type Decoder<T> = (value: unknown, path: string) => T;

// leaves
string, number, integer, boolean, literal(v), enumOf(values), unknownValue

// structure
object(shape), array(inner), tuple(...decoders), record(valueDecoder)

// modality
optional(inner), nullable(inner), withDefault(inner, fallback)

// choice
union(...decoders), variant(tag, cases)

// refinement and transformation
refine(inner, predicate, message), map(inner, fn)
```

The last two carry most of the real-world weight. `refine` is where "a
percentage is between 0 and 100" lives; `map` is where a string becomes a
`Date`, a `URL`, a `BigInt` or a branded id. Note that `map` means input type
and output type differ, which is why serious libraries separate `Input` and
`Output` in their inference types — `z.input` and `z.output` exist precisely
because `z.infer` alone is ambiguous once transformations are allowed.

## 3. The type machinery, piece by piece

```ts
type Infer<D> = D extends Decoder<infer T> ? T : never;

// object: a mapped type over the shape
function object<S extends Record<string, Decoder<unknown>>>(
  shape: S,
): Decoder<{ [K in keyof S]: Infer<S[K]> }>;

// optional keys: partition, then intersect
type OptionalKeys<S> = {
  [K in keyof S]: undefined extends Infer<S[K]> ? K : never;
}[keyof S];
type RequiredKeys<S> = Exclude<keyof S, OptionalKeys<S>>;
type Shaped<S> =
  & { [K in RequiredKeys<S>]: Infer<S[K]> }
  & { [K in OptionalKeys<S>]?: Infer<S[K]> };
```

Three notes on the partition. The `[keyof S]` at the end of `OptionalKeys` is
an indexed access that turns the mapped type into a union of its values — the
standard trick for "keys whose value satisfies a condition". `undefined extends
X` is the test, not `X extends undefined`, because you are asking whether
`undefined` is *one of* the possibilities. And it produces the wrong answer for
`any` (everything is optional) and for `unknown` (nothing is), which is a good
reason not to allow an `any` decoder into a shape.

## 4. Worked example: an API response

```ts
const decodeMoney = map(integer, (cents) => ({ cents, display: cents / 100 }));

const decodeOrder = object({
  id: brandedId("Order"),
  total: decodeMoney,
  placedAt: map(isoDateString, (s) => new Date(s)),
  status: enumOf(["pending", "shipped", "cancelled"] as const),
  note: optional(string),
  lines: array(object({ sku: string, quantity: positiveInteger })),
});

type Order = Infer<typeof decodeOrder>;
// {
//   id: OrderId;
//   total: { cents: number; display: number };
//   placedAt: Date;
//   status: "pending" | "shipped" | "cancelled";
//   note?: string;
//   lines: { sku: string; quantity: number }[];
// }
```

Nobody wrote that type. It is a consequence of the decoder, which means a
change to the decoder is a change to the type, which means every consumer is
re-checked. That property is the entire return on investment.

## 5. Where hand-rolled schemas go wrong

- **Paths built by string concatenation with no array syntax.** `items.2.email`
  is harder to read and impossible to feed back into a form library. Use
  `items[2].email`.
- **`typeof value === "object"` without the `null` check.** Still the most
  common bug in this territory.
- **Using `in` instead of `Object.hasOwn`.** `"constructor" in {}` is `true`.
- **Following a `__proto__` segment in a path walker or a merge helper.**
- **Reusing the input object as the output.** Strips nothing; leaks everything.
- **Throwing strings instead of an error class.** Callers cannot distinguish a
  decode failure from a bug in the decoder.
- **Checking `Array.isArray` and then trusting element types.** An array of the
  wrong thing is still an array.
- **Deep recursion without a depth cap.** A hostile payload nested ten thousand
  levels deep will blow the stack of a naive recursive decoder; this is a real
  denial-of-service class, and it is why `JSON.parse` itself has limits.

## 6. When not to parse

Parsing costs time proportional to the payload, and it is not free. Reasonable
places to skip it:

- **Hot internal loops** where the data was parsed once at the boundary and has
  not left the process since. Parse at the edge, not at every function.
- **Data you produced yourself in the same process**, such as an object you
  just built and are about to serialise.
- **Very large payloads where a streaming check is the only option** — a
  hundred-megabyte NDJSON file wants per-line parsing, not one schema over the
  whole thing.
- **Trusted binary protocols with their own schema** (protobuf, Avro), where the
  codec already produced typed values; re-parsing duplicates work.

Everywhere else — HTTP request and response bodies, environment variables,
localStorage, query strings, message queues, webhook payloads, files on disk,
anything from a database driver that returns `any` — parse.

## 7. Interview answers

**"What is the difference between `unknown` and `any`?"** Both accept anything;
`unknown` permits nothing until you narrow it, and does not spread through
unions. `any` disables checking for every expression it touches.

**"How would you type a JSON API response?"** Not with a type argument on
`fetch`. Define a decoder, derive the static type from it with `Infer`, and
make the decoder the only way to construct the domain type.

**"Is a type predicate safe?"** Only as safe as its body — the compiler does
not verify it. That is an argument for deriving predicates from schemas rather
than writing them by hand.

**"Why strip unknown keys?"** So that data you never validated cannot reach
your database, your logs, or a response you serialise. Strict mode is stronger
but makes additive changes breaking; strip is the right default for public
inputs.

**"What is a branded type and what does it cost?"** An intersection with a
phantom marker that only the parser can produce, giving nominal behaviour in a
structural type system. It costs nothing at runtime and is defeated by a cast,
so it prevents accidents rather than attacks.

## 8. Check yourself

1. Why is `const raw: unknown = JSON.parse(text)` better than letting the `any` flow?

# The long read: schemas, evidence, and the shape of a boundary

Static types describe a program's interior. The moment data crosses into that
interior from outside — a socket, a file, a form, another team's service — the
types stop describing anything and start *asserting* something. This essay is
about how the ecosystem arrived at the current answer to that problem, what the
answer costs, and where it stops working.

## A short history

The earliest TypeScript codebases handled boundaries with casts, because casts
were all there was. `const user = <User>JSON.parse(body)` was idiomatic in
2013. The obvious defect — that the cast was unchecked — was well understood
and generally tolerated, in the same spirit as `@ts-ignore`: a known gap, in
exchange for adoption.

The first serious response was **io-ts** (2017), which brought the Haskell/Scala
codec idea into TypeScript: a value that is simultaneously a runtime validator
and a static type, related by `t.TypeOf<typeof codec>`. It was correct, it was
principled, and it was hard to adopt, because its error handling used
`Either` from fp-ts and its type errors were long. It was right about the
mechanism and wrong about the ergonomics.

**Zod** (2020) kept the mechanism and rewrote the ergonomics: method chaining
instead of combinator application, exceptions or a `safeParse` result instead of
`Either`, and error messages designed for humans. It became the default
essentially at once, and its `z.infer` popularised the phrase "single source of
truth" for schemas.

Since then the field has split along axes rather than replacing the idea.
**Valibot** attacks bundle size by making every combinator a separate importable
function, so tree-shaking can discard what you do not use — a real difference on
a client where zod's chained API pulls in a large object. **ArkType** compiles
schemas to optimised validation functions and parses TypeScript-like syntax at
the type level. **Ajv** takes the other route entirely: JSON Schema, a
language-independent standard, compiled to JavaScript for speed, with types
bolted on afterwards — the right choice when the schema must be shared with
non-TypeScript consumers or published in an OpenAPI document. And in 2024 the
**Standard Schema** specification gave these libraries a common interface so
frameworks can accept any of them.

Knowing this map matters at design time. If your schema must be published,
JSON Schema wins. If bundle size dominates, valibot. If developer experience
dominates, zod. If you need three primitives and no dependency, the decoder in
this sector is about eighty lines and you have now written it.

## How the type derivation works underneath

Every one of those libraries does the same two things: a runtime object that
knows how to check, and a phantom type parameter that carries the result type.
In zod, `ZodString` extends `ZodType<string, ZodStringDef, string>`; the first
parameter is the output type, and `z.infer` is a conditional type that reads it
back out. In our decoder the phantom is the return type of the function, which
is simpler and slightly less capable — it cannot express input/output
divergence without a second parameter.

The mapped type over the shape is the part that makes nesting work. When you
write `object({ user: object({ name: string }) })`, the outer mapped type calls
`Infer` on the inner decoder, whose type is itself a mapped type, and
TypeScript resolves the whole tree lazily on demand. That laziness is why
schemas of a few hundred fields are usable at all, and its limits are why very
large schemas make editors slow: each hover forces a resolution, and the
resolved type is not cached across files in older versions.

## Performance, honestly

Parsing is not free, and teams do notice.

A hand-written decoder like the one in this sector runs a closure per field per
object. For a payload of a thousand objects with ten fields each, that is ten
thousand closure invocations plus ten thousand property writes — sub-millisecond
in practice, and irrelevant next to the network. The cost becomes visible at
different scales: parsing a 50 MB JSON export field by field can take seconds,
and doing it on the main thread of a browser will drop frames.

The mitigations, in the order worth trying: parse once at the boundary and pass
typed values inward; use a compiled validator (ajv compiles to specialised
JavaScript, and typia generates code at build time) when throughput matters;
stream instead of buffering for large files; and for genuinely enormous
untrusted data, validate structurally at the edge and refine lazily per record
as it is consumed.

The type-level cost is often the bigger one. A schema with a hundred fields,
several unions and a few generics can add hundreds of milliseconds to editor
responsiveness in that file. `tsc --generateTrace` will show it. The usual fix
is to annotate the derived type explicitly at the module boundary — write
`export type Order = { ... }` and `satisfies` the decoder against it — so
downstream files use the cheap annotation instead of re-resolving the
conditional chain.

## What parsing does not give you

It is worth being precise about the guarantees, because the phrase "type-safe
API" is oversold.

A parser proves that *this value, at this moment,* had this shape. It says
nothing about whether the shape is *correct* — a schema expecting `price:
number` will happily accept a price in the wrong currency. It says nothing
about consistency between fields unless you write a `refine`. It cannot survive
a later cast, a mutation, or an `any` reintroduced three modules downstream.
And it does not authenticate: a well-formed payload from an attacker is still
from an attacker.

There is also a subtler limit. Deriving types from schemas moves the source of
truth into the schema, which is excellent until you need to *publish* the
type — to another team, another language, another service. At that point the
schema is an implementation detail of one codebase and you need a shared
description: OpenAPI, JSON Schema, protobuf, or a shared package. Teams
frequently discover this a year in, and the migration is unpleasant. If you
know at the outset that the contract is cross-language, start from the shared
description and generate both the types and the validator.

One more limit deserves naming, because it surprises people who have just
adopted a schema library: parsing changes *when* a failure happens, not
*whether*. Before schemas, a malformed payload produced a `TypeError` deep in
business logic, hours of debugging away from its cause. After schemas, it
produces a clear failure at the door. That is an enormous improvement in
diagnosis and no improvement at all in availability — the request still fails.
Teams sometimes respond by making decoders lenient, coercing where they should
reject, and end up with the worst of both: the ceremony of a schema and the
uncertainty of no schema. If a field is genuinely optional, model it as
optional. If a default is genuinely correct, apply it explicitly. Do not teach
your parser to guess.

## When to stop

The discipline has a natural boundary: parse at the edge, once, into domain
types, and then trust the interior. Programs that parse defensively at every
layer are slow and, worse, they teach their authors that the types are not
believable, which erodes the value of having them. The interior of a program
should be a place where a `User` really is a `User` — and the way you get that
is a small number of well-guarded doors, not a checkpoint in every corridor.

exercises.prompt:
## ex1 — a decoder, and an error that says where

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Lay the foundation the rest of the sector builds on:

```ts
export type Decoder<T> = (value: unknown, path: string) => T;
export class DecodeError extends Error { readonly path: string; }
```

`new DecodeError("$.id", "expected a string, got number")` has
`message === "$.id: expected a string, got number"`, `name === "DecodeError"`,
and `path === "$.id"`.

Then four decoders and one factory:

- `decodeString: Decoder<string>`
- `decodeNumber: Decoder<number>` — rejects `NaN` and `±Infinity`
- `decodeInteger: Decoder<number>` — a finite number with no fractional part
- `decodeBoolean: Decoder<boolean>`
- `decodeLiteral<const L extends string | number | boolean>(literal: L): Decoder<L>`

Messages are asserted, so match them exactly:

- `decodeString(7, "$.name")` throws `$.name: expected a string, got number`
- `decodeString(null, "$.name")` throws `$.name: expected a string, got null`
- `decodeNumber([], "$")` throws `$: expected a finite number, got array`
- `decodeNumber(NaN, "$")` throws `$: expected a finite number, got NaN`
- `decodeInteger(1.5, "$.n")` throws `$.n: expected an integer, got 1.5`
- `decodeLiteral("gpt")( "gpt", "$.model")` → `"gpt"`, typed `"gpt"`
- `decodeLiteral("gpt")("other", "$.model")` throws
  `$.model: expected "gpt", got "other"`

Write one `describe(value: unknown): string` helper for the "got ..." half:
`null`, `array`, `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, and otherwise `typeof value`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate ex1
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with `describe`, because every message routes through it and the two
JavaScript warts in this sector both live there: `typeof null === "object"` and
`typeof NaN === "number"`. Getting those two special cases right first makes
the four decoders mechanical.

## Hint 2

`decodeLiteral` is the first generic in the sector, and it wants a `const` type
parameter for the same reason the route table did — without it,
`decodeLiteral("gpt")` is a `Decoder<string>` and the literal you cared about is
gone before the function returns.

## Hint 3

Note the shape of a decoder: `(value: unknown, path: string) => T`, annotated
on the *const*, not inferred from the arrow. Writing `export const decodeString:
Decoder<string> = (value, path) => {...}` means the two parameters are
contextually typed and you never write `unknown` by hand. That is the same
mechanism as the callbacks in the previous sector, pointed at a variable
declaration.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## ex2 — walking `unknown` without opening a hole

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Three functions that let you look inside a value you do
not trust:

```ts
export function isRecord(value: unknown): value is Record<string, unknown>
export function hasOwn<K extends string>(
  value: Record<string, unknown>,
  key: K,
): value is Record<string, unknown> & Record<K, unknown>
export function getPath(value: unknown, path: readonly (string | number)[]): unknown
```

- `isRecord({})` → `true`; `isRecord(null)` → `false`; `isRecord([])` → `false`;
  `isRecord(new Date())` → `true`
- `hasOwn({ a: 1 }, "a")` → `true`
- `hasOwn({}, "toString")` → `false` — this is the whole reason the function
  exists; `"toString" in {}` is `true`
- `hasOwn(Object.create(null) as Record<string, unknown>, "a")` → `false` and
  must not throw
- `getPath({ user: { tags: ["a", "b"] } }, ["user", "tags", 1])` → `"b"`
- `getPath({ user: {} }, ["user", "name"])` → `undefined`
- `getPath({ a: [1] }, ["a", "0"])` → `undefined` — a string segment never
  indexes an array
- `getPath({}, ["__proto__", "polluted"])` → `undefined`, always, even though
  `({}).__proto__` exists

Forbidden segments are `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`: `getPath`
returns `undefined` the moment it meets one.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`isRecord` needs three conditions in a specific order, and the order is forced
by a JavaScript wart you have met before: `typeof null === "object"`. Arrays are
objects too, so they need excluding explicitly if the rest of the sector is
going to treat "record" and "array" as different shapes.

## Hint 2

The safe own-property test does not use `in` and does not call the object's own
method:

```ts
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(value, key)
```

Calling `value.hasOwnProperty(key)` breaks for `Object.create(null)`, which has
no prototype and therefore no such method, and can be shadowed by a payload
that defines its own `hasOwnProperty`.

## Hint 3

`getPath` is a loop with a `let current: unknown = value`. Each iteration
decides based on the segment type: a `number` requires `Array.isArray(current)`
and an in-range index; a `string` requires `isRecord(current)` plus the
forbidden-key check plus `hasOwn`. Any failure returns `undefined` immediately.

Left to you: whether a negative numeric segment counts from the end. The gate
does not test it, so pick a behaviour and be consistent — but notice that
"undefined for anything out of range" is the option that cannot surprise a
caller.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The predicate signature on `hasOwn` is doing real work. Returning `value is
Record<string, unknown> & Record<K, unknown>` means that after the check, the
compiler knows `value[key]` exists, so downstream code reads it without a cast
and without optional chaining. A plain `boolean` return would compile and would
help nobody.

## Hint 2

Think about why the string/number distinction for segments is worth enforcing.
JavaScript makes `array["0"]` work, so a lax implementation cannot tell the
difference between "the first element" and "a property named 0" — and a payload
that supplies `{"0": "gotcha"}` where you expected an array then reads as valid.
Being strict here is a five-line cost with a real payoff.

## Hint 3

The forbidden list is not paranoia. Prototype pollution — reaching
`Object.prototype` through a `__proto__` segment in a path or a merge — has
produced critical advisories in widely used packages. `constructor` and
`prototype` are on the list because `x.constructor.prototype` is a second route
to the same object.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## ex3 — predicate, assertion, parser: three shapes for one job

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `Session` is `{ userId: string; expiresAt: number }`.
Write the same check three ways and notice what each one gives the caller:

```ts
export function isSession(value: unknown): value is Session
export function assertSession(value: unknown): asserts value is Session
export function parseSession(value: unknown): Session
export const assertSessionRef: (value: unknown) => asserts value is Session
```

Rules:

- `expiresAt` must be a finite integer; `userId` must be a non-empty string
- `isSession({ userId: "u1", expiresAt: 1 })` → `true`
- `isSession({ userId: "", expiresAt: 1 })` → `false`
- `assertSession({})` throws `TypeError: not a session`
- `parseSession({ userId: "u1", expiresAt: 1, isAdmin: true })` →
  `{ userId: "u1", expiresAt: 1 }` — a **new** object, the extra key gone
- `parseSession(7)` throws `TypeError: not a session`
- `assertSessionRef` is the same assertion assigned to a `const`; it must carry
  an explicit type annotation or narrowing silently stops working

The type gate checks all three narrowing behaviours: inside `if
(isSession(x))`, after `assertSession(x)`, and on the result of `parseSession`.
It also checks that `parseSession`'s result does **not** have an `isAdmin`
property in its type.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the predicate first and let the other two lean on it. `assertSession` is
`if (!isSession(value)) throw ...`. `parseSession` is the assertion followed by
construction of a fresh object — and the construction is the only one of the
three that changes the value.

## Hint 2

The `const` version needs its type written out, because TypeScript refuses to
apply an assertion whose target is not statically annotated:

```ts
export const assertSessionRef: (value: unknown) => asserts value is Session =
  assertSession;
```

Remove the annotation and the error is *"Assertions require every name in the
call target to be declared with an explicit type annotation"* — a real message
worth recognising on sight.

## Hint 3

After `assertSession(value)` inside `parseSession`, the compiler treats `value`
as `Session` for the rest of the function, so `return { userId: value.userId,
expiresAt: value.expiresAt }` needs no cast and no optional chaining.

Left to you: whether `parseSession` should reject a negative `expiresAt`. The
gate does not test it; deciding on purpose is the exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the compiler verifies about each signature. For the predicate it
checks only that `Session` and `unknown` are related — a body of `return true`
compiles. For the assertion it checks the same, plus that every code path
either returns or throws. Neither one proves the check is right. That is why
this sector ends with schemas: the predicate should be generated, not written.

## Hint 2

The ergonomics differ more than the types do. A predicate composes —
`sessions.filter(isSession)` narrows an array. An assertion reads as a
precondition and narrows for a whole block. A parser is the only shape that can
strip keys, convert a string to a `Date`, or attach a brand. Choose by what the
caller needs to do next.

## Hint 3

The `isAdmin` requirement is the point of the whole exercise. If `parseSession`
returns its input, the returned object still carries whatever the caller sent —
a privilege flag, an id belonging to someone else, a hundred kilobytes of junk
that will end up in your logs. Building the result is what makes it a boundary
rather than a comment.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## ex4 — the object combinator, and a type derived from it

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Bring `Decoder`, `DecodeError` and two primitive
decoders across from ex1 (they are short; retype them), then add the two pieces
that make a schema library:

```ts
export type Infer<D> = D extends Decoder<infer T> ? T : never;

export function object<S extends Record<string, Decoder<unknown>>>(
  shape: S,
): Decoder<{ [K in keyof S]: Infer<S[K]> }>
```

With

```ts
const decodeUser = object({
  id: decodeNumber,
  name: decodeString,
  address: object({ city: decodeString }),
});
type User = Infer<typeof decodeUser>;
```

- `User` is `{ id: number; name: string; address: { city: string } }` — written
  nowhere by hand
- `decodeUser({ id: 1, name: "ada", address: { city: "london" } }, "$")` returns
  an equal object
- `decodeUser({ id: 1, name: "ada", address: { city: "london" }, admin: true }, "$")`
  returns an object with **no** `admin` key — unknown keys are stripped
- `decodeUser({ id: 1, name: "ada", address: {} }, "$")` throws
  `$.address.city: expected a string, got undefined`
- `decodeUser([], "$")` throws `$: expected an object, got array`
- `decodeUser(null, "$")` throws `$: expected an object, got null`

Key order in the result follows the shape, not the input.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two independent halves. At runtime, iterate the *shape's* keys — not the
input's — and call each decoder on the corresponding property. At the type
level, the return type is a mapped type that runs `Infer` over the same shape.
Iterating the shape is what makes stripping automatic: unknown keys are never
visited.

## Hint 2

`Infer` is one conditional type reading the return type back out of a function
type:

```ts
type Infer<D> = D extends Decoder<infer T> ? T : never;
type A = Infer<typeof decodeString>;                 // string
type B = Infer<Decoder<{ city: string }>>;           // { city: string }
```

It composes with nesting for free, because the nested decoder's own type is
already a mapped type.

## Hint 3

`Object.keys(shape)` gives `string[]`, and TypeScript will not let you index a
generic `S` with a plain `string`. One assertion —
`Object.keys(shape) as Array<keyof S & string>` — buys you a checked
`shape[key]` for the whole loop.

Left to you: what the error path looks like for a missing key. The gate expects
`$.address.city: expected a string, got undefined`, which falls out if you pass
`source[key]` straight through rather than special-casing absence.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build the runtime part with a plain fixed shape first —
`{ id: decodeNumber }` typed concretely — and only then make it generic. Most
of the difficulty in this exercise is in the last step, and it is much easier to
see what the generic version must do when a working non-generic one is sitting
next to it.

## Hint 2

You will need exactly two assertions: one on `Object.keys`, and one on the
accumulator when you return it. If you find yourself adding a third, the loop
is probably reading the input's keys instead of the shape's.

## Hint 3

Watch the return assertion. Going from `Record<string, unknown>` to a generic
mapped type is not a relationship TypeScript can verify, so a single `as` will
be rejected as possibly mistaken and you need `as unknown as`. That is
uncomfortable, and it should be — it is the one place in the library where the
compiler is taking your word for it, which is exactly why it belongs in one
line of one function rather than at every call site.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## ex5 — arrays, modality and choice

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Retype the small preamble (`Decoder`, `Infer`,
`DecodeError`, `decodeString`, `decodeNumber`) and add four combinators:

```ts
export function array<T>(inner: Decoder<T>): Decoder<T[]>
export function optional<T>(inner: Decoder<T>): Decoder<T | undefined>
export function nullable<T>(inner: Decoder<T>): Decoder<T | null>
export function union<D extends readonly Decoder<unknown>[]>(
  ...decoders: D
): Decoder<Infer<D[number]>>
```

Behaviour:

- `array(decodeString)(["a", "b"], "$")` → `["a", "b"]`, typed `string[]`
- `array(decodeString)(["a", 2], "$")` throws
  `$[1]: expected a string, got number`
- `array(decodeString)("a", "$")` throws `$: expected an array, got string`
- `optional(decodeString)(undefined, "$.note")` → `undefined`
- `optional(decodeString)(null, "$.note")` **throws** — `null` is not absence
- `nullable(decodeNumber)(null, "$.age")` → `null`
- `union(decodeString, decodeNumber)(7, "$.id")` → `7`, typed `string | number`
- `union(decodeString, decodeNumber)(true, "$.id")` throws
  `$.id: no variant matched (expected a string, got boolean; expected a finite number, got boolean)`

Note the array path syntax: `$[1]`, not `$.1`. Note also that `union`'s failure
message lists every variant's reason, in order, with the paths removed.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each combinator takes a decoder and returns a decoder — that is the whole
pattern, and it is why they compose to arbitrary depth without any special
support. `array(object({ tags: array(decodeString) }))` works because nothing in
`array` knows what `inner` is.

## Hint 2

The path is where the value of this design shows up:

```ts
return items.map((item, index) => inner(item, `${path}[${index}]`));
```

An error twelve levels deep arrives with `$.orders[3].lines[0].sku` attached,
and nobody had to plumb anything.

## Hint 3

`union` needs a `try`/`catch` per variant, collecting the reasons. To strip the
path from a collected message, remember that `DecodeError` carries `path` as a
field, so the detail is the message with the `${path}: ` prefix removed — or,
more robustly, store the detail on the error too.

Left to you: whether `union` should try variants in order or attempt a
discriminant lookup first. Order works and is O(n); the challenge shows the
faster shape.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`optional` and `nullable` look interchangeable and are not. JSON has `null` and
JavaScript has both `null` and `undefined`, and a missing key reads as
`undefined` while an explicit `"note": null` reads as `null`. Deciding which
your API accepts is a contract decision; the gate's fifth case exists to make
you make it.

## Hint 2

The type of `union` is the interesting part. `D[number]` is the union of the
decoder types you passed, and `Infer` distributes across it because the checked
type is a naked type parameter — so `Infer<Decoder<string> | Decoder<number>>`
resolves to `string | number` rather than to `never`. Try writing `Infer` with
the parameter wrapped in a tuple and watch distribution stop.

## Hint 3

For the error text, work backwards from the assertion: the expected message
joins the variants' details with `"; "` inside parentheses. That means you need
the *detail* rather than the full message, which is a nudge to store both on
`DecodeError` — a small design change that pays for itself the first time you
render errors in a form.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## ex6 — report every problem, not the first

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. A form with four bad fields should not take four round
trips. Rebuild the object combinator so it accumulates:

```ts
export interface Issue { readonly path: string; readonly message: string }

export class DecodeError extends Error {
  readonly issues: readonly Issue[];
}

export type ParseResult<T> =
  | { readonly ok: true; readonly value: T }
  | { readonly ok: false; readonly issues: readonly Issue[] };

export function safeParse<T>(decoder: Decoder<T>, value: unknown): ParseResult<T>
export function objectAll<S extends Record<string, Decoder<unknown>>>(
  shape: S,
): Decoder<{ [K in keyof S]: Infer<S[K]> }>
```

`new DecodeError([{ path: "$.a", message: "x" }, { path: "$.b", message: "y" }])`
has `message === "$.a: x; $.b: y"`.

With `const decodeForm = objectAll({ email: decodeString, age: decodeInteger })`:

- `safeParse(decodeForm, { email: "a@b", age: 30 })` →
  `{ ok: true, value: { email: "a@b", age: 30 } }`
- `safeParse(decodeForm, { email: 7, age: "x" })` →
  `{ ok: false, issues: [{ path: "$.email", message: "expected a string, got number" },
  { path: "$.age", message: "expected a finite number, got string" }] }`
- `safeParse(decodeForm, null)` →
  `{ ok: false, issues: [{ path: "$", message: "expected an object, got null" }] }`
- Nested `objectAll`s merge: a failure two levels down appears once, with its
  full path, alongside failures from sibling fields

`safeParse` catches `DecodeError` only. Anything else — a bug inside a
decoder — propagates, because turning a programmer error into a validation
issue is how bugs get reported as user input problems.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The change is small and the consequences are not. Instead of letting the first
field's error escape, wrap each field's decode in a `try`, push whatever issues
come back into a list, and throw once at the end if the list is non-empty.

## Hint 2

Merging nested failures is the reason `DecodeError` carries an *array* rather
than a single path and message:

```ts
catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof DecodeError) issues.push(...error.issues);
  else throw error;
}
```

A nested `objectAll` throws one error containing several issues, and spreading
flattens the tree in one line.

## Hint 3

`safeParse` is the boundary between the throwing world and the value world.
Catch `DecodeError`, return `{ ok: false, issues: error.issues }`; on success
return `{ ok: true, value }`. Note the discriminant is a literal `true` and a
literal `false`, not `boolean` — otherwise nothing narrows.

Left to you: whether a field that throws should still contribute a key to the
partially built result. It cannot, and thinking about why is the reason the
whole operation has to fail rather than returning a half-object.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice which errors are values and which stay exceptions. A payload with a bad
email is *expected* — it is data, it deserves a structured issue list, and the
caller will render it. A `TypeError` from a bug inside a decoder is *not*
expected, and swallowing it into the issue array would show a user "cannot read
property of undefined" as though they had typed it.

## Hint 2

The `Issue` shape matters more than it looks. `{ path, message }` with a
JSONPath-ish string is directly consumable by form libraries, can be sent over
the wire, and sorts sensibly. Compare with a flat `string[]`, which forces the
consumer to parse your prose.

## Hint 3

If your nested failures arrive with truncated paths, the cause is almost always
that the inner decoder was called with `path` instead of `${path}.${key}`.
Build one deliberately-broken fixture with an error at `$.address.city` and a
sibling error at `$.email`, and check both appear, once each, in that order.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## ex7 — brands: parsed data that cannot be confused with raw data

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Two strings and a number that must never be swapped:

```ts
export type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly [brandKey]: B };
export type Email = Brand<string, "Email">;
export type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">;
export type PositiveInt = Brand<number, "PositiveInt">;

export function asEmail(value: unknown, path?: string): Email
export function asUserId(value: unknown, path?: string): UserId
export function asPositiveInt(value: unknown, path?: string): PositiveInt
export function localPart(email: Email): string
export function sendTo(email: Email, id: UserId): string
```

`path` defaults to `"$"`. Rules and behaviour:

- An email is a non-empty string with exactly one `@`, with something on each
  side of it, and no whitespace
- A user id matches `/^u_[0-9a-f]{8}$/`
- A positive integer is a finite integer strictly greater than zero
- `asEmail("ada@example.com")` → the same string, typed `Email`
- `asEmail("nope")` throws `TypeError: $: expected an email, got "nope"`
- `asPositiveInt(0, "$.qty")` throws `TypeError: $.qty: expected a positive integer, got 0`
- `localPart(asEmail("ada@example.com"))` → `"ada"`
- `sendTo(asUserId("u_0f1e2d3c"), asEmail("a@b.co"))` is a **compile error** —
  the arguments are the wrong way round, even though both are strings at runtime
- `localPart("ada@example.com")` is a **compile error**
- `localPart("ada@example.com" as Email)` compiles — say why in a comment

The brand key must be a module-private `unique symbol`, so no other module can
name it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A brand is an intersection with a property that exists only in the type system:

```ts
declare const brandKey: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly [brandKey]: B };
```

`declare const` means there is no runtime value — nothing is allocated, nothing
is wrapped, and `asEmail(x)` returns the very same string it received.

## Hint 2

Each `as*` function is a check plus a single assertion. The assertion is
justified by the check immediately above it, which is the same bargain the
whole sector runs on — but note that this one cannot be avoided, because there
is no way to *construct* a value carrying a phantom property.

## Hint 3

The last requirement is the honest one. `"x" as Email` compiles, because the
brand is a type-level marker and assertions bypass the type level by design. A
brand raises the cost of an accident; it is not a defence against someone who
means it.

Left to you: the email rule. The prompt gives a deliberately crude one. Real
email validation is a swamp — the practical advice is "one `@`, then send a
confirmation" — and encoding that reasoning in the comment is part of the
exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about why the string type alone is not enough. In a system with
`UserId`, `OrderId`, `Sku` and `Email` all typed `string`, every function that
takes two of them has a silent bug waiting: swap the arguments and nothing
complains. TypeScript is structural, so the only way to get nominal behaviour is
to add something structural that only one factory can produce.

## Hint 2

Compare the three implementations of nominal typing before you pick this one. A
class wrapper (`class Email { constructor(readonly value: string) {} }`) gives
real runtime identity and costs an allocation and an unwrap at every use. A
brand costs nothing and is defeated by a cast. An opaque type behind a module
boundary sits between the two. For ids flowing through a large codebase, brands
win on ergonomics by a wide margin.

## Hint 3

`sendTo(email: Email, id: UserId)` exists purely so the gate can prove the
swap is caught. When you test it by hand, notice the error message names the
brand strings — `"UserId"` is not assignable to `"Email"` — which is why the
second type parameter should be a readable name rather than a number.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## ex8 — optional keys that are genuinely optional

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `optional(decodeString)` produces `string | undefined`,
and a shape containing it produces `{ note: string | undefined }` — which
forces every caller to write `note: undefined` explicitly. Fix it at the type
level:

```ts
export type OptionalKeys<S> = ...
export type RequiredKeys<S> = ...
export type Shaped<S> = ...
export type Prettify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {};

export function object<S extends Record<string, Decoder<unknown>>>(
  shape: S,
): Decoder<Prettify<Shaped<S>>>
```

With `const decodeProfile = object({ name: decodeString, note: optional(decodeString) })`:

- `Infer<typeof decodeProfile>` is `{ name: string; note?: string | undefined }`
- `const p: Infer<typeof decodeProfile> = { name: "ada" }` compiles
- `const q: Infer<typeof decodeProfile> = { note: "hi" }` is a compile error
- `decodeProfile({ name: "ada" }, "$")` → `{ name: "ada" }`, and
  `Object.hasOwn(result, "note")` is `false` — the key is **absent**, not
  present-and-undefined
- `decodeProfile({ name: "ada", note: "hi" }, "$")` → `{ name: "ada", note: "hi" }`
- `decodeProfile({ note: "hi" }, "$")` throws
  `$.name: expected a string, got undefined`

Every field whose decoded type includes `undefined` becomes an optional key;
every other field stays required.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The trick is a mapped type that maps each key to itself or to `never`, then
indexes the result to collapse it into a union:

```ts
type KeysWhere<S> = { [K in keyof S]: Test<S[K]> extends true ? K : never }[keyof S];
```

`never` members vanish from a union, so what survives is exactly the keys that
passed.

## Hint 2

The test is `undefined extends Infer<S[K]>`, in that direction. You are asking
whether `undefined` is *one of the possibilities* for that field, and `string |
undefined` satisfies it while `string` does not. Writing it the other way round
(`Infer<S[K]> extends undefined`) asks whether the field is *only* undefined,
and gives you an empty set.

## Hint 3

`Shaped<S>` is an intersection of two mapped types — the required keys mapped
normally, the optional keys mapped with a `?` modifier. `Prettify` then flattens
the intersection so tooltips show one object instead of `A & B`.

Left to you: the runtime half. Omitting a key when its decoded value is
`undefined` is one line, and it is what makes `Object.hasOwn(result, "note")`
false. Decide whether an explicit `{ note: undefined }` in the input should
produce a present key — the gate does not test it, and both answers are
defensible.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build the type in a scratch file with a fixed shape before making it generic.
Write out `{ name: Decoder<string>; note: Decoder<string | undefined> }` by hand
and check that `OptionalKeys` on it is exactly `"note"`. Every later problem is
easier to see once that one case is proven.

## Hint 2

Two values behave badly in the `undefined extends X` test and both are worth
knowing. If a decoder's type is `any`, `undefined extends any` is true and the
key becomes optional. If it is `unknown`, the test is also true — `undefined` is
assignable to `unknown` — so an `unknown` field silently becomes optional. That
is a decent argument for never putting a bare `unknown` decoder into a shape
without wrapping it.

## Hint 3

`Prettify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] } & {}` looks like a no-op and is not: the
homomorphic mapped type preserves `?` and `readonly` while forcing the
intersection to be resolved, and the `& {}` prevents the alias being displayed
by name. If your tooltip still shows `Shaped<S>` rather than the fields, that
`& {}` is the missing piece.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a discriminated-union schema with a strict key policy (hard)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Two combinators and one worked schema.

```ts
export function strictObject<S extends Record<string, Decoder<unknown>>>(
  shape: S,
): Decoder<{ [K in keyof S]: Infer<S[K]> }>

export function variant<K extends string, C extends Record<string, Decoder<unknown>>>(
  tagKey: K,
  cases: C,
): Decoder<Infer<C[keyof C]>>
```

`strictObject` behaves like the stripping `object` from ex4 except that an
unknown key is an error rather than a silent removal:

- `strictObject({ id: decodeInteger })({ id: 1, extra: 2 }, "$")` throws
  `$: unexpected key "extra"`
- Several unexpected keys report the first in shape-independent input order

`variant` reads `tagKey` off the value, looks up the matching case decoder and
runs it — one lookup, not a linear scan through every variant:

- `variant("kind", cases)({ kind: "nope" }, "$")` throws
  `$.kind: expected one of "click", "key", "close", got "nope"`
- `variant("kind", cases)(7, "$")` throws `$: expected an object, got number`
- A body error keeps its own path: `{ kind: "click", x: "a", y: 0 }` throws
  `$.x: expected a finite number, got string`

Then build the schema and consume it:

```ts
export const decodeEvent = variant("kind", {
  click: strictObject({ kind: decodeLiteral("click"), x: decodeInteger, y: decodeInteger }),
  key:   strictObject({ kind: decodeLiteral("key"), code: decodeString }),
  close: strictObject({ kind: decodeLiteral("close") }),
});
export type AppEvent = Infer<typeof decodeEvent>;
export function render(event: AppEvent): string;
```

- `AppEvent` is the three-member discriminated union, written by hand nowhere
- `render` uses a `switch` on `kind` with an `assertNever` default
- `render({ kind: "click", x: 1, y: 2 })` → `"click at 1,2"`;
  `render({ kind: "key", code: "Escape" })` → `"key Escape"`;
  `render({ kind: "close" })` → `"close"`
- Add a fourth case to the schema and `render` must fail to compile

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`variant` is `union` with the linear scan replaced by a lookup. That is not
only faster; it is the reason the error message can be useful. A `union` that
tried three variants can only say "none matched, here are three reasons"; a
`variant` knows the tag was wrong and can name the ones it accepts.

## Hint 2

The return type is simpler than it looks:

```ts
Decoder<Infer<C[keyof C]>>
```

`C[keyof C]` is the union of the case decoders, and `Infer` distributes across
it, so the result is the union of what they produce. Because each case is a
`strictObject` containing a `decodeLiteral` for the tag, that union is a proper
discriminated union and `switch` narrows it.

## Hint 3

For `strictObject`, decode the known keys exactly as `object` does, then
compare the input's own keys against the shape's. `Object.keys(source).find((key)
=> !Object.hasOwn(shape, key))` is the check; report the first one found.

Left to you: whether the unexpected-key check runs before or after the field
decoding. Running it first means a payload with both problems reports the
unexpected key; running it last means it reports the bad field. Pick one, and
notice that the gate's fixtures only ever have one problem at a time — real
schemas should be less forgiving of that ambiguity than the gate is.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the consumer and work backwards. `render` needs `event.kind` to be a
literal in each branch, which means each case decoder must produce a literal
`kind`, which means `decodeLiteral` must keep its literal type, which means it
needs a `const` type parameter. If the union collapses to `{ kind: string; ...
}`, that chain broke somewhere and the first place to look is the literal.

## Hint 2

The `assertNever` default is what makes the last requirement work:

```ts
function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`unhandled variant: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}
```

Add a fourth case to the schema and the union grows; the `switch` then leaves a
member unhandled, the default's argument is no longer `never`, and the error
names exactly the variant you forgot. That is a compile-time to-do list
generated by a runtime schema.

## Hint 3

Think about which policy you would ship. Strict is excellent between services
you own — a typo in a client's field name becomes a loud failure instead of a
silently ignored setting. On a public API it is hostile: adding an optional
field to a request becomes a breaking change for every caller that sends it
early. Most teams end up strict internally and stripping at the edge, and being
able to justify that split is the point of implementing both.

exercises.prompt:
## Review — a webhook that arrives as text and leaves as a domain object

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Same discipline, new angle: this time the parser
*transforms*, so the wire format and the domain type are different types.

Implement three combinators and one schema:

```ts
export function refine<T>(inner: Decoder<T>, predicate: (value: T) => boolean, message: string): Decoder<T>
export function map<A, B>(inner: Decoder<A>, transform: (value: A) => B): Decoder<B>
export function enumOf<const V extends readonly string[]>(values: V): Decoder<V[number]>
export const decodeIsoDate: Decoder<Date>
export const decodeWebhook: Decoder<Webhook>
export type Webhook = Infer<typeof decodeWebhook>;
export function parseWebhook(body: string): Webhook
```

`Webhook` must come out as
`{ id: string; type: "order.created" | "order.cancelled"; occurredAt: Date; totalCents: number }`.

- `decodeIsoDate("2024-03-01T09:30:00.000Z", "$.at")` → a `Date`, and the
  round trip `date.toISOString()` equals the input
- `decodeIsoDate("2024-02-31T00:00:00.000Z", "$.at")` throws
  `$.at: expected an ISO date, got "2024-02-31T00:00:00.000Z"` — `Date.parse`
  rolls that over to 2 March, and a parser must not accept a date it would
  print differently
- `decodeIsoDate("yesterday", "$.at")` throws with the same message shape
- `enumOf(["a", "b"])("c", "$.t")` throws `$.t: expected one of "a", "b", got "c"`
- `refine(decodeInteger, (n) => n >= 0, "expected a non-negative integer")` on
  `-1` throws `$.totalCents: expected a non-negative integer, got -1`
- `parseWebhook('{"id":"evt_1","type":"order.created","occurredAt":"2024-03-01T09:30:00.000Z","totalCents":1250}')`
  → the domain object, with `occurredAt instanceof Date` true
- `parseWebhook("not json")` throws a `DecodeError` at `$`, not a `SyntaxError`

`parseWebhook` is the only function in the file that touches `JSON.parse`, and
the value it produces is `unknown` before anything else happens to it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb02_parse_dont_validate review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`refine` and `map` differ in one word. `refine` runs a predicate and returns the
*same* value with the same type; `map` runs a transform and returns a
*different* type. Everything else in this exercise is built from those two plus
the combinators you already have.

## Hint 2

The date check is the interesting one, and the trick is a round trip:

```ts
const date = new Date(text);
if (Number.isNaN(date.getTime()) || date.toISOString() !== text) throw ...;
```

`new Date("2024-02-31T00:00:00.000Z")` is a valid `Date` — it is 2 March — so
validity alone is not enough. Comparing the canonical form catches rollovers,
missing timezones and sloppy separators in one line.

## Hint 3

`parseWebhook` is three statements: `JSON.parse` inside a `try` that rethrows as
a `DecodeError` at `$`, an assignment to a variable annotated `unknown`, and a
call to `decodeWebhook(raw, "$")`.

Left to you: whether `enumOf` should be built on `union(...values.map(literal))`
or written directly with a `Set`. The second gives a better error message and
is O(1); the first is two lines. Try both and read the failures.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice what this exercise proves that ex4 could not. Once a decoder transforms,
the input type and the output type are different, and `Infer` only tells you
about the output. That is exactly why zod exposes `z.input` and `z.output`
separately, and why a schema used for *both* validating a request and
serialising a response needs two types, not one.

## Hint 2

Build `decodeWebhook` bottom-up and check the derived type at each step by
hovering `Infer<typeof decodeWebhook>`. If `occurredAt` shows as `string`, the
`map` is missing; if `type` shows as `string`, the `enumOf` lost its literals
and the `const` type parameter is the place to look.

## Hint 3

The `parseWebhook("not json")` case is a small but real design statement. A
caller of your boundary should have to handle exactly one failure type. Letting
a `SyntaxError` escape means every call site needs two `catch` branches, and the
one for malformed JSON will be the one nobody writes.

lessons.title: V3·TB3 — Result types, error modelling and the cost of throwing
lessons.summary: TypeScript has no checked exceptions, so a function's failures are invisible in its type. Result types make them visible: the failure becomes a value the caller cannot ignore, with a union you can exhaustively handle. This sector builds the whole toolkit, and argues honestly about when to keep throwing.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·TB3 — Result types, error modelling and the cost of throwing

Look at this signature and say what can go wrong:

```ts
declare function loadUser(id: string): Promise<User>;
```

You cannot. The type says it produces a `User`; it does not say that the id
might be malformed, that the row might be missing, that the database might time
out, or that a bug in the driver might throw a `TypeError`. Java had checked
exceptions and people hated them. TypeScript has nothing at all: `throw` is
invisible to the type system, and `catch` gives you `unknown`.

That is not an argument for never throwing. It is an argument for deciding,
per failure, whether it is **expected** — part of the contract, something a
caller will handle — or **exceptional** — a bug, an invariant violation, an
unrecoverable state. Expected failures belong in the return type. Exceptional
ones belong in a `throw`, where they will travel up to whatever handles
catastrophes.

```ts
declare function loadUser(id: string): Promise<Result<User, NotFound | Timeout>>;
```

Now the caller can see the failures, cannot read the user without handling
them, and gets a compile error when a new failure mode is added to the union.

## Concept — Result is a discriminated union, and the discriminant is literal

You met the shape in the unions sector. The full version has two type
parameters:

```ts
export interface Ok<T> { readonly ok: true; readonly value: T }
export interface Err<E> { readonly ok: false; readonly error: E }
export type Result<T, E> = Ok<T> | Err<E>;
```

Both variants pin `ok` to a *literal*, which is what makes `if (result.ok)`
narrow. Write `ok: boolean` in both and everything still compiles and nothing
narrows — the single most instructive mistake in this territory.

The constructors deserve their odd-looking types:

```ts
export const ok = <T,>(value: T): Result<T, never> => ({ ok: true, value });
export const err = <E,>(error: E): Result<never, E> => ({ ok: false, error });
```

`never` is right because `ok(1)` genuinely cannot carry an error. It works
because `never` is assignable to everything, so `Result<number, never>` fits
anywhere a `Result<number, string>` is wanted. If you write `unknown` there
instead, every call site has to widen by hand.

## Concept — model errors as data, not as a class hierarchy

The instinct from other languages is a tree of error classes. In TypeScript the
better default is a discriminated union of plain objects:

```ts
type AppError =
  | { code: "not_found"; resource: string; id: string }
  | { code: "forbidden"; action: string }
  | { code: "timeout"; ms: number }
  | { code: "invalid"; issues: readonly string[] };
```

Four advantages over subclassing `Error`. It is exhaustively checkable, so
adding `code: "rate_limited"` produces compile errors everywhere you handle
errors. It survives serialisation — an `Error` subclass sent through
`JSON.stringify`, a worker `postMessage`, or a server boundary arrives as a
plain object with the class gone. It carries *per-variant* data with no
optional fields. And it avoids the `instanceof` cross-realm problem entirely.

What you give up is a stack trace, and that matters. The pragmatic compromise
most codebases land on: unions for expected failures, `Error` objects (with
`cause`) for the unexpected ones, and a `normalizeError(unknown): Error` at
every `catch`.

## Concept — the combinators, and the two ways to combine failures

A `Result` is only pleasant to use if you rarely have to open it. Five
functions do most of the work:

```ts
map(result, fn)          // change the value, keep the error
mapErr(result, fn)       // change the error, keep the value
andThen(result, fn)      // run another fallible step: Result<U, E | F>
orElse(result, fn)       // recover
match(result, handlers)  // collapse to one type
```

`andThen` is the one to understand: it *widens the error union*, which is
exactly what you want, because a pipeline of three fallible steps really can
fail in three ways and the type should say so.

Combining several results splits into two different operations, and confusing
them is a design bug rather than a coding one. **Short-circuit** (`all`) stops
at the first error — right for sequential dependencies. **Accumulate**
(`allSettled`, validation-style) collects every error — right for forms and
config, where showing the user one problem at a time is a bad experience. The
functional-programming names for these are the monadic and applicative
combinations; you do not need the vocabulary, but you do need the distinction.

## The trap

The trap is doing this halfway. A codebase where some functions return
`Result` and others throw, with no rule about which, is worse than either
discipline alone: callers must handle both, and they will forget one. Pick a
boundary — usually "the domain layer returns Results, the transport layer
translates them into HTTP responses, and everything unexpected throws" — and
hold it.

There is also a guarantee people claim that does not exist. TypeScript has no
equivalent of Rust's `#[must_use]`, so calling a `Result`-returning function as
a bare statement and dropping the value compiles without complaint. The
compiler stops you *reading* a success you have not proved; it does not stop
you ignoring the whole thing. Lint rules and review close that gap, and it is
worth knowing which half of the promise is enforced by the machine.

The second trap is ceremony. `Result` costs you a wrapper at every step, and
TypeScript has no `?` operator to make it disappear. If a function has exactly
one failure mode and every caller wants to give up, `throw` may genuinely be
the better tool. The exercises below build the whole apparatus; the reading
argues, at length, about when not to use it.

# Reading - typescript/v3tb03_result_error_modelling

Notes on the mechanism, on variance, on async, and on the honest costs.

## Notes

**`catch` gives you `unknown`, and that is `strict`'s doing.**
`useUnknownInCatchVariables` (on under `strict` since 4.4) types the catch
binding as `unknown` rather than `any`, because JavaScript can throw anything —
a string, `undefined`, a `Symbol`, a frozen object. Every `catch` therefore
needs a normalisation step before the value is useful. Code that reads
`error.message` in a catch without checking is one `throw "boom"` away from a
second exception inside the handler.

**`never` in the constructors is a variance argument.** `Result<T, E>` is
covariant in both parameters, so `Result<number, never>` is assignable to
`Result<number, AppError>`, and `ok(1)` slots into any position expecting a
richer error type. The same reasoning explains why `err(e)` is `Result<never,
E>`. Try writing the constructors with `unknown` and watch every call site
sprout an explicit type argument.

**`andThen` grows the error union on purpose.** `andThen<T, E, U, F>(r:
Result<T, E>, fn: (v: T) => Result<U, F>): Result<U, E | F>` — the result can
fail the first way or the second way. In a four-step pipeline this produces a
four-member union, which is precisely the documentation you want. If the union
becomes unwieldy, that is a signal to `mapErr` intermediate steps into a common
domain error, not a signal to widen to `Error`.

**Short-circuit versus accumulate.** `all(results): Result<T[], E>` returns the
first error and discards the rest. `allSettled(results): Result<T[], E[]>`
returns every error. A form validator that short-circuits will annoy users four
times; a database pipeline that accumulates will run steps that had no business
running. The operation you want depends on whether the steps are independent.

**Async: `Promise<Result<T, E>>`, not a rejected promise.** A rejected promise
is a `throw` with extra steps: the failure is invisible in the type, the
`catch` binding is `unknown`, and `Promise.all` short-circuits in a way you
often do not want. Returning `Promise<Result<T, E>>` keeps expected failures in
the type. The cost is `await` plus a narrowing at every step, which is why
`andThenAsync` earns its place. Note that `Promise.all` over `AsyncResult`s
waits for everything — you cannot cancel work that is already in flight — so
"first error wins" means first *by index*, not first by time, unless you use
`Promise.race`.

**`Error.cause` is the underused feature.** `new Error("could not load user",
{ cause: original })` preserves the chain without stringifying it, and Node
prints the whole chain. It landed in ES2022 and in Node 16.9; use it instead of
`new Error(original.message)`, which throws away the stack of the thing that
actually failed.

**`instanceof Error` fails across realms.** In an iframe, a worker, or Node's
`vm` module, there are two `Error` constructors and an error from the other
side fails `instanceof`. Library code hedges with a structural check. This is
one more argument for modelling expected errors as data.

## ex1 — errors as a union with an exhaustive handler

`matchError(error, handlers)` typed as `{ [K in Code]: (e: Extract<AppError,
{ code: K }>) => R }` is the pattern worth memorising: the handler map is a
mapped type over the discriminant, so omitting one is a compile error and each
handler receives the *narrowed* variant. The one cast in the implementation —
looking up a handler by a runtime tag — is unavoidable and is the same cast
every state machine library contains.

## ex2 — the core, and why `unwrapOr` must not use `??`

The gate checks `unwrapOr(ok(0), 99)` and `unwrapOr(ok(undefined), 5)` for the
same reason the previous volume did: the decision belongs to the discriminant,
never to the truthiness or nullishness of the value. Type predicates `isOk` and
`isErr` exist because `filter` cannot narrow without them.

## ex3 — combinators

Four small functions, and the interesting one is `orElse`, whose type is the
mirror image of `andThen`: it widens the *value* union and replaces the error.
Getting the two type signatures the right way round is most of the exercise.

## ex4 — combining a collection, and combining a record

`all` is a loop with an early return. `allObject` is the same idea over a
record, and its type needs two helper conditional types that read the value and
error out of a `Result`. They must be written to distribute — `R extends { ok:
true; value: infer T } ? T : never` — so the `Err` half of each union
contributes `never` and vanishes.

## ex5 — accumulate

The switch from short-circuit to accumulate is four lines of implementation and
a different API contract. Note the return type `Result<T[], E[]>`: a failure
carries *several* errors, which is why the error type parameter is an array
rather than a union.

## ex6 — meeting the throwing world

`fromThrowable` wraps a function; `fromPromise` wraps a promise;
`normalizeError` turns the `unknown` from a `catch` into an `Error` you can
log. The subtlety is that `fromThrowable` must not swallow *everything* in real
code — a `RangeError` from your own bug should probably not become a domain
failure — but at a library boundary, converting once and classifying afterwards
is the practical choice.

## ex7 and ex8 — async, and a growing error union

`andThenAsync` is `andThen` with two `await`s, and the type is identical. The
pipeline in ex8 is where the sector's argument becomes visible: after three
steps the return type names all three failure modes, an exhaustive `match`
handles them, and adding a fourth step breaks the handler at compile time.

## challenge and review1

The challenge is the full boundary: parse, authorise, load, render, then
translate the error union into HTTP status codes exhaustively. The review comes
at the same ideas from the side-effect direction — a small transaction that
must roll back completed steps when a later one fails, which is where "errors
as values" stops being a style preference and starts being a correctness tool.

## Further reading

- [Rust book: recoverable errors with `Result`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors-with-result.html) — the design this pattern is borrowed from, including the `?` operator TypeScript lacks.
- [neverthrow](https://github.com/supermacro/neverthrow) — the most widely used TypeScript implementation; read its `ResultAsync` for the async shape.
- [MDN: `Error.cause`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Error/cause) — chaining errors without losing stacks.
- [TypeScript 4.4 release notes: `useUnknownInCatchVariables`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-4.html) — why your catch bindings changed type.
- [Effect](https://effect.website/) — the maximalist version: typed errors, dependencies and interruption in one effect type, and a good place to see where this road ends.
