# V3·TB3 — Result types and error modelling (archive)

The deep version: the taxonomy, the full API, async, interop, HTTP mapping,
costs, and a self-test bank.

## 1. A taxonomy of failure

Before choosing a mechanism, classify the failure. Three buckets cover almost
everything:

**Expected domain failures.** The user does not exist. The password is wrong.
The order is already cancelled. These are part of the contract; every caller
must decide what to do; they belong in the return type.

**Environmental failures.** The database is down. The network timed out. The
disk is full. Recoverable in principle, usually with a retry, and usually
handled at one layer rather than at every call site. Either bucket works; the
deciding question is whether the *immediate* caller can do something useful.

**Programmer errors.** A null that the types said could not be null. An
exhaustive switch that was not. An invariant broken by a bad refactor. These
should `throw`, loudly, and be reported to your error tracker. Turning them
into values means somebody will handle them politely and ship the bug.

The single most common mistake in this area is putting bucket three into
bucket one, which produces a program that carefully returns
`{ ok: false, error: "something went wrong" }` while a stack trace that would
have found the bug is discarded.

## 2. The API, in full

```ts
interface Ok<T> { readonly ok: true; readonly value: T }
interface Err<E> { readonly ok: false; readonly error: E }
type Result<T, E> = Ok<T> | Err<E>;

// construction
ok<T>(value: T): Result<T, never>
err<E>(error: E): Result<never, E>

// interrogation
isOk<T, E>(r: Result<T, E>): r is Ok<T>
isErr<T, E>(r: Result<T, E>): r is Err<E>

// extraction
unwrapOr<T, E>(r: Result<T, E>, fallback: T): T
unwrapOrElse<T, E>(r: Result<T, E>, recover: (e: E) => T): T
expect<T, E>(r: Result<T, E>, message: string): T           // throws

// transformation
map<T, E, U>(r: Result<T, E>, fn: (v: T) => U): Result<U, E>
mapErr<T, E, F>(r: Result<T, E>, fn: (e: E) => F): Result<T, F>
andThen<T, E, U, F>(r: Result<T, E>, fn: (v: T) => Result<U, F>): Result<U, E | F>
orElse<T, E, U, F>(r: Result<T, E>, fn: (e: E) => Result<U, F>): Result<T | U, F>

// combination
all<T, E>(rs: readonly Result<T, E>[]): Result<T[], E>          // short-circuit
allSettled<T, E>(rs: readonly Result<T, E>[]): Result<T[], E[]> // accumulate
partition<T, E>(rs: readonly Result<T, E>[]): { values: T[]; errors: E[] }

// interop
fromThrowable<A extends readonly unknown[], T>(fn: (...a: A) => T): (...a: A) => Result<T, Error>
fromPromise<T>(p: Promise<T>): Promise<Result<T, Error>>
toPromise<T, E>(r: Result<T, E>): Promise<T>
```

Twenty functions, none longer than five lines. That is the entire library, and
writing it once is why using someone else's stops feeling like magic.

## 3. Worked example: a request handler

```ts
type HandlerError =
  | { code: "bad_request"; issues: readonly string[] }
  | { code: "unauthorised" }
  | { code: "not_found"; id: string }
  | { code: "conflict"; reason: string };

function handle(raw: unknown, session: Session): Result<Response, HandlerError> {
  return andThen(parseBody(raw), (body) =>
    andThen(authorise(session, body), (actor) =>
      map(loadOrder(body.orderId, actor), (order) => render(order)),
    ),
  );
}

function toHttp(result: Result<Response, HandlerError>): { status: number; body: unknown } {
  if (result.ok) return { status: 200, body: result.value };
  switch (result.error.code) {
    case "bad_request":  return { status: 400, body: { issues: result.error.issues } };
    case "unauthorised": return { status: 401, body: {} };
    case "not_found":    return { status: 404, body: { id: result.error.id } };
    case "conflict":     return { status: 409, body: { reason: result.error.reason } };
    default:             return assertNever(result.error);
  }
}
```

Two properties are worth noticing. The status-code mapping is exhaustive, so a
new error variant fails the build until somebody decides what status it
deserves. And `handle` cannot forget to handle a failure, because there is no
way to reach `result.value` without narrowing.

The nesting is the ugly part, and it is the honest cost. Rust writes this with
`?`. TypeScript's nearest equivalents are a fluent wrapper class with `.andThen`
methods, generator-based `do` notation (what Effect provides), or simply early
returns:

```ts
const body = parseBody(raw);
if (!body.ok) return body;
const actor = authorise(session, body.value);
if (!actor.ok) return actor;
```

That version is longer, flatter and, in most teams, the one people actually
read. Note that `return body` type-checks: `Result<Body, BadRequest>` narrowed
to `Err<BadRequest>` is assignable to the wider return type.

## 4. Async

```ts
type AsyncResult<T, E> = Promise<Result<T, E>>;

async function andThenAsync<T, E, U, F>(
  r: AsyncResult<T, E>,
  fn: (v: T) => AsyncResult<U, F>,
): AsyncResult<U, E | F> {
  const awaited = await r;
  return awaited.ok ? fn(awaited.value) : awaited;
}
```

Three async-specific points:

- `Promise.all` over `AsyncResult`s never rejects on a domain failure, so you
  get every result and choose which error to report. That is usually better
  than rejection, but it also means no cancellation: work already started keeps
  running. If you need to stop early, you need an `AbortController`, not a
  combinator.
- An `async` function that returns `Result` can still reject. Wrapping the body
  in `fromPromise` at the outermost layer is what makes the signature honest.
- Do not build `Promise<Result<T, E>>` and then `throw` inside it "for
  convenience". Half a discipline is worse than none.

## 5. Costs, stated plainly

- **Ceremony.** Every fallible call needs unwrapping. In a codebase without a
  fluent API this is genuinely more code.
- **No stack traces** unless the error variant carries one. Add a `cause` field
  to environmental errors.
- **Interop friction.** Every library you use throws. The boundary functions in
  ex6 are mandatory, not optional.
- **Type noise in tooltips.** A five-step pipeline's error union is a wall of
  text on hover. `mapErr` into a domain error at layer boundaries.
- **Team cost.** It is a convention; conventions need enforcement. A lint rule
  banning `throw` outside a designated module is worth more than a style guide
  paragraph.

## 6. Interview answers

**"Why not just use exceptions?"** Because TypeScript has no checked
exceptions, so a throwing function's failure modes are invisible in its type
and cannot be exhaustively handled. Results move expected failures into the
return type, where the compiler enforces handling.

**"Should everything return a Result?"** No. Expected, per-call-site failures
should. Programmer errors and unrecoverable states should throw, so they reach
your error tracker with a stack.

**"Why is `ok()` typed `Result<T, never>`?"** Because a success carries no
error, and `never` is assignable to every type, so the value fits wherever a
richer error type is expected without an explicit type argument.

**"Difference between `all` and `allSettled` here?"** Short-circuit versus
accumulate. Use short-circuit when the steps depend on each other, accumulate
when they are independent and the caller wants every problem at once.

**"What is `catch (e)` typed as, and why?"** `unknown`, under
`useUnknownInCatchVariables`, because JavaScript can throw any value. Normalise
before use.

## 7. Common mistakes

- `ok: boolean` in both variants, so nothing narrows.
- `unwrapOr` implemented with `??` or `||`.
- Catching `unknown` and reading `.message` without a check.
- Mixing throwing and Result-returning APIs with no boundary rule.
- Using `Result` for programmer errors, so bugs are swallowed politely.
- `new Error(original.message)` instead of `{ cause: original }`.
- `instanceof MyError` across a worker or iframe boundary.
- An error union so wide (`Result<T, Error>`) that exhaustiveness buys nothing.
- Accumulating errors for steps that were sequentially dependent, so later
  errors are just noise from work that should not have run.

## 8. Check yourself

1. Why does `ok: boolean` break narrowing, and what is the fix?
2. Why is `ok<T>(value: T): Result<T, never>` better than `Result<T, unknown>`?
3. Give the exact type of `andThen` and explain the `E | F`.
4. When is short-circuiting the wrong combination strategy?
5. What is `catch (e)` typed as under `strict`, and what must you do first?
6. Name two things an error union gives you that an `Error` subclass tree does not.
7. Name one thing the subclass tree gives you that the union does not.
8. Why does `Promise.all` over `AsyncResult`s not cancel in-flight work?
9. How do you write an exhaustive HTTP status mapping that fails the build when a new error is added?
10. When would you deliberately throw in a Result-based codebase?
11. What does `Error.cause` do that string concatenation does not?
12. Why does `instanceof Error` sometimes return false for a genuine error?

# The long read: what "errors as values" really costs and really buys

The debate about exceptions is older than JavaScript. It is worth understanding
the history, because most of the arguments people have about `Result` in
TypeScript were already had, with better data, about other languages.

## Where the idea comes from

Exceptions arrived in mainstream languages as an answer to a real problem: C's
convention of returning an error code was easy to ignore, and ignoring it was
the default. Exceptions made failure impossible to ignore *accidentally* — an
unhandled one terminates the program — at the cost of making control flow
invisible.

Java tried to have both with checked exceptions: the compiler forces you to
handle or declare. The experiment is widely judged a failure, and the reasons
are instructive. Checked exceptions did not compose with generics or with
lambdas; the standard library declared exceptions too coarsely; and the escape
hatch, wrapping everything in `RuntimeException`, was so much easier than doing
it properly that it became the norm. C# looked at all this and deliberately
omitted checked exceptions.

The functional lineage went the other way. ML and Haskell modelled failure as
an ordinary value — `option`, `Either`, `Result` — with the language providing
enough syntax that unwrapping is not painful. Rust's `Result` plus the `?`
operator is the version most TypeScript engineers have met: failure is in the
type, exhaustively matchable, and one character of syntax propagates it.

TypeScript sits awkwardly between these worlds. It has the union types to
express `Result` beautifully and none of the syntax to make it ergonomic. That
tension explains everything about how the pattern is used in practice: it is
excellent at boundaries, tiring in the middle of a function, and it lives or
dies on whether the team agrees where the boundary is.

## What the type system can and cannot enforce

A `Result` gives you three real guarantees.

You cannot read the success value without narrowing, so a failure cannot be
silently ignored — the compiler stops you at the property access. You get
exhaustiveness: with `assertNever` in a `default` branch, adding an error
variant produces a compile error at every handler. And the failure modes are
*documented in the signature*, which is worth as much as either guarantee when
someone new reads the code.

What it cannot do is stop you dropping the whole result on the floor.
`doThing()` as a statement, ignoring the returned `Result`, compiles fine.
TypeScript has no `#[must_use]`. The mitigations are lint rules
(`no-floating-promises` has a cousin for this in several plugins) and code
review. Do not claim the guarantee you do not have.

It also cannot stop a `throw` from inside a function that returns a `Result`.
Any library you call can throw; `JSON.parse` throws; a getter can throw. A
function whose signature says `Result<T, E>` and whose body calls unwrapped
third-party code is telling a small lie, and the fix is a `try` at that call,
not optimism.

## Performance

This comes up and it is mostly a non-issue, but the details are worth knowing.

Allocating a `{ ok: true, value }` object per call is cheap — these are
short-lived objects in the nursery, exactly the case generational garbage
collectors are optimised for — but it is not free, and in a hot loop over a
million items you can measure it. The usual fix is to keep the loop body
throwing (or returning a sentinel) and to wrap once at the outside.

Exceptions, meanwhile, are cheap to *set up* and expensive to *use*. `try`
blocks cost almost nothing when nothing throws; V8 has long since stopped
deoptimising functions that contain them. Capturing a stack trace is the
expensive part — `new Error()` walks frames — which is why an error-per-item
validation loop that constructs `Error` objects can be an order of magnitude
slower than one returning plain objects. If you are building thousands of
errors, build data, not `Error`s.

Async adds one more consideration. `Promise<Result<T, E>>` allocates a promise
and a result object; a rejected promise allocates a promise and an error with a
stack. For very high throughput services the Result version is usually the
cheaper one, which surprises people who expect the "functional" option to cost
more.

## When not to use it

Some honest cases for staying with exceptions.

**Scripts and one-off tools.** If the answer to every failure is "print
something and exit", throwing is shorter and just as safe.

**Deeply nested pure computation.** If a failure ten frames down should abort
the whole operation and nothing in between can do anything useful, an exception
is the correct control-flow construct — that is what it is for.

**Framework boundaries you do not control.** React error boundaries, Express
error middleware, and test frameworks are all built around throwing. Fighting
them buys nothing.

**Invariants.** `assertNever`, `invariant(cond, msg)` and friends should throw.
A violated invariant means the program's model of the world is wrong, and
continuing carefully is worse than stopping.

**When the team will not maintain it.** A half-adopted convention where callers
must handle both mechanisms is measurably worse than either one applied
consistently. If you cannot get agreement, pick exceptions plus a strict
normalisation layer and spend the effort elsewhere.

## The migration problem

Nobody adopts this on a green field. The realistic situation is a codebase of
throwing functions and a team that wants typed errors, and the way that goes
well is bottom-up and boundary-first. Pick one module whose failures are
genuinely part of its contract — an authentication check, a payment call, a
parser — and convert only it, exposing `fromPromise` and `toPromise` shims at
both edges so callers are unaffected. The module's tests get shorter, because
asserting on a returned value beats asserting that a call rejects with the
right shape. Then convert the module that calls it, and delete a shim.

Two failure patterns are worth naming so you can spot them early. The first is
converting the *leaves* — small utilities that everything calls — which floods
every call site with unwrapping and produces a revolt before any benefit shows.
The second is converting the *transport* layer first, which gives you a
`Result` whose error type is `Error` and therefore no exhaustiveness at all;
the value is in the domain union, not in the wrapper. Start where the failure
modes are interesting and few, and let the discipline spread outward from
there.

## Where the road ends

Once a codebase has typed errors, the next questions arrive quickly: what about
dependencies, cancellation, retries, resource cleanup, and tracing? Libraries
like Effect answer all of them with one type — an effect that carries its
success type, its error type and its requirements — and the result is powerful,
coherent, and a substantial commitment. It is worth reading even if you never
adopt it, because it shows what the pattern in this sector looks like taken to
its conclusion, and because it makes the tradeoff explicit: everything the type
system knows, it knows because you told it, and telling it takes time.

The moderate position, and the one most production TypeScript ends up at, is
this. Model expected failures as a small union per module. Return `Result` from
domain functions. Translate to exceptions exactly once, at the framework
boundary. Normalise every `catch`. Throw for bugs. Keep the error unions narrow
enough that exhaustive handling is a help rather than a chore. That is not a
philosophy; it is a set of habits, and it is what the next ten missions install.

## ex1 — errors as data, handled exhaustively

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Model the failures of a small service as a union, then
build a handler map the compiler checks:

```ts
export type AppError =
  | { readonly code: "not_found"; readonly resource: string; readonly id: string }
  | { readonly code: "forbidden"; readonly action: string }
  | { readonly code: "timeout"; readonly ms: number }
  | { readonly code: "invalid"; readonly issues: readonly string[] };

export type ErrorHandlers<R> = { [K in AppError["code"]]: (error: Extract<AppError, { code: K }>) => R };

export function matchError<R>(error: AppError, handlers: ErrorHandlers<R>): R
export function describeError(error: AppError): string
export function statusOf(error: AppError): number
```

- `describeError({ code: "not_found", resource: "order", id: "o1" })` →
  `"order o1 was not found"`
- `describeError({ code: "forbidden", action: "cancel" })` →
  `"not allowed to cancel"`
- `describeError({ code: "timeout", ms: 250 })` → `"timed out after 250ms"`
- `describeError({ code: "invalid", issues: ["a", "b"] })` → `"invalid: a, b"`
- `statusOf` maps the four codes to `404`, `403`, `504` and `422`
- Both must be written **with** `matchError`, not with a `switch`
- Omitting one key from a handler map is a compile error naming the key
- Each handler receives the narrowed variant: the `timeout` handler can read
  `.ms` and cannot read `.issues`

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`ErrorHandlers<R>` is a mapped type over the *discriminant*, not over the
union. `AppError["code"]` is the union of the four literal codes, and
`Extract<AppError, { code: K }>` pulls out the single variant matching each
one — which is what gives every handler a precisely narrowed parameter.

## Hint 2

`Extract` is a conditional type that distributes over a union:

```ts
type Timeout = Extract<AppError, { code: "timeout" }>;
// { code: "timeout"; ms: number }
```

Every member that is not assignable to `{ code: "timeout" }` becomes `never`
and disappears.

## Hint 3

The implementation is two lines, one of which is a cast. Looking up
`handlers[error.code]` gives a union of function types, and TypeScript will not
let you call a union of functions with a union argument, because it cannot
prove the pairing. Assert once to `(error: AppError) => R` and call it.

Left to you: whether the cast should be a `as` or an intermediate variable with
an annotation. Neither is safer; one reads better in review.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Compare the handler map against the obvious alternative, a `switch` with a
`default: assertNever`. Both are exhaustive. The map wins when you want to
*pass* the handling around — a table of handlers is a value you can compose,
override in tests, or build per-transport. The switch wins on readability
inside one function. Knowing why you would choose each is the exercise.

## Hint 2

Write the union first and write it with `readonly` on every field. Errors are
values that get logged, serialised and compared; nothing should mutate one
after it is created, and making that structural rather than conventional costs
you nothing here.

## Hint 3

If `statusOf` seems like an odd thing to build twice with the same map shape,
that is the point: `matchError` is generic in `R`, so the same exhaustiveness
machinery produces a string in one call and a number in another. When a fifth
error code is added, both fail to compile, and both failures name the key.

## ex2 — the core type, and the extraction functions

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Build the foundation:

```ts
export interface Ok<T> { readonly ok: true; readonly value: T }
export interface Err<E> { readonly ok: false; readonly error: E }
export type Result<T, E> = Ok<T> | Err<E>;

export function ok<T>(value: T): Result<T, never>
export function err<E>(error: E): Result<never, E>
export function isOk<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>): result is Ok<T>
export function isErr<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>): result is Err<E>
export function unwrapOr<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>, fallback: T): T
export function unwrapOrElse<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>, recover: (error: E) => T): T
export function expectOk<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>, message: string): T
```

- `unwrapOr(ok(0), 99)` → `0`, and `unwrapOr(ok(undefined), 5)` → `undefined`
- `unwrapOr(err("boom"), 5)` → `5`
- `unwrapOrElse(err({ code: 404 }), (e) => e.code)` → `404`
- `expectOk(ok(1), "wanted a number")` → `1`
- `expectOk(err("boom"), "wanted a number")` throws an `Error` whose message is
  `wanted a number: "boom"`
- `[ok(1), err("x"), ok(2)].filter(isOk).map((r) => r.value)` → `[1, 2]`, typed
  `number[]` — that only works because `isOk` is a type predicate
- `const r: Result<number, string> = ok(1)` compiles with no type argument —
  that is what `Result<T, never>` buys

## Hint 1

Two literal discriminants, `true` and `false`. Write `ok: boolean` in both
interfaces and every function in this file stops narrowing, while continuing to
compile — try it once, read the error you get on `result.value`, and then put
the literals back.

## Hint 2

`never` in the constructors is not decoration:

```ts
export function ok<T>(value: T): Result<T, never> {
  return { ok: true, value };
}
const r: Result<number, AppError> = ok(1);   // fine: never is assignable to AppError
```

Write `Result<T, unknown>` instead and that assignment fails, because `unknown`
is assignable to almost nothing.

## Hint 3

`unwrapOr` is one conditional on `result.ok`. Resist `result.value ?? fallback`
— the two gate cases with `0` and `undefined` exist to catch exactly that, and
they are the same two values that caught it in the previous volume.

Left to you: whether `expectOk` should throw an `Error` or a custom class. The
gate only checks the message; a custom class would let callers distinguish an

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the `filter(isOk)` requirement and work backwards, because it is the
one that constrains the design. `filter` cannot narrow an array on its own —
its signature has no way to say "the predicate proves something" — so `isOk`
must be declared as a type predicate returning `result is Ok<T>`, and `Ok<T>`
must therefore be a *named* type rather than an inline object literal.

## Hint 2

Note what `expectOk` is for. It is the deliberate escape hatch: a place where
you assert that a failure here means a bug, and you want a stack trace rather
than a value. Every Result library has one, every one of them is named
something like `expect` or `unwrap`, and every code review should ask why a
particular call is using it.

## Hint 3

`JSON.stringify` on the error in `expectOk`'s message is what makes the assert
readable when the error is an object rather than a string. It also means an
error containing a circular reference will throw *inside* your error path,
which is a genuine production footgun worth a comment.

## ex3 — the four combinators

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Bring the core across from ex2 and add the functions
that let callers work with a `Result` without opening it:


- `orElse(err("cold"), () => ok(0))` → `ok(0)`
- `orElse(ok(1), () => ok(0))` → `ok(1)` and `fn` is never called

`divide(a: number, b: number): Result<number, "div0">` and

## Hint 1

Each combinator is a one-line conditional, and the whole exercise is in the
type signatures. Write all four signatures first, with the bodies as
`throw new Error("todo")`, and check that the `andThen` example's type comes
out as a two-member union before you implement anything.

## Hint 2

The important line in the whole sector:

```ts
export function andThen<T, E, U, F>(
  result: Result<T, E>,
  fn: (value: T) => Result<U, F>,
): Result<U, E | F> {
  return result.ok ? fn(result.value) : result;
}
```

`E | F` because the chain can fail either way. Returning `result` in the else
branch type-checks because `Err<E>` is assignable to `Result<U, E | F>`.

## Hint 3

`orElse` is the mirror: it can *recover*, so the value type widens to `T | U`
and the error type becomes just `F`. Getting `map`/`mapErr` right and then
writing `orElse` by symmetry with `andThen` is the fastest route.

Left to you: whether `map` should return the original object when the result is
an error, or construct a fresh one. Returning the original is cheaper and means
`map(e, f) === e`, which some tests rely on and others find surprising.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about why these functions exist at all. Without them, every call site
that wants to transform a success writes an `if`, and a five-step pipeline is
fifteen lines of narrowing. With them the pipeline reads as a pipeline, and the
compiler assembles the error union as it goes.

## Hint 2

`divide` and `sqrtResult` are deliberately trivial, and their error types are
deliberately string literals rather than a shared `Error`. That is what makes
the union in the combined type readable — `"div0" | "negative"` tells you
exactly what can go wrong, where `Error | Error` tells you nothing.

## Hint 3

Check `map(err("x"), (n: number) => n * 3)` carefully. The annotation on the
callback parameter is needed because `err("x")` is `Result<never, string>` and
`T` is inferred as `never`, so the parameter has no useful type. That is not a
bug in your signature — it is the same "one inference site wins" behaviour from
the first sector, showing up in a place people find surprising.

## ex4 — combining many results, and a record of them

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Two shapes of combination, plus the helper types that
make the second one work:

```ts
export type OkOf<R> = R extends { ok: true; value: infer T } ? T : never;
export type ErrOf<R> = R extends { ok: false; error: infer E } ? E : never;

export function all<T, E>(results: readonly Result<T, E>[]): Result<T[], E>
export function partition<T, E>(results: readonly Result<T, E>[]): { values: T[]; errors: E[] }
export function allObject<S extends Record<string, Result<unknown, unknown>>>(
  entries: S,
): Result<{ [K in keyof S]: OkOf<S[K]> }, ErrOf<S[keyof S]>>
```

- `all([ok(1), ok(2)])` → `ok([1, 2])`
- `all([ok(1), err("a"), err("b")])` → `err("a")` — the **first** error, and
  the rest are not inspected
- `all([])` → `ok([])`
- `partition([ok(1), err("a"), ok(2)])` → `{ values: [1, 2], errors: ["a"] }`
- `allObject({ port: ok(8080), host: ok("localhost") })` →
  `ok({ port: 8080, host: "localhost" })`, typed
  `Result<{ port: number; host: string }, never>`
- `allObject({ port: ok(8080), host: err("missing HOST") })` →
  `err("missing HOST")`
- `allObject({ a: ok(1), b: err("x"), c: err("y") })` → `err("x")` — insertion
  order decides

The typed result of `allObject` is the point: `{ port: number; host: string }`,
key by key, not `Record<string, unknown>`.

## Hint 1

`OkOf` and `ErrOf` have to *distribute*. Given `Result<number, string>`, which

That vanishing is what makes the helper work at all.

## Hint 2

The mapped type over the record is the same trick as the schema sector:

```ts
Result<{ [K in keyof S]: OkOf<S[K]> }, ErrOf<S[keyof S]>>
```

The success type maps each key's result to its value type; the error type is the
union over all keys, because any one of them could be the failure.

## Hint 3

In the implementation, annotate the loop variable explicitly:

```ts
const result: Result<unknown, unknown> = entries[key];
```

An unresolved indexed access like `S[keyof S & string]` does not narrow on
`.ok` the way a concrete union does; the annotation gives the checker something
it can narrow.

Left to you: whether `all` should stop iterating at the first error or keep
going. The prompt says it must not inspect the rest — which matters if the
"results" are lazy or expensive, and is a habit worth having even when they are
not.

## Hint 1

`partition` is the function that looks trivial and teaches the most. Two
`filter` passes would be shorter and would lose the types — `results.filter((r)

Check the `never` in the type of the all-success case. `allObject({ port:
ok(8080) })` is `Result<{ port: number }, never>`, which means the compiler

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 — accumulate instead of short-circuit

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `all` from ex4 answers "did anything fail". A form needs
"what *all* failed". Same core type, different contract:

```ts
export function allSettled<T, E>(results: readonly Result<T, E>[]): Result<T[], E[]>

export interface Rule<T> { readonly message: string; readonly test: (value: T) => boolean }
export function validate<T>(value: T, rules: readonly Rule<T>[]): Result<T, string[]>

export function collect<T, E>(
  entries: Readonly<Record<string, Result<T, E>>>,
): Result<Record<string, T>, Record<string, E>>
```

- `allSettled([ok(1), ok(2)])` → `ok([1, 2])`
- `allSettled([ok(1), err("a"), err("b")])` → `err(["a", "b"])` — both, in
  order
- `allSettled([])` → `ok([])`
- With `const password = [{ message: "too short", test: (s: string) => s.length >= 8 },
  { message: "needs a digit", test: (s: string) => /\d/.test(s) }]`:
  - `validate("hunter2!", password)` → `ok("hunter2!")`
  - `validate("abc", password)` → `err(["too short", "needs a digit"])`
- `collect({ email: err("required"), age: err("not a number"), name: ok("ada") })`
  → `err({ email: "required", age: "not a number" })` — keyed by field, with
  successful fields absent
- `collect({ name: ok("ada"), age: ok(41) })` → `ok({ name: "ada", age: 41 })`

Note the error type of `allSettled` is `E[]`, not `E`. A failure now carries
several errors, and the type says so.


## Hint 1

The implementation difference from `all` is two lines: instead of returning on
the first error, push it into a list and keep going; at the end, return the
error list if it is non-empty and the values otherwise. The *contract*
difference is much bigger than the code difference, which is the lesson.

## Hint 2

`validate` runs every rule and keeps the messages of the ones that failed:

```ts
const failures = rules.filter((rule) => !rule.test(value)).map((rule) => rule.message);
```

Then it is one conditional. Notice the rules are data — a value you can build
per locale, per tenant, or per test — which is the same argument the handler
map made in ex1.

## Hint 3

`collect` is keyed rather than positional, which is what a form needs: the
consumer must know that `email` failed, not that "the second one" failed. Build
two objects as you walk, and decide at the end which one to return.

Left to you: whether an empty `entries` object should be `ok({})`. It should,
for the same reason `all([])` is `ok([])` — the identity element of "everything
succeeded" is "nothing failed" — and being able to explain that saves an
argument in code review.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask when each strategy is *wrong*, because that is how you choose. Accumulating
over sequentially dependent steps runs code that should never have run: if
loading the user failed, "the user has no orders" is not a second problem, it is
noise. Short-circuiting over independent fields makes a user fix one typo at a
time. The rule is whether step two makes sense when step one failed.

## Hint 2

Watch the shape of the failure type. `Result<T[], E[]>` says a failure carries
one or more errors, and the type cannot express "at least one" — so an empty
error array is representable and meaningless. Some libraries use a non-empty
array type (`readonly [E, ...E[]]`) to close that hole. Consider whether the
extra precision is worth the friction here; there is no single right answer.

## Hint 3

In `collect`, the successful fields disappearing from the error object is
deliberate. A form renderer wants a map from field name to message and nothing
else; including successful keys with `undefined` values makes every consumer
filter. Design the failure payload for the code that renders it.

exercises.prompt:
## ex6 — meeting the world that throws

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Every library you use throws, and `catch` hands you
`unknown`. Build the boundary:

```ts
export function normalizeError(thrown: unknown): Error
export function fromThrowable<A extends readonly unknown[], T>(
  fn: (...args: A) => T,
): (...args: A) => Result<T, Error>
export function fromPromise<T>(promise: Promise<T>): Promise<Result<T, Error>>
export function toPromise<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>): Promise<T>
```

`normalizeError` rules:

- an `Error` is returned unchanged, same object identity
- a `string` becomes `new Error(thatString)`
- anything else becomes `new Error("non-error thrown: <JSON>")` with the
  original attached as `cause`
- `normalizeError(undefined).message` → `"non-error thrown: undefined"`
- `normalizeError({ a: 1 }).cause` is the original object

Then:

- `fromThrowable(JSON.parse)("{}")` → `ok({})`
- `fromThrowable(JSON.parse)("nope")` → an `err` whose error is a `SyntaxError`
- The wrapped function keeps its signature: `fromThrowable(JSON.parse)()` is a
  compile error
- `await fromPromise(Promise.resolve(1))` → `ok(1)`
- `await fromPromise(Promise.reject("boom"))` → `err(Error("boom"))`
- `await toPromise(ok(1))` → `1`; `toPromise(err("x"))` rejects with an `Error`
  whose message is `"x"` and whose `cause` is the original error value

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`catch (error)` is typed `unknown` under `strict`, and the reason is that
JavaScript really can throw anything — a string, `undefined`, a `Symbol`, a
DOM node. `normalizeError` exists so that the rest of your program never has to
think about that again.

## Hint 2

`Error.cause` is the piece people miss:

```ts
new Error("non-error thrown: 42", { cause: 42 });
```

It preserves the original without stringifying it, and Node's default printer
walks the chain. It has been available since ES2022 and Node 16.9, and it is
strictly better than embedding the message of one error inside another.

## Hint 3

`fromThrowable` reuses the argument-tuple trick from the first sector, so the
returned function keeps arity and parameter names. The body is a `try` that
returns `ok(fn(...args))` and a `catch` that returns
`err(normalizeError(error))`.

Left to you: whether `fromThrowable` should really catch *everything*. A
`RangeError` from a bug in your own code becoming a domain failure is not
obviously right; some codebases rethrow anything that is not an expected error
type. The prompt takes the simple line; the reading argues the other side.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`JSON.stringify(undefined)` returns `undefined`, not the string `"undefined"`,
which is exactly the case the gate checks. Build the message with `String(...)`
for primitives and `JSON.stringify` for objects, or handle the special case
directly — either way, discover it now rather than in a log line at 3am.

## Hint 2

`toPromise` is the reverse boundary and it matters more than it looks. It is
what lets a Result-based domain layer sit underneath a framework that expects
rejections — Express error middleware, a React error boundary, a test runner.
Being able to cross in both directions is what makes the discipline adoptable
one module at a time.

## Hint 3

Preserving object identity for an `Error` input is a real requirement, not
pedantry. Wrapping an error you were handed loses its stack in some tooling and
double-wraps in others, so the first check in `normalizeError` should be
`instanceof Error` and the first action should be `return thrown`. Note the
cross-realm caveat: in a worker or iframe this check can be false for a genuine
error, which is why library code sometimes adds a structural fallback.

## ex7 — asynchronous results

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. A rejected promise is a `throw` with extra steps.
Keep expected failures in the type instead:

```ts
export type AsyncResult<T, E> = Promise<Result<T, E>>;

export function mapAsync<T, E, U>(
  result: AsyncResult<T, E>,
  fn: (value: T) => U | Promise<U>,
): AsyncResult<U, E>

export function andThenAsync<T, E, U, F>(
  result: AsyncResult<T, E>,
  fn: (value: T) => AsyncResult<U, F>,
): AsyncResult<U, E | F>

export function allAsync<T, E>(results: readonly AsyncResult<T, E>[]): AsyncResult<T[], E>

export function withTimeout<T, E>(
  result: AsyncResult<T, E>,
  ms: number,
): AsyncResult<T, E | { readonly code: "timeout"; readonly ms: number }>
```

- `await mapAsync(Promise.resolve(ok(2)), (n) => n * 2)` → `ok(4)`
- `await mapAsync(Promise.resolve(ok(2)), async (n) => n * 2)` → `ok(4)` — the
  callback may be async
- `await mapAsync(Promise.resolve(err("x")), (n: number) => n)` → `err("x")`,
  and the callback never runs
- `await andThenAsync(Promise.resolve(ok("12")), parseAsync)` → `ok(12)`; the
  declared error type is the union of both steps' errors
- `await allAsync([Promise.resolve(ok(1)), Promise.resolve(err("a")), Promise.resolve(err("b"))])`
  → `err("a")` — first **by index**, and every promise still settles
- `await withTimeout(slow, 50)` → `err({ code: "timeout", ms: 50 })` when `slow`
  takes longer than 50ms, and the underlying promise is not cancelled

The comment in `allAsync` must say why "first error" means first by index and
not first in time.

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`AsyncResult<T, E>` is just `Promise<Result<T, E>>` — there is no new
machinery, only `await` in the right places. `andThenAsync` is `andThen` with
two awaits, and its type signature is character-for-character the same.

## Hint 2

```ts
export async function andThenAsync<T, E, U, F>(
  result: AsyncResult<T, E>,
  fn: (value: T) => AsyncResult<U, F>,
): AsyncResult<U, E | F> {
  const settled = await result;
  return settled.ok ? fn(settled.value) : settled;
}
```

An `async` function returning `Promise<X>` may `return` either an `X` or a
`Promise<X>`; that is why returning `fn(...)` directly type-checks.

## Hint 3

`allAsync` is `Promise.all` followed by the synchronous `all`. That ordering is
what makes "first by index" true: every promise has already settled by the time
you look at any of them.

`withTimeout` needs `Promise.race` between the work and a timer that resolves
to an error result. Remember to `clearTimeout` on the happy path, or a Node
process will stay alive waiting for a timer nobody needs.

Left to you: whether `withTimeout` should try to cancel the slow work. It
cannot, with promises alone — you would need an `AbortController` threaded into
whatever started the work — and pretending otherwise is a common source of
"why is the server still doing that".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Compare the two async failure styles before implementing. A rejected promise
carries an `unknown`, is invisible in the signature, and makes `Promise.all`
abandon results you already paid for. `Promise<Result<T, E>>` carries a typed
error, shows up in the signature, and lets `Promise.all` return everything. The
cost is one `await` and one narrowing per step.

## Hint 2

An `async` function that returns a `Result` can still reject — if its body
throws, or if a library it calls does. That means the signature is a promise
you have to keep, usually by wrapping the body in the `fromPromise` boundary
from ex6. A function whose type says `AsyncResult` and whose body calls
unwrapped third-party code is telling a small lie.

## Hint 3

For the timeout, think about what the type is saying:
`E | { code: "timeout"; ms: number }` means the caller now has one more case to
handle, and the compiler will tell them. That is the whole argument of this
sector in one signature — a new failure mode is a type change, and a type change
is a compile error at every site that cares.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 — a pipeline whose error union grows as you build it

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Nested `andThen` calls are correct and unreadable. Wrap
them:

```ts
export interface Chain<T, E> {
  map<U>(fn: (value: T) => U): Chain<U, E>;
  mapErr<F>(fn: (error: E) => F): Chain<T, F>;
  andThen<U, F>(fn: (value: T) => Result<U, F>): Chain<U, E | F>;
  match<R>(handlers: { ok: (value: T) => R; err: (error: E) => R }): R;
  done(): Result<T, E>;
}

export function chain<T, E>(result: Result<T, E>): Chain<T, E>
```

Then write three fallible steps with **different** error types and use them:

```ts
export function parseAmount(text: string): Result<number, { code: "not_a_number"; text: string }>
export function checkRange(amount: number): Result<number, { code: "out_of_range"; amount: number }>
export function toCents(amount: number): Result<number, { code: "too_precise"; amount: number }>
export function parseCents(text: string): Result<number, PipelineError>
```

- `parseAmount("12.50")` → `ok(12.5)`; `parseAmount("x")` →
  `err({ code: "not_a_number", text: "x" })`
- `checkRange` rejects anything outside `0 < amount <= 1_000_000`
- `toCents` rejects an amount with more than two decimal places
- `parseCents("12.50")` → `ok(1250)`
- `parseCents("x")`, `parseCents("-3")` and `parseCents("1.005")` each return
  the matching error variant
- `PipelineError` is the union of the three step errors, and `parseCents` is
  written as one `chain(...).andThen(...).andThen(...).done()` expression
- `describe(error: PipelineError)` uses a `switch` with an `assertNever`
  default; adding a fourth step's error to the union must break it

The declared return type of the chain expression, before you annotate anything,
must already be the three-member union. Check it by hovering.

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`chain` is a closure over one `Result` returning an object of methods, each of
which builds a new `Chain` from a new `Result`. Nothing is mutated; every method
returns a fresh wrapper, which is why the type parameters can change from one
link to the next.

## Hint 2

The method that carries the sector's argument:

```ts
andThen<U, F>(fn: (value: T) => Result<U, F>): Chain<U, E | F> {
  return chain<U, E | F>(result.ok ? fn(result.value) : result);
}
```

Each link adds its own failure type to the union. After three links the type
lists all three, and nobody wrote that union by hand.

## Hint 3

`toCents` is the fiddly step: `Math.round(amount * 100)` is right, and testing
"more than two decimals" with `Math.round(amount * 100) !== amount * 100` fails
for floating-point reasons on values like `1.005`. Compare against a rounded
string, or check `Number.isInteger(Math.round(amount * 1000) / 10)` — and write
down which one you chose and why.

Left to you: whether `chain` should also have an `orElse`. It is four lines and
it is the recovery path; the gate does not require it, but a chain without one
forces every caller back to `done()` to handle failures.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build the three steps before the wrapper. Each one is small, each has exactly
one failure mode, and each failure is a variant with the data needed to explain
it — `{ code: "not_a_number", text }` rather than `"bad input"`. Errors that
carry their context are what make the final `describe` useful.

## Hint 2

Watch what happens to the union if you make all three steps return
`Result<number, string>`. Everything still compiles, the chain still works, and
the exhaustive `describe` becomes impossible, because `string` has no variants
to enumerate. Precision in the error type is not decoration; it is the thing
that makes the compiler able to help.

## Hint 3

The floating-point trap in `toCents` is worth sitting with. `1.005 * 100` is
`100.49999999999999`, so a naive rounding check reports "too precise" for a
value the user typed as two decimals — or accepts three, depending on which way
you wrote it. Money in floating point is a whole discipline; the honest
production answer is to parse the *string* and never multiply at all.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a request handler with an exhaustive status map (hard)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Four fallible steps, one error union, and a
transport boundary the compiler polices.

```ts
export type HandlerError =
  | { readonly code: "bad_request"; readonly issues: readonly string[] }
  | { readonly code: "unauthorised" }
  | { readonly code: "not_found"; readonly id: string }
  | { readonly code: "conflict"; readonly reason: string };

export interface Session { readonly userId: string; readonly scopes: readonly string[] }
export interface Order { readonly id: string; readonly ownerId: string; readonly status: "open" | "cancelled" }
export interface CancelRequest { readonly orderId: string }

export function parseRequest(raw: unknown): Result<CancelRequest, HandlerError>
export function authorise(session: Session): Result<Session, HandlerError>
export function loadOrder(orders: ReadonlyMap<string, Order>, id: string, session: Session): Result<Order, HandlerError>
export function cancel(order: Order): Result<Order, HandlerError>
export function handle(raw: unknown, session: Session, orders: ReadonlyMap<string, Order>): Result<Order, HandlerError>
export function toHttp(result: Result<Order, HandlerError>): { status: number; body: unknown }
```

Rules:

- `parseRequest` needs an object with a non-empty string `orderId`; otherwise
  `bad_request` with every problem listed: `parseRequest({})` →
  `err({ code: "bad_request", issues: ["orderId is required"] })`, and
  `parseRequest({ orderId: 7 })` → `issues: ["orderId must be a string"]`
- `authorise` requires the scope `"orders:write"`, else `unauthorised`
- `loadOrder` returns `not_found` when the id is absent **and** when the order
  belongs to another user — the same error either way
- `cancel` on an already-cancelled order → `conflict` with reason
  `"order is already cancelled"`; otherwise a **new** order object with
  `status: "cancelled"`
- `handle` composes the four steps; a failure at any step is returned unchanged
- `toHttp` maps success to `{ status: 200, body: order }` and the four codes to
  `400`, `401`, `404`, `409`, with an `assertNever` default

Add a fifth variant to `HandlerError` and `toHttp` must fail to compile, naming
the code you forgot.

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write `toHttp` first. It is the part with the compile-time guarantee, and
having it in front of you makes the error union concrete before you write a
single step. A `switch` on `result.error.code` with `default: return
assertNever(result.error)` is the whole mechanism.

## Hint 2

`handle` can be written with nested `andThen`s or with early returns. The early
return version is flatter and type-checks for a reason worth understanding:

```ts
const request = parseRequest(raw);
if (!request.ok) return request;
```

`request` is narrowed to `Err<HandlerError>`, which is assignable to
`Result<Order, HandlerError>` — so returning it needs no wrapping.

## Hint 3

`parseRequest` must accumulate rather than short-circuit, because a request with
two problems should report two. That is the ex5 shape: collect issues into an
array and decide at the end.

Left to you: whether `cancel` mutates the order or returns a copy. The prompt
says a new object; think about what a handler that mutates its input does to a
caller holding a reference, and to a retry.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The `not_found`-for-someone-else's-order rule is a security decision disguised
as an error code. Returning `403` when the order exists but is not yours tells
an attacker that the id is real — an enumeration oracle. Returning `404` for
both cases leaks nothing. Encoding that in the type means nobody can
accidentally "improve" the error later without changing the union.

## Hint 2

Notice what the boundary function buys you organisationally. Every HTTP status
in this service is decided in one place, from a union the domain layer owns.
Compare with throwing `NotFoundError` subclasses and mapping them in middleware
by `instanceof`: same behaviour, no exhaustiveness, and a new error class that
nobody maps becomes a 500 in production.

## Hint 3

If `toHttp`'s `assertNever` complains before you have added a fifth variant,
the usual cause is a non-literal `code`. Check that `HandlerError`'s members
pin `code` to string literals and that nothing along the way widened them — a
missing `as const` on a helper that builds errors is the classic culprit.

## Review — a transaction that rolls back

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Same ideas, from the side where they stop being a
style preference: steps with side effects, where a failure halfway through has
to be undone.

```ts
export interface Step<S> {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly run: (state: S) => Result<S, string>;
  readonly undo: (state: S) => S;
}

export interface TxFailure {
  readonly failedAt: string;
  readonly error: string;
  readonly rolledBack: readonly string[];
}

export function runTransaction<S>(initial: S, steps: readonly Step<S>[]): Result<S, TxFailure>
```

Semantics:

- Steps run in order, each receiving the state the previous one returned
- On success, the final state is returned: `runTransaction(0, [inc, inc])` →
  `ok(2)` for a step whose `run` adds one
- On failure at step *n*, the completed steps `0..n-1` are undone in **reverse**
  order, each `undo` receiving the state the rollback has reached so far
- The failing step is not undone — it never completed
- `rolledBack` lists the undone step names in the order they were undone
- `runTransaction(0, [])` → `ok(0)`
- A failure in the first step returns `rolledBack: []`

Given `charge` (adds 100, then fails), the sequence
`[reserve, charge, ship]` where `charge` fails returns
`err({ failedAt: "charge", error: "card declined", rolledBack: ["reserve"] })`
and the state observed by `reserve.undo` is the state *before* `charge` ran.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb03_result_error_modelling review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Keep a list of the steps that have completed, alongside the current state. The
list is the rollback plan; without it, a failure has no way to know what to undo.

## Hint 2

The rollback loop walks the completed list backwards, threading state:

```ts
for (let i = completed.length - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {
  state = completed[i].undo(state);
  rolledBack.push(completed[i].name);
}
```

Reverse order matters: undoing a reservation before undoing the charge that
depended on it would apply the compensations in an order the system never saw.

## Hint 3

The failing step is not in `completed`, so it is not undone — which is correct
only if `run` is atomic. If a step can fail halfway through its own side
effects, no rollback plan built from step boundaries can save you; that is why
real systems make each step idempotent and retriable.

Left to you: what `runTransaction` should do if an `undo` itself throws. The
gate does not test it. Every production implementation has to answer it, and
"log loudly and keep undoing the rest" is usually better than "abort the
rollback".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice why this exercise belongs to this sector rather than to a general
"write a loop" one. The failure is *data*: it carries which step failed, why,
and what was undone. A thrown exception could carry the same information only
by inventing a custom class, and the caller would have no compile-time hint
that any of it exists.

## Hint 2

Think about the state threading in the rollback. Each `undo` takes the current
state and returns the state as it was before its step — so the state flows
backwards through the same list it flowed forwards through. Getting this wrong
usually shows up as an `undo` seeing a state that includes the failed step's
partial effects.

## Hint 3

This shape is the saga pattern, and knowing the name is worth something in an
interview. Distributed systems use it where a real transaction is impossible:
each step has a compensating action, the compensations run in reverse, and the
system is eventually consistent rather than atomic. The type here — a `Result`
whose error describes the compensation that happened — is what makes it
auditable.

# V3·TB4 — Typing configuration and environment

The previous sector taught you to parse data arriving from the network. This
one is about data arriving from the operator, and it is worse in three specific
ways.

First, everything is a string. `process.env` is typed
`Record<string, string | undefined>`, and there is no other type it could
honestly have — the operating system hands your process a list of byte strings.
A port is a string. A boolean is a string. A timeout is a string.

Second, the failures happen at the worst possible time. A missing
`DATABASE_URL` read lazily inside a request handler is discovered when the
first request arrives, in production, after the deploy was declared green.

Third, the traps are silent. Every JavaScript coercion you might reach for
returns a plausible wrong answer rather than failing:

```ts
Number("")        // 0        - an empty variable becomes a port of zero
Number("8080abc") // NaN      - but parseInt("8080abc") is 8080
Boolean("false")  // true     - every non-empty string is truthy
parseInt("08")    // 8        - fine now; a decade ago it was 0
Number(" 42 ")    // 42       - whitespace is silently trimmed
Number(null)      // 0        - and Number(undefined) is NaN
```

There is no combination of these that gives you "read a port, fail loudly if
it is not a port". You have to write it.

## Concept — the honest starting type

Every config read begins as `string | undefined`, and the first job is to
decide, per key, which of three things it is:

```ts
required     // absent is a boot failure
optional     // absent is a legitimate `undefined`
withDefault  // absent means this value, and the result is never undefined
```

The third one is where types usually go wrong. A key with a default must not
be typed `number | undefined` — the whole point of the default is that the
value exists. Getting that right means the *spec* has to carry the information,
and the output type has to be derived from the spec rather than written by
hand:

```ts
const spec = {
  PORT: withDefault(asPort, 3000),
  DATABASE_URL: required(asUrl),
  LOG_LEVEL: withDefault(asEnum(["debug", "info", "warn"]), "info"),
  SENTRY_DSN: optional(asUrl),
} as const;

type Config = ConfigOf<typeof spec>;
// { PORT: number; DATABASE_URL: URL; LOG_LEVEL: "debug" | "info" | "warn";
//   SENTRY_DSN: URL | undefined }
```

That derivation is the same mechanism as the schema sector — a mapped type over
a record of specs — pointed at a different problem.

## Concept — fail fast, in one place, with every error

Config validation should happen once, at process start, before the server
listens. Two properties follow from that, and both are design decisions rather
than accidents.

**Every key is checked, even if the first one is broken.** An operator who
fixes `PORT`, redeploys, and then discovers `DATABASE_URL` is also wrong has
had a bad afternoon that one error message could have prevented. The loader
accumulates.

**The result is frozen and passed explicitly.** A module that reads
`process.env` at the point of use is untestable and unauditable — there is no
list of what the program needs, and no way to construct a different
configuration for a test. A single `loadConfig(process.env)` at the entry
point, with the result threaded through, gives you both.

## Concept — layers, secrets and per-environment shapes

Real configuration has more than one source, and precedence is a contract:
built-in defaults, then a config file, then environment variables, then command
line flags — each one overriding the last. Expressing that in types means a
`DeepPartial` of the config for the override layers and a merge that respects
nesting.

Secrets need one more idea. A `Redacted<string>` — a branded type whose value
cannot be logged by accident, with an explicit `reveal()` at the point of use —
turns "do not log the database password" from a code review comment into a
compile error. The runtime half is a `toLogSafe` that replaces every redacted
value before the object reaches a logger.

Finally, some requirements are conditional: production needs a TLS certificate
and staging does not. A discriminated union on `env` says that in the type, so
`config.tlsCert` is a `string` in the production branch and does not exist in
the others — and the code that reads it must narrow first.

There is one more shape worth naming before the exercises, because it is the
difference between a config system people use and one they route around: the
spec is a *value*. A record of variable declarations is an ordinary object, so
you can iterate it, print it, diff it against a deployment manifest, or
generate a `.env.example` from it. None of that is possible when configuration
is two hundred `process.env` reads scattered through the codebase, and the
inability to answer "what does this service actually need" is what makes those
codebases frightening to deploy.

## The trap

The trap in this sector is `declare global { namespace NodeJS { interface
ProcessEnv { DATABASE_URL: string } } }`. It compiles. It makes
`process.env.DATABASE_URL` a `string` everywhere. It checks nothing at all —
you have written a cast that applies to your whole program, and the first time
the variable is missing you get `undefined` flowing into code that the compiler
promised could not receive it. Declaration merging on `ProcessEnv` is
acceptable *only* when something validates at boot; on its own it is the
`parseJson<T>` of configuration, and it fails in exactly the same way, for
exactly the same reason: the caller supplied the type and nothing supplied the
evidence.

# Reading - typescript/v3tb04_typed_config_env

Notes on coercion, on deriving the config type, on layering, and on secrets.

## Notes

**`process.env` values are strings or `undefined`, and an empty string is
ambiguous.** `FOO=` sets `FOO` to `""`, which is present-but-empty. Most
loaders treat empty as absent, because an operator who leaves a blank in a
deployment template means "I did not set this". That is a convention, not a
law, so write it down; the exercises here treat empty as absent and say so.

**Every coercion needs an explicit failure.** The rule of thumb: never use
`Number`, `parseInt`, `Boolean` or `JSON.parse` on config without a check
immediately afterwards. `parseInt` in particular is the wrong tool — it stops
at the first non-digit, so `"8080abc"` becomes `8080` and `"1e3"` becomes `1`.
`Number` is stricter but maps `""` to `0` and trims whitespace. The reliable
recipe is: reject empty, then `Number`, then `Number.isFinite`, then whatever
domain rule applies.

**Booleans need a vocabulary.** `Boolean(raw)` is useless. Pick an accepted set
— `"1" | "true" | "yes" | "on"` against `"0" | "false" | "no" | "off"`,
case-insensitive — and reject everything else. Accepting anything else silently
is how a flag set to `"False"` turns a feature on.

**Durations want units.** `TIMEOUT=30` is ambiguous and someone will read it as
seconds and someone else as milliseconds. A parser that accepts `"30s"`,
`"1500ms"`, `"5m"` and rejects a bare number removes an entire class of
incident.

**The output type is a mapped type over the spec.** `{ [K in keyof S]:
Output<S[K]> }`, where `Output` is a conditional type reading the parsed type
out of each variable's declaration. The interesting part is optionality: a
`withDefault` variable's output must not include `undefined`, which means the
three constructors need to produce three distinguishable spec types.

**Layering is a fold with a precedence order.** `[defaults, file, env, flags]`
reduced left to right with a deep merge, where later layers win. Two subtleties:
arrays should usually be *replaced* rather than concatenated (nobody wants a
CIDR list that grows every layer), and `undefined` in a later layer should mean
"no opinion" rather than "unset", or an optional flag will clobber a good value.

**Freezing is shallow.** `Object.freeze(config)` protects the top level only; a
nested object stays mutable. A recursive freeze is five lines and worth it for
a value that lives for the process lifetime.

**Redaction is a brand plus a discipline.** The brand stops `logger.info({
password })` from compiling; `toLogSafe` stops the value from reaching a
serialiser by another route. Neither stops `String(secret)`, so the pair is a
guard rail rather than a guarantee — the same honest limit branded types had in
the parsing sector.

## ex1 — the three modalities

The exercise looks trivial and encodes two real decisions: empty string means
absent, and a missing required key throws a `ConfigError` naming the key rather
than a generic message. Naming the key matters more than any other detail in
this sector, because the person reading the error is deploying at the time.

## ex2 — coercions and their traps

Six small functions, each of which exists because a built-in does the wrong
thing. The port range check (1 to 65535) and the leading-zero case are the ones
people skip; `PORT=0` is legal to `Number` and means "any free port" to some
servers, which is almost never what a config file intended.

## ex3 — variable specs

`required`, `optional` and `withDefault` produce three shapes carrying a parse
function and enough type information for the loader to derive an output type.
The design decision worth noticing: the default is stored as an already-parsed
value, not as a string to be parsed later, so a typo in a default is a compile
error rather than a boot error.

## ex4 — the loader

One pass over the spec, one issue list, one derived type. The error message is
the deliverable: every bad or missing key, one per line, with the key name and
the reason.

## ex5 — layers

The merge is recursive and the precedence is left to right. `DeepPartial<T>` is
the type of every layer above the base, and writing it correctly means handling
arrays (do not make their elements partial) and primitives (do not recurse).

## ex6 — freezing and secrets

`deepFreeze` needs a `WeakSet` if you want it to survive a cyclic object, and
the type signature is more interesting than the body: it should return
`DeepReadonly<T>` so the compiler knows what the runtime just enforced.

## ex7 — per-environment shapes

A discriminated union on `env` makes conditional requirements structural. The
payoff is that `config.tlsCertPath` simply does not exist outside the
production branch, so the code that needs it must prove where it is.

## ex8 — documenting the spec

Generating a `.env.example` from the spec, and an `explain` that says where each
value came from, are the two things that make a config system usable by people
who did not write it. They also demonstrate that a spec is data: once
configuration is a value rather than a scatter of reads, you can compute over
it.

## Further reading

- [The Twelve-Factor App: config](https://12factor.net/config) — the argument for environment variables, and its limits.
- [Node docs: `process.env`](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#processenv) — including the string-coercion behaviour on assignment.
- [envalid](https://github.com/af/envalid) — a small library shaped almost exactly like the loader in this sector.
- [dotenv](https://github.com/motdotla/dotenv) — and the important note that it should not run in production.
- [MDN: `Object.freeze`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/freeze) — shallow, and silent in sloppy mode.

# V3·TB4 — Typing configuration and environment (archive)

The deep version: the coercion table, the derivation, layering, secrets,
containers, and a self-test bank.

## 1. The coercion table

| you want | do not use | use | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| integer | `parseInt(raw)` | reject empty, `Number(raw)`, `Number.isInteger` | `parseInt("8080abc")` is `8080` |
| number | `Number(raw)` alone | plus `Number.isFinite` | `Number("")` is `0`, `Number("x")` is `NaN` |
| port | `Number(raw)` | integer plus `1 <= n <= 65535` | `PORT=0` means "any free port" to some servers |
| boolean | `Boolean(raw)` | an explicit accepted vocabulary | every non-empty string is truthy |
| duration | `Number(raw)` | a unit-suffixed parser | a bare number is ambiguous |
| url | `new URL(raw)` alone | in a `try`, plus a protocol allowlist | `new URL("javascript:...")` succeeds |
| enum | `raw as Level` | membership test against a `const` array | a cast checks nothing |
| list | `raw.split(",")` | split, trim, drop empties | `"a,,b"` and trailing commas |
| json | `JSON.parse(raw)` | parse then decode with a schema | `any` from the parser |

Every row is a production incident somebody has already had.

## 2. Deriving the config type from the spec

```ts
interface Required_<T>   { readonly kind: "required";  readonly parse: Parse<T> }
interface Optional_<T>   { readonly kind: "optional";  readonly parse: Parse<T> }
interface Defaulted_<T>  { readonly kind: "default";   readonly parse: Parse<T>; readonly value: T }

type Var<T> = Required_<T> | Optional_<T> | Defaulted_<T>;

type Output<V> =
  V extends Required_<infer T>  ? T :
  V extends Defaulted_<infer T> ? T :
  V extends Optional_<infer T>  ? T | undefined :
  never;

type ConfigOf<S> = { [K in keyof S]: Output<S[K]> };
```

The order of the conditional branches matters: `Defaulted_` must be tested
before `Optional_` if their shapes overlap structurally, and keeping a literal
`kind` on each variant removes the ambiguity entirely. That is the same
discriminated-union discipline as everywhere else in this volume, applied to a
type-level dispatch.

## 3. A complete loader

```ts
export function loadConfig<S extends Record<string, Var<unknown>>>(
  env: Readonly<Record<string, string | undefined>>,
  spec: S,
): ConfigOf<S> {
  const issues: string[] = [];
  const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};

  for (const key of Object.keys(spec)) {
    const variable = spec[key];
    const raw = env[key];
    const present = raw !== undefined && raw !== "";
    try {
      if (present)                        out[key] = variable.parse(raw, key);
      else if (variable.kind === "default") out[key] = variable.value;
      else if (variable.kind === "optional") out[key] = undefined;
      else issues.push(`${key} is required`);
    } catch (error) {
      issues.push(error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error));
    }
  }

  if (issues.length > 0) throw new ConfigError(issues);
  return out as ConfigOf<S>;
}
```

Twenty lines, one cast, and every property of a good config system: fail fast,
report everything, name the keys, produce a typed object.

## 4. Layering

```ts
type DeepPartial<T> =
  T extends readonly unknown[] ? T :
  T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> } :
  T;

function mergeLayers<T>(base: T, ...layers: readonly DeepPartial<T>[]): T;
```

Precedence is the argument order. Three rules that avoid arguments later:

- **Arrays replace, they do not concatenate.** An override that adds one entry
  to an allowlist should say so explicitly, not by accident of merge order.
- **`undefined` means "no opinion".** A layer that does not set a key must not
  unset it. If you need explicit unsetting, use `null` and say so.
- **Merging stops at class instances.** A `URL` or a `Date` in the config should
  be replaced wholesale, never merged property by property.

## 5. Secrets

```ts
declare const secret: unique symbol;
export type Redacted<T> = T & { readonly [secret]: true };

export function redact<T>(value: T): Redacted<T>;
export function reveal<T>(value: Redacted<T>): T;
export function toLogSafe<T>(value: T): unknown;   // replaces redacted values with "***"
```

The brand stops the value being passed where a plain `string` is expected —
including into most logger signatures — so `logger.info({ dsn: config.dsn })`
fails to compile and `reveal(config.dsn)` is a visible, greppable decision.

Two things it does not do. `String(secret)` and template interpolation still
produce the raw text, because the brand is erased. And a structured logger that
takes `unknown` will happily serialise it, which is why `toLogSafe` exists as
the runtime half.

For serious deployments, remember that environment variables are visible in
`/proc/<pid>/environ`, in container inspect output, in crash dumps and often in
CI logs. Files mounted from a secret store, read once at boot, are strictly
better; the type-level work in this sector applies identically to them.

## 6. Containers, dotenv and the twelve-factor argument

Twelve-factor's "store config in the environment" was written against a
platform where the alternative was config files baked into the artifact. It
remains good advice with two caveats the essay predates: environment variables
are a poor place for large or structured values (they are a flat string map with
size limits), and they are a poor place for secrets for the reasons above.

`dotenv` is a development convenience. In production, the environment should
come from the orchestrator, and calling `dotenv.config()` there is a way to
have your local `.env` file win over the deployed configuration on the one day
somebody copies it into an image. Load it conditionally, and validate the
result either way.

## 7. Interview answers

**"How do you type `process.env`?"** You do not improve it by declaration
merging alone; that is an unchecked cast over the whole program. You read it as
`string | undefined`, validate once at boot with a spec, and pass a derived,
frozen config object explicitly.

**"Where should config validation happen?"** At process start, before anything
listens or connects, accumulating every problem so an operator sees them all.

**"Why not `parseInt`?"** It stops at the first non-digit, so invalid input
produces a plausible number instead of an error.

**"How do you type a key with a default?"** So that the output type does not
include `undefined`. That requires the spec to distinguish defaulted from
optional and the output type to be derived from the spec.

**"How do you keep secrets out of logs?"** A branded type that will not fit a
plain-string parameter, plus a runtime scrubber before serialisation, plus not
putting them in environment variables if you can mount files instead.

## 8. Common mistakes

- Reading `process.env` deep inside modules, so nothing knows what the program
  needs and tests cannot vary it.
- Declaration-merging `ProcessEnv` and treating the result as validation.
- `Number(raw) || 3000` — which silently accepts `"abc"` and also rejects `0`.
- Treating `""` and absent differently by accident rather than by decision.
- Failing on the first bad key.
- A default typed as a string that is parsed at boot, so a typo in the default
  is a runtime error.
- Merging layers with `Object.assign` and losing nested values.
- Logging the config object at startup "for debugging".
- Freezing shallowly and assuming the whole tree is protected.

## 9. Check yourself

1. What is the type of `process.env.PORT`, and why can it be nothing else?
2. Give three inputs where `Number` and `parseInt` disagree.
3. Why must a defaulted key's output type exclude `undefined`?
4. Write `Output<V>` for a three-variant `Var` type.
5. Why should the loader accumulate errors instead of throwing at the first?
6. What should a later layer's `undefined` mean, and why?
7. Why do arrays replace rather than merge?
8. What does declaration merging on `ProcessEnv` actually guarantee?
9. Name two ways a redacted value can still leak.
10. Why is `Object.freeze` insufficient for a nested config?
11. When is `dotenv` the wrong thing to run?
12. How would you express "production requires a TLS certificate" in types?

# The long read: configuration as a boundary, and why it is always worse than you think

Configuration is the part of a system that changes without a code review. That
single fact explains almost every incident in this area: the code was tested,
the deployment was tested, and then somebody set a variable to a value nobody
had ever considered.

## The shape of the problem

An operating system gives a process a flat map of strings to strings. That is
the entire contract. Everything above it — types, structure, defaults,
validation — is something your program invents, and it can only invent it at
runtime.

This makes configuration structurally identical to the network payload problem
in the previous sector, with three differences that make it harder rather than
easier. There is no schema negotiation: nobody versioned the environment. The
producer is a human under time pressure rather than another program. And the
consequence of a bad value is often not a rejected request but a subtly wrong
system — a cache TTL of zero, a retry count of one, a feature flag that is on
in the wrong region.

The type system can do exactly one thing about this, and it is the same thing
as before: make the validated value the only way to obtain a config. If
`config.port` is a `number`, it is because something checked; if any module can
read `process.env.PORT` directly, the guarantee is gone.

## Where defaults belong

There is a long-running argument about whether a default should live in code or
in the deployment manifest, and both positions are defensible.

Defaults in code mean the program runs with no configuration at all, which is
excellent for local development and for tests, and it means the default is
reviewed. The risk is that a value tuned for a laptop leaks into production
because nobody set it there — a 10-connection pool, a 5-second timeout, an
in-memory cache.

Defaults in the deployment manifest mean production is explicit, which is what
you want for anything with a capacity or cost implication, and it means the
program refuses to start when a value is missing. The cost is ceremony for
every developer.

The rule that survives contact with practice: **safe, environment-independent
values get defaults in code; anything with a cost, a capacity or a security
implication is required.** A log level has a default. A database URL does not.
A connection pool size probably should not, however tempting.

## Fail fast, and what "fast" means

"Validate at boot" is easy to say and has a wrinkle: a process that exits
immediately on a bad config, inside an orchestrator that restarts it, becomes a
crash loop, and crash loops are noisy and slow to diagnose. The behaviours that
work well in practice:

- Validate everything before opening any listener or connection.
- Print every problem, formatted for a terminal, to stderr.
- Exit with a distinct non-zero code so the orchestrator's logs distinguish
  configuration failure from a crash.
- Never retry a configuration failure; it will not fix itself.

The last point is worth stating because retry logic is often applied wholesale.
A missing `DATABASE_URL` is not a transient error, and treating it as one turns
a clear failure into a slow one.

## Testing configuration

The single most valuable consequence of a spec-based loader is that
configuration becomes testable. `loadConfig(fakeEnv, spec)` is a pure function
of its input, so you can assert that a missing required key produces the right
message, that a default applies, that a bad port is rejected. Codebases that
read `process.env` inline cannot do this without global mutation, which is why
they usually do not do it at all.

Two tests worth writing for any real service. One that loads the spec against
an environment built from your production manifest, catching drift between the
two. And one that asserts the *set of keys* the spec declares, so that adding a
required variable is a visible, reviewable change rather than a surprise at
deploy time.

## Performance and other non-issues

Configuration loading happens once, so its performance does not matter — with
one exception worth knowing. Programs that call `loadConfig` lazily from inside
a hot path, "just in case it changed", pay for it repeatedly and gain nothing:
`process.env` is a snapshot taken at process start, and in Node reading from it
is a native call that is slower than a property read on a plain object. Load
once, freeze, pass the object.

Hot reloading is a different matter and is usually a mistake for anything
except log levels. A configuration change that takes effect mid-request means
two halves of one operation ran under different rules. If you need dynamic
values, model them as a feature-flag service with its own consistency story,
not as configuration.

## The drift problem

The failure mode that survives every technique in this sector is drift between
the spec and the deployment. The program knows it needs `DATABASE_URL`; the
Helm chart, the Terraform module, the CI secrets page and the developer's
`.env` file each know something slightly different; and nothing checks that the
four agree. Adding a required variable is the moment this bites, because the
code deploys fine in staging where somebody set it by hand.

Three practices reduce it, none of them clever. Generate the `.env.example`
from the spec and commit it, so a diff appears in the pull request that adds a
variable. Write a test that loads the spec against an environment constructed
from the production manifest, so the two are compared by machine rather than by
memory. And make the loader print, at startup, the *source* of every value —
environment, default, or absent — because the alternative is an operator
grepping logs to find out whether their variable was picked up at all.

None of this is type system work, and that is the point: types make the values
correct once they are in the process, and nothing in the language can tell you
what the orchestrator will hand you. The spec-as-data design is what lets you
close that gap with ordinary code, which is why the last exercise in this
sector generates documentation rather than parsing anything.

## When not to do all of this

The apparatus in this sector is worth roughly an afternoon and pays back over
the life of a service. For a script, a build tool, or a Lambda with two
variables, it is overkill: read the two values, check them, move on. The
threshold is roughly when one of these becomes true — more than about five
variables, more than one deployment environment, more than one person
deploying, or any secret at all. Below that, a `requireEnv` helper and a couple
of `if` statements are the right amount of engineering, and knowing where the
line is matters as much as knowing how to build the machinery above it.

The way to tell you have crossed the line is not a count of variables but a
question: could a new engineer, given only your repository, produce a working
configuration for a fresh environment without asking anyone? If the answer is
no — if the knowledge lives in a colleague's shell history or in a wiki page
last edited two years ago — the spec is worth building, whatever the variable
count says. That is a documentation argument as much as a typing one, and it is
the reason the exercises finish where they do.
