exercises.prompt:
## ex1 — three ways a variable can be absent

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Nothing in this sector touches the real `process.env`;
every function takes the environment as an argument, which is what makes it
testable.

```ts
export type Env = Readonly<Record<string, string | undefined>>;

export class ConfigError extends Error { readonly issues: readonly string[]; }

export function requireEnv(env: Env, key: string): string
export function optionalEnv(env: Env, key: string): string | undefined
export function envWithDefault(env: Env, key: string, fallback: string): string
```

`new ConfigError(["PORT is required", "HOST is required"])` has
`message === "invalid configuration:\n  - PORT is required\n  - HOST is required"`
and `name === "ConfigError"`.

Behaviour, with `const env = { PORT: "8080", EMPTY: "", SPACED: "  " }`:

- `requireEnv(env, "PORT")` → `"8080"`
- `requireEnv(env, "MISSING")` throws a `ConfigError` with the single issue
  `"MISSING is required"`
- `requireEnv(env, "EMPTY")` throws the same — an empty value counts as absent
- `requireEnv(env, "SPACED")` throws too: values are trimmed before the
  emptiness test, and the trimmed value is what is returned
- `optionalEnv(env, "EMPTY")` → `undefined`
- `envWithDefault(env, "MISSING", "3000")` → `"3000"`
- `envWithDefault(env, "PORT", "3000")` → `"8080"`

Write a one-line comment where you decide that empty means absent, because it
is a convention rather than a law and the next reader deserves to know you
chose it.

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every one of the three functions is the same two questions in a different
order: is the value present, and what happens when it is not. Write one private
`read(env, key): string | undefined` that handles trimming and emptiness, and
the three public functions become one line each.

## Hint 2

The error class carries a list even though these functions only ever produce
one issue:

```ts
export class ConfigError extends Error {
  readonly issues: readonly string[];
  constructor(issues: readonly string[]) {
    super(`invalid configuration:\n${issues.map((i) => `  - ${i}`).join("\n")}`);
    this.name = "ConfigError";
    this.issues = issues;
  }
}
```

ex4 will throw one of these carrying every problem at once, and having the
shape right now saves rewriting it.

## Hint 3

`optionalEnv` returns `string | undefined`, and that is the honest type. Do not
be tempted to return `""` for absence — the caller then cannot distinguish "not
set" from "set to nothing", which is exactly the ambiguity this function exists
to resolve.

Left to you: whether trimming is right. It usually is, because deployment
templates introduce trailing spaces; but a variable holding a password or a
delimiter would be damaged by it. Note your decision.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice the shape of the signatures before you write anything: `env` is a
parameter, not a global. That one choice is what lets a test construct six
different environments in six lines, and it is the difference between
configuration you can reason about and configuration you can only deploy and
watch.

## Hint 2

`Readonly<Record<string, string | undefined>>` is exactly what an environment
is. The `| undefined` is not pessimism — index a map with a key that is not
there and that is what you get — and under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` you would
get it whether you asked or not. Starting from the honest type is what makes
the rest of the sector possible.

## Hint 3

The `SPACED` case is small and real. A YAML deployment template with
`PORT: "8080 "` produces a value that `Number` accepts, so a naive loader
starts a server on port 8080 and a strict one rejects a configuration that was
almost certainly intended to work. Trim first, then decide.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 — six coercions, six traps

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Each of these exists because a JavaScript built-in
returns a plausible wrong answer. Signature shape is
`(raw: string, key: string) => T`, and every failure throws a `ConfigError`
naming the key.

```ts
export function asInt(raw: string, key: string): number
export function asPort(raw: string, key: string): number
export function asBoolean(raw: string, key: string): boolean
export function asDuration(raw: string, key: string): number      // milliseconds
export function asEnum<const V extends readonly string[]>(values: V): (raw: string, key: string) => V[number]
export function asUrl(raw: string, key: string): URL
```

- `asInt("42", "N")` → `42`; `asInt("8080abc", "N")` throws — note `parseInt`
  would have returned `8080`
- `asInt("1e3", "N")` throws; `asInt("4.5", "N")` throws; `asInt("-7", "N")` → `-7`
- `asPort("8080", "PORT")` → `8080`; `asPort("0", "PORT")` and
  `asPort("70000", "PORT")` throw
- `asBoolean` accepts `true/false/1/0/yes/no/on/off`, case-insensitively;
  `asBoolean("False", "F")` → `false`; `asBoolean("maybe", "F")` throws
- `asDuration("30s", "T")` → `30000`; `asDuration("1500ms", "T")` → `1500`;
  `asDuration("5m", "T")` → `300000`; `asDuration("2h", "T")` → `7200000`;
  `asDuration("30", "T")` throws — a bare number is ambiguous
- `asEnum(["debug", "info", "warn"])("info", "LEVEL")` → `"info"`, typed
  `"debug" | "info" | "warn"`
- `asUrl("https://example.com", "U")` → a `URL`; `asUrl("not a url", "U")`
  throws; `asUrl("javascript:alert(1)", "U")` throws — only `http:` and
  `https:` are accepted

Error messages name the key and what was expected, for example
`PORT must be a port between 1 and 65535, got "70000"`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb04_typed_config_env ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The reliable integer recipe is three steps in this order: reject an empty
string, convert with `Number` (not `parseInt`), then check `Number.isInteger`.
`Number` is the strict one — it returns `NaN` for `"8080abc"` where `parseInt`
happily returns `8080` — and it is also the one that maps `""` to `0`, which is
why emptiness is rejected first.

## Hint 2

`asDuration` is a small regular expression plus a lookup:

```ts
const match = /^(\d+)(ms|s|m|h)$/.exec(raw);
const multipliers = { ms: 1, s: 1000, m: 60_000, h: 3_600_000 } as const;
```

Rejecting a bare number is the design point: `TIMEOUT=30` has been read as
seconds by one team and milliseconds by another in the same system.

## Hint 3

`asEnum` returns a *function*, so it is the only one of the six with a
different shape. It needs a `const` type parameter, or the array widens to
`string[]` and the return type stops being a literal union.

Left to you: whether `asUrl` should return a `URL` or a validated string. A
`URL` is parsed once and cannot be malformed afterwards, which is the whole
argument of the previous sector; a string is easier to log and compare.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the failing cases before the passing ones. `""`, `"abc"`, `"8080abc"`,
`"1e3"`, `"4.5"`, `"0"`, `"70000"`, `"False"`, `"30"`, `"javascript:alert(1)"`
— every one of them is a value some built-in accepts and your loader must not.
A coercion function is defined by what it refuses.

## Hint 2

The protocol allowlist in `asUrl` is a security control, not tidiness.
`new URL` succeeds for `javascript:`, `data:` and `file:` URLs, and a
configuration value that later becomes an `href`, a fetch target or a redirect
is a real attack surface. Allowlist, never blocklist.

## Hint 3

Keep the error text uniform: `<KEY> must be <expectation>, got <JSON of the
raw>`. Quoting the raw value with `JSON.stringify` shows trailing spaces and
empty strings that a bare interpolation hides — which is exactly the class of
value that produced the error in the first place.

exercises.prompt:
## ex3 — variable specs, and an output type derived from them

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. A variable is not just a parser; it also knows what
absence means. Model that as data:

```ts
export type Parse<T> = (raw: string, key: string) => T;

export interface RequiredVar<T>  { readonly kind: "required"; readonly parse: Parse<T> }
export interface OptionalVar<T>  { readonly kind: "optional"; readonly parse: Parse<T> }
export interface DefaultedVar<T> { readonly kind: "default";  readonly parse: Parse<T>; readonly value: T }
export type Var<T> = RequiredVar<T> | OptionalVar<T> | DefaultedVar<T>;

export function required<T>(parse: Parse<T>): RequiredVar<T>
export function optional<T>(parse: Parse<T>): OptionalVar<T>
export function withDefault<T>(parse: Parse<T>, value: T): DefaultedVar<T>

export type Output<V> = ...
export function readVar<T>(env: Env, key: string, spec: Var<T>): T | undefined
```

`Output` must satisfy all three of these:

- `Output<RequiredVar<number>>` is `number`
- `Output<DefaultedVar<number>>` is `number` — **not** `number | undefined`
- `Output<OptionalVar<number>>` is `number | undefined`

`readVar` returns the parsed value when the key is present, the default when it
is absent and the spec is defaulted, `undefined` when it is absent and
optional, and throws a `ConfigError` when it is absent and required.

- `readVar({ PORT: "8080" }, "PORT", required(asPort))` → `8080`
- `readVar({}, "PORT", withDefault(asPort, 3000))` → `3000`
- `readVar({}, "DSN", optional(asUrl))` → `undefined`
- `readVar({}, "DSN", required(asUrl))` throws `DSN is required`
- `withDefault(asPort, "3000")` is a **compile error** — the default is stored
  already parsed, so a typo in it fails the build rather than the boot

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb04_typed_config_env ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Output` is a chain of conditional types, and the literal `kind` on each
interface is what makes the branches unambiguous — without it, three shapes
that all carry a `parse` would overlap structurally and the first branch would
swallow the rest.

## Hint 2

```ts
export type Output<V> =
  V extends RequiredVar<infer T> ? T :
  V extends DefaultedVar<infer T> ? T :
  V extends OptionalVar<infer T> ? T | undefined :
  never;
```

Check each of the three cases in a scratch file before moving on. If
`Output<DefaultedVar<number>>` comes out as `number | undefined`, a branch is
in the wrong order or a `kind` is missing.

## Hint 3

`readVar` is a `switch` on `spec.kind` in the absent case and a single
`spec.parse(raw, key)` in the present case. The whole point of the three
variants is that this function has exactly one place where absence is
interpreted.

Left to you: whether `withDefault` should also validate its default by running
it through `parse`. It cannot — the default is already a `T`, not a string —
which is precisely the property that makes a bad default a compile error.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The type-level requirement is the interesting half, so test it first. Write

```ts
type A = Output<DefaultedVar<number>>;
const a: A = 3;          // must compile
const b: A = undefined;  // must NOT compile
```

and get those two lines right before implementing anything at runtime.

## Hint 2

Think about why storing the default already parsed matters. The alternative —
`withDefault(asPort, "3000")` with the string parsed at boot — means a typo in
a default is discovered in production by the one deployment that did not set
the variable. Types can only catch what you give them; here you give them the
default's type.

## Hint 3

`readVar`'s return type is `T | undefined` for all three kinds, which looks like
a defeat after all that work on `Output`. It is not: `readVar` is the low-level
primitive, and ex4's loader is where `Output` turns the union back into a
precise per-key type. Keeping the primitive simple is what makes the loader
short.

exercises.prompt:
## ex4 — the loader: one pass, every error, a derived type

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Bring the spec machinery across and add the function
the whole sector has been building towards:

```ts
export type ConfigOf<S> = { [K in keyof S]: Output<S[K]> };

export function loadConfig<S extends Record<string, Var<unknown>>>(
  env: Env,
  spec: S,
): ConfigOf<S>
```

With

```ts
const spec = {
  PORT: withDefault(asPort, 3000),
  DATABASE_URL: required(asUrl),
  LOG_LEVEL: withDefault(asEnum(["debug", "info", "warn"]), "info" as const),
  SENTRY_DSN: optional(asUrl),
};
```

- `loadConfig({ DATABASE_URL: "https://db" }, spec)` →
  `{ PORT: 3000, DATABASE_URL: URL, LOG_LEVEL: "info", SENTRY_DSN: undefined }`
- The static type is
  `{ PORT: number; DATABASE_URL: URL; LOG_LEVEL: "debug" | "info" | "warn"; SENTRY_DSN: URL | undefined }`
  — nobody writes that interface
- `loadConfig({}, spec)` throws a `ConfigError` whose `issues` are
  `["DATABASE_URL is required"]`
- `loadConfig({ PORT: "abc", LOG_LEVEL: "silly" }, spec)` throws with **three**
  issues, in spec order: the bad port, the bad level, and the missing database
  URL
- `loadConfig({}, {})` → `{}`

The accumulation is the requirement. An operator who fixes one variable and
redeploys only to find a second one broken has had an afternoon your loader
could have given back.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb04_typed_config_env ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One loop over `Object.keys(spec)`, one `issues` array, one `try`/`catch` per
key so that a throwing parser contributes an issue instead of aborting the
loop. At the end, throw once if there is anything to report.

## Hint 2

Indexing a generic record needs the same two moves as the schema sector:

```ts
for (const key of Object.keys(spec) as Array<keyof S & string>) {
  const variable: Var<unknown> = spec[key];
```

The annotation on `variable` is what lets `switch (variable.kind)` narrow — an
unresolved indexed access has no union for control flow to split.

## Hint 3

Catch `ConfigError` specifically and spread its `issues`; rethrow anything
else. A `TypeError` from a bug inside a parser is not a configuration problem,
and reporting it as one sends an operator hunting for a variable that is
perfectly fine.

Left to you: whether the loader should also report *unknown* keys in the
environment. It cannot sensibly — the environment is full of `PATH` and `HOME`
— but a loader over a config *file* absolutely should, for the same reason the
strict object policy exists.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The derived type is the deliverable, so check it before the runtime behaviour.
Hover `loadConfig(env, spec)` and confirm four things: `PORT` is `number` and
not `number | undefined`, `SENTRY_DSN` is `URL | undefined`, `LOG_LEVEL` is the
three-member union, and nothing is `unknown`. If `LOG_LEVEL` is `string`, the
`as const` on the default is missing.

## Hint 2

There is exactly one cast in the function, on the accumulator at the end.
`Record<string, unknown>` to `ConfigOf<S>` cannot be verified — the compiler
has no idea your loop visited every key — so it needs `as unknown as`. That is
the same single blind spot the object decoder had, in the same place, for the
same reason.

## Hint 3

Think about where this function is called: once, in the entry point, before
anything listens. Everything downstream receives the returned object as a
parameter. If you find yourself wanting to call `loadConfig` from inside a
module, that is a signal the config should have been threaded through instead —
and the fact that `env` is a parameter rather than a global is what makes that
possible.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## ex5 — layers, and a precedence you can defend

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Real configuration has more than one source. Express
the merge in types and in behaviour:

```ts
export type DeepPartial<T> =
  T extends readonly unknown[] ? T :
  T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> } :
  T;

export function mergeLayers<T extends object>(base: T, ...layers: readonly DeepPartial<T>[]): T
```

Precedence is left to right: later layers win. With

```ts
interface Settings {
  port: number;
  db: { host: string; pool: { min: number; max: number } };
  origins: string[];
  createdAt: Date;
}
const base: Settings = {
  port: 3000,
  db: { host: "localhost", pool: { min: 1, max: 10 } },
  origins: ["http://localhost"],
  createdAt: new Date(0),
};
```

- `mergeLayers(base, { port: 8080 })` → `port` is `8080`, everything else
  unchanged
- `mergeLayers(base, { db: { pool: { max: 50 } } })` → `db.host` is still
  `"localhost"` and `db.pool.min` is still `1` — nested objects merge
- `mergeLayers(base, { origins: ["https://app"] })` → `origins` is
  `["https://app"]` — arrays **replace**, they do not concatenate
- `mergeLayers(base, { port: undefined })` → `port` is still `3000` — an
  `undefined` in a layer means "no opinion", not "unset"
- `mergeLayers(base, { createdAt: new Date(1) })` → the whole `Date` is
  replaced; it is not merged property by property
- `mergeLayers(base, { port: 8080 }, { port: 9090 })` → `9090`
- The base is not mutated: `base.port` is still `3000` afterwards

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb04_typed_config_env ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three rules decide every case, and each one is in the prompt for a reason:
arrays replace, `undefined` is silence, and anything that is not a *plain*
object is replaced wholesale. Get those written down before you write the
recursion.

## Hint 2

"Plain object" is the load-bearing predicate, and `typeof x === "object"` is
not enough:

```ts
const proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(value);
return proto === Object.prototype || proto === null;
```

That is what keeps a `Date`, a `URL`, a `Map` or a class instance from being
walked property by property and rebuilt as a broken plain object.

## Hint 3

`DeepPartial` needs the array branch *first*. Without it, `string[]` matches the
object branch and you get `{ 0?: string; length?: number; ... }`, which is both
wrong and a memorable thing to see once.

Left to you: whether `null` in a layer should mean "unset this". It is a
reasonable convention and it needs the output type to admit `null`; the prompt
does not require it, and choosing deliberately is the exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Work out what each rule prevents. Concatenating arrays means an allowlist grows
every time a layer is added, and nobody can see the final value in any one
file. Treating `undefined` as "unset" means an optional command-line flag that
was not passed erases a good value from the file layer. Merging a `Date` means
`createdAt` becomes an object with no methods.

## Hint 2

The immutability requirement is not decoration either. A merge that mutates
`base` makes the function order-dependent in a way that bites when the same
defaults object is used twice — in a test suite, for example, where the second
test inherits the first test's overrides. Copy at every level.

## Hint 3

If the recursion type-checks but the runtime result loses nested keys, the
usual cause is spreading only the layer (`{ ...layer }`) instead of spreading
the base and then applying the layer's keys. The merge is base-first,
layer-second, per level.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## ex6 — freezing the result and keeping secrets out of logs

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Two independent protections for a value that lives as
long as the process.

```ts
export type DeepReadonly<T> =
  T extends (...args: never[]) => unknown ? T :
  T extends readonly (infer U)[] ? readonly DeepReadonly<U>[] :
  T extends object ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> } :
  T;

export function deepFreeze<T>(value: T): DeepReadonly<T>

export class Redacted<T> {
  constructor(value: T);
  reveal(): T;
  toString(): string;
  toJSON(): string;
}

export function toLogSafe(value: unknown): unknown
```

- `deepFreeze({ a: { b: 1 } })` freezes both levels:
  `Object.isFrozen(result.a)` is `true`
- `deepFreeze` returns the same object it was given, and survives a cycle
  without recursing forever
- The returned type is deeply readonly: `result.a.b = 2` is a compile error
- `new Redacted("hunter2").toString()` → `"[redacted]"`
- `JSON.stringify({ pw: new Redacted("hunter2") })` → `'{"pw":"[redacted]"}'`
- `` `${new Redacted("hunter2")}` `` → `"[redacted]"`
- `new Redacted("hunter2").reveal()` → `"hunter2"`
- `const s: string = new Redacted("hunter2")` is a **compile error**
- `toLogSafe({ user: "ada", pw: new Redacted("x"), nested: { token: new Redacted("y") } })`
  → `{ user: "ada", pw: "[redacted]", nested: { token: "[redacted]" } }`, with
  arrays and non-plain objects handled sensibly

Write a comment comparing this class with the branded `Redacted<T>` from the
parsing sector, and say what each one can and cannot stop.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb04_typed_config_env ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`deepFreeze` needs a `WeakSet` of visited objects, or a config with a cycle —
which is rarer than in general data but not impossible — takes the process
down. Freeze the node first, then recurse into its values.

## Hint 2

The class does its runtime work through two well-known hooks:

```ts
toString(): string { return "[redacted]"; }
toJSON(): string { return "[redacted]"; }
```

`JSON.stringify` calls `toJSON`; template literals and `String()` call
`toString`. Between them they cover most accidental leaks — which is more than
a type-level brand can do, because a brand is erased before any of that runs.

## Hint 3

A `#private` field is what makes the class *nominal*: two classes with the same
public shape are still not assignable to each other if either has a private
field, and `Redacted<string>` is not assignable to `string`. That is the
compile-time half.

Left to you: whether `toLogSafe` should recurse into arrays and class
instances. The prompt says "sensibly"; the defensible line is to walk plain
objects and arrays, replace `Redacted` values, and leave everything else alone.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Compare the two designs deliberately, because this is the second time this
volume has offered them. The brand from the parsing sector costs nothing at
runtime, needs no unwrapping, and disappears entirely once compiled — which
means a logger that takes `unknown` will serialise the secret happily. The
wrapper costs an allocation and an explicit `reveal()`, and it defends at
runtime too. Secrets are the case where the runtime half is worth paying for.

## Hint 2

Note what neither design stops. `secret.reveal()` is available to anyone who
types it, and that is the point — the goal is to make disclosure *visible and
greppable*, not impossible. A code review that can search for `.reveal()` and
find eleven call sites is in a much better position than one searching for
every place a string might be logged.

## Hint 3

`DeepReadonly` needs its branches in the right order: functions first (or they
match the object branch and lose their call signatures), then arrays, then
objects, then everything else. Test it against a config type containing a
function, an array of objects, and a `Date` before you trust it.

## ex7 — requirements that depend on the environment

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. "Production needs a TLS certificate" is a rule that
usually lives in a wiki. Put it in the type:

```ts
export type AppConfig =
  | { readonly env: "development"; readonly port: number; readonly hotReload: boolean }
  | { readonly env: "staging"; readonly port: number; readonly baseUrl: URL }
  | { readonly env: "production"; readonly port: number; readonly baseUrl: URL;
      readonly tlsCertPath: string; readonly tlsKeyPath: string };

export function loadAppConfig(env: Env): AppConfig
export function isProduction(config: AppConfig): config is Extract<AppConfig, { env: "production" }>
export function describeConfig(config: AppConfig): string
```

`loadAppConfig` reads `APP_ENV` (one of the three, required) and then the keys
that variant needs:

- development: `PORT` (default 3000), `HOT_RELOAD` (default `true`)
- staging: `PORT` (default 3000), `BASE_URL` (required)
- production: `PORT` (default 443), `BASE_URL`, `TLS_CERT_PATH`,
  `TLS_KEY_PATH` (all required)

Behaviour:

- `loadAppConfig({ APP_ENV: "development" })` →
  `{ env: "development", port: 3000, hotReload: true }`
- `loadAppConfig({ APP_ENV: "production", BASE_URL: "https://x" })` throws a
  `ConfigError` listing **both** missing TLS keys
- `loadAppConfig({ APP_ENV: "test" })` throws naming the three accepted values
- `config.tlsCertPath` is a **compile error** unless the code has narrowed to
  the production variant first
- `describeConfig` is a `switch` on `env` with an `assertNever` default; adding
  a fourth environment must break it

`describeConfig` returns, respectively, `"dev on 3000 (hot reload on)"`,
`"staging on 3000 at https://x/"` and `"production on 443 at https://x/ with tls"`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The union is doing the work that a pile of optional fields would do badly.
Compare with `{ env: string; tlsCertPath?: string }`: that shape permits a
production config with no certificate and a development config with one, and
every consumer has to defend against both.

## Hint 2

`loadAppConfig` reads the discriminant first, then branches, and each branch
builds a different object. Inside the production branch, collect the missing
keys into one list before throwing so the operator sees both at once — the same
accumulate-then-fail shape as ex4.

## Hint 3

`isProduction` uses `Extract` to name the variant rather than repeating its
fields:

```ts
Extract<AppConfig, { env: "production" }>
```

Repeating the shape would compile and would drift the first time a field is
added.

Left to you: whether `staging` and `production` should share a base interface
that both extend. It removes repetition and makes the union slightly harder to
read; both styles appear in real codebases and the argument is worth having
once.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what this buys at the call site. Code that sets up HTTPS has to
prove it is in production before it can read the certificate path, so a
refactor that moves that code into a shared path fails to compile rather than
throwing `undefined is not a string` on a Tuesday deploy.

## Hint 2

The default port differing per environment (3000 in dev, 443 in production) is
a small illustration of a bigger rule: defaults belong in code when they are
environment-independent and safe. A port is borderline — some teams require it
everywhere precisely because a wrong default binds the wrong socket.

## Hint 3

If `describeConfig`'s `assertNever` complains before you have added a fourth
environment, the union has been widened somewhere. The usual culprit is
building the object without a literal `env` — `{ env: appEnv, ... }` where
`appEnv` is typed `string` collapses the discriminant. Parse `APP_ENV` into the
literal union first, then branch on it.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 — a spec is data, so compute over it

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Once configuration is a value rather than a scatter of
reads, you can generate documentation and diagnostics from it.

```ts
export interface Documented { readonly doc: string; readonly example: string }
export type DocVar<T> = Var<T> & Documented;

export type Source = "environment" | "default" | "absent" | "invalid";

export function describeSpec<S extends Record<string, DocVar<unknown>>>(spec: S): string
export function explain<S extends Record<string, Var<unknown>>>(
  env: Env,
  spec: S,
): Readonly<Record<keyof S & string, Source>>
```

`describeSpec` produces a `.env.example` file, one block per key, in spec
order, blocks separated by a blank line:

```
# PORT - the port to listen on
# optional, default 3000
PORT=8080

# DATABASE_URL - postgres connection string
# required
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/app
```

- A `required` variable's second line is `# required`
- An `optional` variable's second line is `# optional`
- A `default` variable's second line is `# optional, default <JSON of value>`
- The third line is always `KEY=<example>`

`explain` says where each value came from, without throwing:

- present and parseable → `"environment"`
- absent with a default → `"default"`
- absent and optional → `"absent"`
- absent and required, or present and unparseable → `"invalid"`

`explain({ PORT: "abc", DATABASE_URL: "postgres://x" }, spec)` →
`{ PORT: "invalid", DATABASE_URL: "environment", LOG_LEVEL: "default" }`.

`explain` never throws, because it is what you call when the loader already did.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb04_typed_config_env ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both functions are one loop over `Object.keys(spec)`. The difference is that
`describeSpec` produces text and `explain` produces a record — and neither one
needs a cast until the final return, where `explain`'s key type comes from `S`.

## Hint 2

The requirement line is a `switch` on `variable.kind`:

```ts
case "default": return `# optional, default ${JSON.stringify(variable.value)}`;
```

`JSON.stringify` rather than interpolation, so a default of `""` or `"3000"`
prints as something an operator can distinguish from `3000`.

## Hint 3

`explain` must swallow parse failures rather than propagate them — it reports
`"invalid"` and continues, because its job is to describe the whole environment
even when parts of it are broken. That is the opposite contract from the
loader, on purpose.

Left to you: whether `describeSpec` should print secrets' examples. It should
not print a real one; a placeholder like `changeme` is the convention, and
deciding how the spec expresses that is a small design exercise of its own.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice what these two functions prove about the design. Nothing about
generating a `.env.example` or diagnosing an environment was anticipated when
the spec type was written — they are possible because the spec is an ordinary
object rather than a hundred scattered `process.env` reads. That is the real
argument for the whole apparatus, and it is worth being able to make it.

## Hint 2

`explain` is the function operators will actually run. Think about what it is
like to read at 2am: a table saying `DATABASE_URL: environment`, `PORT:
default`, `SENTRY_DSN: absent` answers "is my variable being picked up" in one
line, which is otherwise a twenty-minute conversation.

## Hint 3

The return type `Readonly<Record<keyof S & string, Source>>` keeps the keys
precise, so `report.DATABASE_URL` is checked and `report.DATABAES_URL` is a
compile error. Widening it to `Record<string, Source>` would compile and would
throw that away — a small illustration of the first sector's rule that a type
parameter should express a relationship.

## Challenge — boot a service: layers, secrets, and a frozen result (hard)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Everything in the sector, in the order a real
process does it.

```ts
export interface DbConfig {
  readonly host: string;
  readonly port: number;
  readonly password: Redacted<string>;
}

export type ServiceConfig =
  | { readonly kind: "development"; readonly port: number; readonly db: DbConfig; readonly logLevel: LogLevel }
  | { readonly kind: "production"; readonly port: number; readonly db: DbConfig; readonly logLevel: LogLevel;
      readonly tls: { readonly certPath: string; readonly keyPath: string } };

export type LogLevel = "debug" | "info" | "warn" | "error";

export function mergeEnv(...layers: readonly Env[]): Env
export function bootstrap(env: Env, fileLayer?: Env): ServiceConfig
export function describeBoot(config: ServiceConfig): unknown
```

`mergeEnv` combines string layers left to right, later wins, and an empty or
whitespace-only value never overrides a real one:

- `mergeEnv({ PORT: "1" }, { PORT: "2" })` → `{ PORT: "2" }`
- `mergeEnv({ PORT: "1" }, { PORT: "" })` → `{ PORT: "1" }`
- `mergeEnv({ PORT: "1" }, { HOST: "h" })` → `{ PORT: "1", HOST: "h" }`

`bootstrap(env, fileLayer)` merges `fileLayer` **under** `env` — the process
environment wins over the file — and then validates:

- `APP_ENV` required, `"development"` or `"production"`
- `PORT` defaults to `3000` in development and `443` in production
- `DB_HOST` required; `DB_PORT` defaults to `5432`; `DB_PASSWORD` required and
  wrapped in `Redacted`
- `LOG_LEVEL` defaults to `"debug"` in development and `"info"` in production
- production additionally requires `TLS_CERT_PATH` and `TLS_KEY_PATH`
- every problem is reported in one `ConfigError`, in the order listed above
- the returned object is deeply frozen: `Object.isFrozen(config.db)` is `true`

`describeBoot` returns the config with secrets replaced, suitable for logging
at startup: `describeBoot(config).db.password` is `"[redacted]"`, and
`JSON.stringify(describeBoot(config))` contains no password.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb04_typed_config_env challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do the merge at the *string* layer, before any parsing. That is what real
systems do — a file, then the environment, then flags, all as flat string maps
— and it means the whole validation stage sees one `Env` and does not need to
know how many sources there were.

## Hint 2

Accumulate first, branch last:

```ts
const issues: string[] = [];
const host = requiredString(merged, "DB_HOST", issues);
// ... every other key ...
if (issues.length > 0) throw new ConfigError(issues);
```

Each helper pushes an issue and returns `undefined` rather than throwing, so
one pass collects everything. The narrowing then happens once, after the throw.

## Hint 3

The per-environment defaults mean you have to know `APP_ENV` before reading
`PORT` and `LOG_LEVEL`. Read and validate the discriminant first, throwing
immediately if it is wrong — there is no useful way to continue collecting
issues when you do not know which variant you are building.

Left to you: whether `bootstrap` should freeze before or after building the
union member. Freezing last is simpler; freezing the `db` object as you build
it is closer to what a layered system does. Both pass.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The ordering of the whole function is the lesson: merge, then validate, then
construct, then freeze. Each stage has one job and none of them reaches back to
an earlier one. Config code that interleaves these — parsing a value, using it
to decide whether to read another, mutating the result later — is the kind that
nobody can safely change two years on.

## Hint 2

Notice why `DB_PASSWORD` is wrapped at construction rather than at use. If the
raw string escapes into the config object even briefly, every consumer sees a
plain `string` and the compile-time protection is gone. Wrapping at the
boundary — the same principle as parsing at the boundary — is what makes the
type meaningful downstream.

## Hint 3

For `describeBoot`, resist writing a bespoke redactor per config shape. A
generic walker that replaces `Redacted` instances works for any future field,
including one added by someone who never reads this file. That is the
difference between a rule and a mechanism, which is the theme of this volume.

exercises.prompt:
## Review — the values that are not scalars

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Configuration is not only ports and booleans. Three
shapes that appear in every real service, each with its own trap:

```ts
export interface Dsn {
  readonly protocol: "postgres" | "postgresql";
  readonly user: string;
  readonly password: Redacted<string>;
  readonly host: string;
  readonly port: number;
  readonly database: string;
  readonly params: Readonly<Record<string, string>>;
}

export function parseDsn(raw: string, key: string): Dsn
export function asList(raw: string, key: string): readonly string[]
export function asFlagSet<const V extends readonly string[]>(
  known: V,
): (raw: string, key: string) => Readonly<Record<V[number], boolean>>
```

- `parseDsn("postgres://ada:pw@db.internal:5432/app?sslmode=require", "DB")` →
  a `Dsn` with `port` `5432`, `params` `{ sslmode: "require" }` and a password
  that prints as `"[redacted]"`
- `parseDsn("postgres://ada:pw@db.internal/app", "DB")` → `port` defaults to
  `5432`
- `parseDsn("mysql://x/y", "DB")` throws naming the accepted protocols
- `parseDsn("postgres://db/app", "DB")` throws — credentials are required
- `asList("a, b ,, c", "ORIGINS")` → `["a", "b", "c"]` — split, trim, drop
  empties
- `asList("", "ORIGINS")` → `[]`
- `asFlagSet(["beta", "newNav"])("beta", "FLAGS")` →
  `{ beta: true, newNav: false }`, typed
  `Readonly<Record<"beta" | "newNav", boolean>>`
- `asFlagSet(["beta"])("beta,ghost", "FLAGS")` throws naming `ghost` — an
  unknown flag is a typo, and a typo that silently does nothing is the worst
  possible outcome for a feature flag

Use `URL` to parse the DSN rather than a regular expression, and write a
comment about the one thing `URL` does to the password that you must undo.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tb04_typed_config_env review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`new URL("postgres://ada:pw@host:5432/app?sslmode=require")` parses non-HTTP
schemes perfectly well, giving you `username`, `password`, `hostname`, `port`,
`pathname` and `searchParams`. Reaching for a regular expression here is the
classic mistake — DSNs have escaping rules, and the URL parser already
implements them.

## Hint 2

The thing to undo: `URL` percent-encodes `username` and `password`, so a
password containing `@` or `:` comes back as `%40` or `%3A`.
`decodeURIComponent` on both is required, and forgetting it produces a
connection failure that looks like a wrong password.

## Hint 3

`url.port` is an empty string when the URL has no port, not `undefined`, and
`url.pathname` is `"/app"` with a leading slash. Both need handling. For
`params`, `url.searchParams.forEach((value, name) => { ... })` is the portable
route — `Object.fromEntries(url.searchParams)` reads better and needs the
`DOM.Iterable` lib, which not every project enables.

Left to you: whether an unknown query parameter should be an error. For a DSN
it should probably pass through — drivers accept many — which is the opposite of
the flag-set decision two lines below, and the difference is worth being able to
explain.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The flag-set rule is the interesting design decision in this exercise. An
unknown flag could reasonably be ignored, and every system that ignores them
eventually ships a release where `FLAGS=newnav` (wrong case) did nothing for
three weeks. Failing at boot converts a silent behavioural bug into a loud
deployment failure, which is the trade this whole sector keeps making.

## Hint 2

`asFlagSet` needs a `const` type parameter so the returned record's keys are
the literal flag names. Without it, `known` widens to `string[]`, `V[number]`
becomes `string`, and the result is `Record<string, boolean>` — which compiles,
and lets `flags.nwNav` through as a typo the compiler could have caught.

## Hint 3

Note that `asList("")` returns `[]` rather than `[""]`. That is not obvious —
`"".split(",")` is `[""]` — and it is why the trim-and-filter step exists. An
empty list and a list containing one empty string behave very differently when
the value is an allowlist of origins.

lessons.summary: A fluent API is a small language, and its type parameters are its grammar. Done well, a builder makes illegal call sequences unsayable and needs no type arguments; done badly it produces error messages nobody can read. This sector builds type-state builders, and argues about when a plain options object wins.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·TB5 — Builders and fluent APIs with generics

Every query builder, HTTP client, form library and router you have used is the
same idea: a chain of method calls that accumulates state, ending in a
`build()`, `execute()` or `send()`. The interesting question is not how to
write the chain — that is a closure and a return statement — but how much of
the *grammar* the type system enforces.

Consider three levels of ambition:

```ts
query().where("id = 1").build();          // 1. runs, fails at runtime: no table
query().where("id = 1").build();          // 2. throws a clear error at runtime
query().where("id = 1").build();          // 3. does not compile
```

The third is what this sector is about. It is called **type state**: the
builder's type carries what has been supplied so far, and methods are available
— or not — depending on it. Rust's builders do this with separate types per
stage; TypeScript does it with a type parameter that changes on every call.

## Concept — the accumulating type parameter

The simplest useful builder threads a growing object type:

```ts
interface Builder<T extends object> {
  with<K extends string, V>(key: K, value: V): Builder<T & { [P in K]: V }>;
  build(): T;
}
```

Each call intersects one more property into `T`, so after
`.with("host", "db").with("port", 5432)` the type is
`Builder<{ host: string } & { port: number }>` and `build()` returns exactly
that. Nothing was annotated; the shape was inferred from the values.

Two details make or break it. The key must be captured as its own type
parameter (`K extends string`), or it widens to `string` and you get an index
signature instead of a property. And the accumulation must be an *intersection*
rather than a reassignment, because a mapped type over a growing union is far
more expensive for the checker.

## Concept — type state as "what is still missing"

To make `build()` unavailable until the required parts are supplied, track the
missing keys and require them to be gone:

```ts
type Required = "url" | "method";

interface RequestBuilder<Missing extends Required> {
  readonly __missing?: Missing;        // phantom: no runtime existence
  url(value: string): RequestBuilder<Exclude<Missing, "url">>;
  method(value: Method): RequestBuilder<Exclude<Missing, "method">>;
  build(this: RequestBuilder<never>): RequestSpec;
}
```

The `this` parameter is the gate: `build` is only callable when the receiver's
type is assignable to `RequestBuilder<never>`.

The phantom property is what makes that gate actually close, and it is the
detail almost every first attempt omits. Without it, the only places `Missing`
appears are the *return types of methods that mention the builder again*, so
checking assignability recurses — and TypeScript's recursion guard assumes
success for a comparison it is already in the middle of. The result is a
builder whose type state compiles beautifully and enforces nothing. Adding one
property that mentions `Missing` directly gives the checker something it can
compare without recursing, and `"method"` is not assignable to `never`.

Writing it as "what is missing" rather than "what is provided" is the second
half. The provided-keys version compares in the wrong direction:
`Builder<"url">` genuinely *is* assignable to `Builder<"url" | "method">`, so
`build()` would be allowed after one call out of two. Get either of these
wrong and the API is decorative — which is why negative tests, guarded with
`@ts-expect-error`, are mandatory here rather than nice to have.

## Concept — the three modifiers, again, in a chain

The generics sector's tools all reappear here, and they matter more, because a
builder has many call sites per usage rather than one.

**`const` type parameters** keep literals: `.token("primary", "#0af")` should
produce `{ primary: "#0af" }`, not `{ primary: string }`.

**`NoInfer`** stops a later method poisoning an earlier decision:
`.oneOf(["red", "green"]).fallback("purple")` must be an error, and it is only
an error if `fallback`'s parameter is excluded from inference.

**Polymorphic `this`** keeps a chain working through subclasses. A base method
declared to return `Query` truncates the chain the moment somebody extends it;
declared to return `this`, it does not.

And one tool that is specific to fluent APIs: **`Omit<..., "method">`** as a
return type removes a method from what the chain offers next, which is how you
say "you may call `select` once".

## The trap

The trap is that all of this is invisible until it fails, and when it fails the
error message is enormous. A rejected `build()` on a deeply generic builder
produces a wall of intersections, and the reader has no idea which of eight
chained calls was wrong. Two mitigations are worth building in from the start:
keep the type parameter small — a union of key names, not the whole
accumulated object — and, when you can, make the failure a *missing method*
rather than a mismatched argument, because "Property 'build' does not exist"
is far more readable than a page of type diffs.

The larger trap is ambition. A builder with four type parameters and six
type-state transitions is a genuine achievement and a liability: it is slow to
check, hard to modify, and impossible for a colleague to extend. The exercises
build the machinery; the reading argues for the plain options object more often
than you might expect.

# Reading - typescript/v3tb05_builders_fluent_apis

Notes on `this` types, on variance in builders, on inference through a chain,
and on the readability cost.

## Notes

**Polymorphic `this` is a type, not a value.** Declaring `select(): this` means
"returns whatever the receiver's type is", so a subclass's methods stay
available through a base method. Two limits: `this` types make a class
invariant in ways that occasionally surprise, and a method returning `this`
cannot return a *different* instance — so `this`-typing and immutability do not
combine. An immutable builder must return a named type.

**Mutable chains and immutable chains are different animals.** The mutable
version pushes into an array and returns `this`; it is cheap, and a builder
that is reused twice produces two overlapping queries. The immutable version
constructs a new object per call; it is safe to branch (`const base =
query().from("t"); base.where("a"); base.where("b")`) and allocates more. For a
builder used a handful of times per request, take immutability.

**Type state needs a phantom, not only good variance.** Modelling *missing*
keys is necessary — the provided-keys version is assignable in the wrong
direction — but it is not sufficient. If the type parameter appears only inside
the return types of the builder's own methods, comparing `Builder<"url">` with
`Builder<never>` recurses immediately, and the recursion guard resolves an
in-progress comparison as successful. The check silently passes. One phantom
member that mentions the parameter directly — `readonly __missing?: Missing` —
gives the checker a non-recursive comparison to fail on. Optional, so no
implementation has to produce it; present in the type, so assignability sees
it.

**`Omit` as a return type is the "call it once" pattern.** `select(cols):
Omit<Query, "select">` removes the method from the returned type. It reads
badly in tooltips — the reader sees a structural type rather than a name — and
it is best applied through a small alias so the name survives.

**Inference degrades when a generic escapes into a callback.** A builder method
taking a callback that receives the accumulated type works beautifully when the
callback is written inline and stops working when it is extracted to a `const`.
That is the contextual typing rule from the first sector, and in a fluent API
it is the most common "it broke when I refactored" report.

**Overloads beat conditional return types in a chain.** In a tooltip, a
conditional return type is displayed unevaluated, so a user hovering
`.expect("one")` sees `M extends "one" ? Row | undefined : Row[]` rather than
an answer. Two overloads show `Row | undefined`. The cost is that overloads do
not compose with further generics, which is why libraries end up with both.

## ex1 — polymorphic `this`

The exercise is small and the failure is instructive: change `select(): this`
to `select(): Query` and the subclass chain stops compiling at the first base
method. It is the cheapest possible demonstration that a return type is a
promise about *identity*, not only about shape.

## ex2 — an accumulating immutable builder

`with<K extends string, V>(key: K, value: V): Builder<T & { [P in K]: V }>`
contains the whole idea. Watch what happens if you drop `K`: the parameter
widens to `string`, the mapped type becomes an index signature, and `build()`
returns something with no known keys at all.

## ex3 — type state by missing keys

The `this` parameter, a "missing" union, and a phantom property. The gate
checks the negative case, which is the only case that matters:
`request().url("/x").build()` must not compile. If it does, either the
parameter is modelling provided keys instead of missing ones, or the phantom is
absent and the assignability check is recursing into itself and giving up in
your favour. Both failures look identical from the outside, which is why the
exercise requires `@ts-expect-error` lines in the file.

## ex4 — `const` in a builder

Design tokens, route tables and permission maps all want the literal. A builder
is the best possible place for a `const` type parameter, because the
alternative is asking every caller to write `as const` at every step.

## ex5 — `NoInfer` in a chain

`.oneOf([...]).fallback(x)` is the colour-picker problem from the first sector,
made worse by distance: the two calls can be many lines apart, so the widening
is even harder to spot by reading. The fix is one word in a signature.

## ex6 — call it once

`Omit` on the return type. The exercise's interesting constraint is that the
type must be recursive without being circular, which is why the methods live on
a helper interface and the exported alias applies the `Omit`. Aliases that
reference themselves through a mapped type are rejected; aliases that reference
themselves through an interface are fine.

## ex7 — overloads versus conditionals

Implement the same API twice and compare. Both work; the difference is what a
user sees on hover and what the error says when they get it wrong. This is the
exercise to remember when someone proposes a clever conditional return type in
review.

## ex8, challenge and review1

ex8 assembles a query builder where `from` must precede `where`, `select` may
be called once, and `build` requires both. The challenge adds inference: a
request builder that carries a decoder so `send()` returns a typed body without
a type argument. The review approaches the same ideas as a form definition,
where the built value's type is a record derived from the fields declared along
the way.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: polymorphic `this` types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/classes.html#this-types) — including the fluent-interface motivation.
- [TypeScript 5.0: `const` type parameters](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-5-0.html#const-type-parameters).
- [TypeScript 5.4: `NoInfer`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-5-4.html#the-noinfer-utility-type).
- [Kysely](https://kysely.dev/) — a production type-safe SQL builder; read its `SelectQueryBuilder` for type state at full scale.
- [Handbook: variance annotations](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-7.html#optional-variance-annotations-for-type-parameters) — why `in` and `out` exist and when to write them.

# V3·TB5 — Builders and fluent APIs (archive)

The deep version: the patterns, the variance argument, error-message
engineering, performance, and a self-test bank.

## 1. Four builder shapes

**Mutable, `this`-returning.** The classic. Cheap, subclass-friendly with
polymorphic `this`, and unsafe to branch.

```ts
class Query {
  private readonly parts: string[] = [];
  select(cols: string): this { this.parts.push(`SELECT ${cols}`); return this; }
}
```

**Immutable, named return.** Each call returns a new object. Safe to branch and
to share; allocates per call.

```ts
interface Query { select(cols: string): Query }
```

**Accumulating generic.** The return type's type argument grows.

```ts
interface Builder<T extends object> {
  with<K extends string, V>(k: K, v: V): Builder<T & { [P in K]: V }>;
  build(): T;
}
```

**Type state.** The type argument tracks *which stage* you are in, and methods
appear or disappear.

```ts
interface Q<Missing extends "from" | "select"> {
  from(t: string): Q<Exclude<Missing, "from">>;
  build(this: Q<never>): string;
}
```

Most real libraries use the last two together.

## 2. The variance argument, in full

Type state is a variance trick, so it is worth being precise.

A type parameter that appears only in **return** positions is covariant:
`Box<Cat>` is assignable to `Box<Animal>`. One that appears only in
**parameter** positions is contravariant: `Sink<Animal>` is assignable to
`Sink<Cat>`. One that appears in both is invariant.

In `Q<Missing>` above, `Missing` appears inside `Exclude<Missing, "from">` in
return positions, so the direction we want is:

```ts
Q<"select">  →  Q<never>   ?   "select" assignable to never ?   No.
Q<never>     →  Q<never>   ?   yes
```

which is precisely the gate we want on `build(this: Q<never>)`.

There is a catch, and it is the single most common reason a hand-written
type-state builder does nothing. If `Missing` occurs *only* inside return types
that mention `Q` again, then checking `Q<"select">` against `Q<never>` requires
checking their `from` methods, which requires checking `Q<"select">` against
`Q<never>` again. TypeScript detects the cycle and resolves the in-progress
comparison as *true*, so the whole check passes and `build()` is allowed in
every state. The fix is one member that mentions the parameter without
recursing:

```ts
interface Q<Missing extends "from" | "select"> {
  readonly __missing?: Missing;      // never assigned at runtime
  from(t: string): Q<Exclude<Missing, "from">>;
  build(this: Q<never>): string;
}
```

Now the comparison hits `__missing?: "select"` against `__missing?: never`
immediately, fails, and the API works. Make it optional and no implementation
needs to produce it.

Now write it the other way, tracking what has been *provided*:

```ts
interface Q2<Provided extends "from" | "select"> {
  from(t: string): Q2<Provided | "from">;
  build(this: Q2<"from" | "select">): string;
}
Q2<"from">  →  Q2<"from" | "select">  ?  "from" assignable to that union ?  Yes.
```

`build()` is allowed after one call out of two. The API compiles, looks
correct, and enforces nothing. If you must model provided keys — sometimes the
rest of the design wants it — force invariance with a phantom member that uses
the parameter in a contravariant position, or add an explicit `in out`
variance annotation.

## 3. Keeping errors readable

A generic builder's error messages are its user interface. Techniques, in order
of value:

- **Prefer a missing method to a mismatched argument.** "Property 'build' does
  not exist on type ..." beats a two-page intersection diff.
- **Keep the type parameter small.** Track a union of key names, not the whole
  accumulated object, wherever the accumulated object is not needed.
- **Name your types.** `Q<"select">` displays better than an anonymous
  structural type; aliases survive in errors more often than inline shapes.
- **Add a branded "you forgot X" type.** Instead of `never`, return
  `{ readonly __error: "call .from() before .where()" }`. The message then
  appears inside the error text.
- **Do not nest conditionals deeply.** Every level shows up unevaluated in
  tooltips.

## 4. Inference through the chain

Two rules cover most surprises.

**Inference happens per call, left to right.** Each method call is its own
inference problem; nothing is inferred "across" the chain. That is why the
accumulation must be encoded in the type parameter — the chain has no other
memory.

**Contextual typing only reaches inline callbacks.** This works:

```ts
builder.where((row) => row.id > 1);          // row is typed
```

and this does not:

```ts
const predicate = (row) => row.id > 1;        // implicit any
builder.where(predicate);
```

The fix at the call site is an annotation; the fix in the API is to accept a
value rather than a callback where possible.

## 5. Performance

Builders are where TypeScript projects most often become slow to check, and the
costs are concrete:

- **Intersections accumulate.** After twenty `.with()` calls the type is a
  twenty-way intersection, and every property access resolves it. Prefer
  flattening with a `Prettify`-style mapped type at the `build()` boundary,
  not on every step.
- **Conditional types re-evaluate per call site.** A conditional return type in
  a method used in five hundred places is five hundred evaluations.
- **Deep recursion hits limits.** Tuple-recursive builders (accumulating a
  tuple of stages) hit the 50-deep instantiation limit faster than people
  expect.
- **`Omit` is a mapped type.** Using it as a return type on every method
  rebuilds the interface at every step.

`tsc --generateTrace` will name the file and the type. The usual remedy is to
reduce what the type parameter carries.

## 6. When a plain options object wins

An options object is better whenever the answer to all of these is yes: the
arguments are independent, there are fewer than about eight, none of them
changes the *type* of the result, and nobody needs to build the value in
pieces. That describes most APIs.

```ts
createServer({ port: 8080, host: "0.0.0.0", tls: { cert, key } });
```

That call is easier to read, easier to type, faster to check, trivially
serialisable, and testable as data. A builder earns its complexity when one of
these is true: the value is assembled across several places; the valid orderings
are a real grammar; or a later call's types depend on an earlier call's values.
A query builder qualifies on all three. A server constructor qualifies on none.

## 7. Interview answers

**"What is a type-state builder?"** One whose type parameter tracks progress
through a protocol, so that methods are available only in valid states and
`build()` is a compile error until the required parts are supplied.

**"Why track missing keys rather than provided ones?"** Variance. With the
parameter in return positions it is covariant, so a partially-built builder is
not assignable to the fully-built one — which is the rejection you need. The
provided-keys version is assignable in the wrong direction and enforces
nothing.

**"What does `this` as a return type do?"** It returns the receiver's own type,
so chains keep working through subclasses. It cannot be used by an immutable
builder, which returns a new object.

**"When would you not build a fluent API?"** When the arguments are independent
and do not affect the result type — an options object is clearer, faster to
check and easier to test.

**"Why do type-heavy builders make editors slow?"** Accumulated intersections
and conditional return types are re-resolved at every call site and every
hover.

## 8. Common mistakes

- Modelling provided keys instead of missing keys, so type state enforces
  nothing.
- Returning the base class instead of `this`, truncating subclass chains.
- Forgetting `K extends string`, so keys widen and the built object gains an
  index signature.
- Mutating shared state in a builder that callers expect to be branchable.
- A conditional return type where two overloads would read better.
- Deep intersections carried all the way through, instead of flattened at
  `build()`.
- An alias that applies `Omit` to itself, producing a circular type error —
  put the methods on an interface first.
- Forgetting `NoInfer` on the argument that should conform rather than define.
- Building the whole apparatus for four independent options.

## 9. Check yourself

1. Why does a `this` return type keep a subclass chain working?
2. Why can an immutable builder not use `this` as a return type?
3. Give the signature of an accumulating `with` and say what each type parameter does.
4. Explain, using variance, why type state tracks missing rather than provided keys.
5. What does `build(this: Q<never>)` mean, and when is it callable?
6. How do you make a method callable only once?
7. Why does an alias applying `Omit` to itself fail, and what fixes it?
8. Where does `NoInfer` belong in a fluent API, and what does it prevent?
9. Why does an extracted callback lose its parameter types?
10. Name two ways to make a builder's error messages readable.
11. Give two reasons a builder can slow an editor down.
12. State the conditions under which an options object is the better API.
